paragraphs.title: Acne Vulgaris
paragraphs.name: [1] Acne Vulgaris — Definition / Overview
paragraphs.text:
Acne Vulgaris — Definition / Overview
- Chronic inflammatory disorder of the pilosebaceous unit with a prolonged course, commonly presenting with comedones, papules, pustules, and nodules. Typically affects the face, upper arms, trunk, and back. Can occur at any age but most common in adolescents.

paragraphs.title: Acne Vulgaris
paragraphs.name: [2] Acne Vulgaris — Epidemiology
paragraphs.text:
Acne Vulgaris — Epidemiology
- Prevalence: 35%–90% in adolescents.  
- Onset: Begins as early as 7–12 years (preadolescent acne), usually resolves by the third decade.  
- Gender: More common in males during adolescence; postadolescent acne predominantly affects females.  
- Geographic: Higher prevalence in urban vs. rural populations.  
- Ethnicity: Asians and Africans more likely to develop severe acne; mild acne more common in White populations.  
- Neonates: Acne can occur but typically resolves spontaneously.  
- Infants/children: Rare; may indicate underlying conditions.

paragraphs.title: Acne Vulgaris
paragraphs.name: [3] Acne Vulgaris — Etiology / Causes
paragraphs.text:
Acne Vulgaris — Etiology / Causes
- Primary factors: Hypersensitivity of sebaceous glands to androgens, *Cutibacterium acnes* (C acnes), inflammation.  
- Contributory factors:  
  - Medications (lithium, steroids, anticonvulsants).  
  - Occlusive wear (e.g., backpacks, headbands).  
  - Oil-based cosmetics, facial massage.  
  - Endocrine disorders (polycystic ovarian syndrome, pregnancy).  
  - Genetic factors (50–90% heritability).  
  - Diet (high milk consumption, high glycemic load).  
  - Psychological stress.  
  - Insulin resistance.  
- Chocolate does not exacerbate acne.

paragraphs.title: Acne Vulgaris
paragraphs.name: [4] Acne Vulgaris — Pathophysiology
paragraphs.text:
Acne Vulgaris — Pathophysiology
- **Four key events**:  
  1. Increased sebum production (seborrhea).  
  2. Follicular hyperkeratinization.  
  3. *C. acnes* colonization.  
  4. Inflammation.  
- **Role of androgens**: Stimulate sebaceous gland growth and sebum production. Most patients have normal androgen levels, but hyperandrogenism (e.g., PCOS) exacerbates acne.  
- **Role of *C. acnes***: Strains (e.g., phylotype IA) trigger innate/adaptive immune responses (TH17 cells, IL-17, cytokines). Biofilm formation linked to antibiotic resistance.  
- **Genetics**: Family history increases risk 3-fold. Upregulation of inflammatory genes (MMP-1, IL-8, beta-defensins).

paragraphs.title: Acne Vulgaris
paragraphs.name: [5] Acne Vulgaris — Clinical Presentation
paragraphs.text:
Acne Vulgaris — Clinical Presentation
- **Lesions**:  
  - Grade 1: Comedones (open/blackheads, closed/whiteheads).  
  - Grade 2: Inflammatory papules.  
  - Grade 3: Pustules.  
  - Grade 4: Nodules/cysts (nodulocystic acne).  
- **Distribution**: Face (T-zone in adolescents), neck, chest, upper back, arms. Adult women often on lower face/neck, linked to menstrual cycles.  
- **Variants**:  
  - Acne conglobata (severe nodules, interconnecting abscesses).  
  - Acne fulminans (ulcerating nodules, systemic symptoms).  
  - Acne excoriée (picked/scarring).  
  - Infantile acne (3–6 months, improves by age 1–2).  
- **Associated features**: Seborrhea, hyperandrogenism (hirsutism, irregular menses), postinflammatory hyperpigmentation (more common in darker skin).

paragraphs.title: Acne Vulgaris
paragraphs.name: [6] Acne Vulgaris — Evaluation / Diagnosis
paragraphs.text:
Acne Vulgaris — Evaluation / Diagnosis
- **Clinical diagnosis**: Based on physical exam (lesion type, distribution).  
- **Laboratory tests**:  
  - For suspected hyperandrogenism (females): Testosterone, LH, FSH, DHEA.  
  - Acne fulminans: CBC, LFTs, ESR, CRP, cholesterol/triglycerides, pregnancy test, imaging for bone/joint involvement.  
- **Skin biopsy**: Not routinely required.

paragraphs.title: Acne Vulgaris
paragraphs.name: [7] Acne Vulgaris — Differential Diagnosis
paragraphs.text:
Acne Vulgaris — Differential Diagnosis
- Rosacea (telangiectasia, no comedones).  
- Perioral dermatitis (perioral papules, lip sparing).  
- Demodex folliculitis (non-responsive to acne treatment).  
- Facial angiofibroma (tuberous sclerosis, pink/red papules).  
- Pseudofolliculitis barbae (beard area, curved hair).  
- Nevus comedonicus (grouped comedones, present at birth/childhood).  
- Sebaceous hyperplasia (umbilicated yellowish papules).  
- Adnexal tumors (flesh-colored facial papules).  
- Favre-Racouchot syndrome (photodamage, upper lateral cheeks).

paragraphs.title: Acne Vulgaris
paragraphs.name: [8] Acne Vulgaris — Management / Treatment
paragraphs.text:
Acne Vulgaris — Management / Treatment
### **Mild Acne**  
- **Topical retinoids** (tretinoin, tazarotene, adapalene, trifarotene): Normalize keratinization, reduce comedones. Monotherapy for comedonal acne; combine with antimicrobials for papulopustular. Apply once daily (night), start every other night to reduce irritation.  
- **Benzoyl peroxide** (2.5%–10%): Comedolytic, antimicrobial. Avoid concurrent tretinoin (oxidation).  
- **Topical clindamycin/erythromycin**: Use with benzoyl peroxide to prevent resistance.  
- **Azelaic acid**: Comedolytic, antimicrobial, whitening (postinflammatory hyperpigmentation).  
- **Salicylic acid**: Alternative to retinoids.  

### **Moderate-to-Severe Acne**  
- **Oral isotretinoin** (0.5–1 mg/kg/day): Targets all pathogenic factors. Contraindicated in pregnancy (teratogenic). Monitor for myalgia, dry skin, hyperlipidemia, hepatic enzymes. Combine with steroids for flare prevention.  
- **Oral antibiotics** (tetracyclines preferred): Doxycycline, minocycline, sarecycline. Limit to 3–4 months; avoid in children <8, pregnancy. Adverse effects: photosensitivity, GI upset, pseudotumor cerebri.  
- **Hormonal therapies**:  
  - **Oral contraceptives**: FDA-approved options (ethinyl estradiol with norethindrone, norgestimate, drospirenone). Avoid in thrombophilic disorders.  
  - **Spironolactone** (25–100 mg/day): Anti-androgen; reduces sebum by 50%. Adverse effects: breast tenderness, menstrual irregularities. Combine with contraceptives.  

### **Management of Complications**  
- **Hyperpigmentation**: Photoprotection, retinoids, azelaic acid, hydroquinone, chemical peels.  
- **Scars**: Ice-pick (CROSS with TCA), rolling (subcision, fillers), boxcar (excision, lasers), hypertrophic/keloidal (laser, triamcinolone).

paragraphs.title: Acne Vulgaris
paragraphs.name: [9] Acne Vulgaris — Complications
paragraphs.text:
Acne Vulgaris — Complications
- Psychological (depression, anxiety, low self-esteem).  
- Acne fulminans (ulcerating nodules, fever, arthralgia, osteolytic lesions).  
- Solid facial edema (Morbihan’s disease).  
- Gram-negative folliculitis (resistant to antibiotics, *Pseudomonas*, *Proteus*).

paragraphs.title: Acne Vulgaris
paragraphs.name: [10] Acne Vulgaris — Prognosis
paragraphs.text:
Acne Vulgaris — Prognosis
- Generally good with treatment, but may leave scars.  
- Potential association between teenage acne and prostate cancer (limited evidence).  
- Scars are challenging to treat once established.

paragraphs.title: Acne Vulgaris
paragraphs.name: [11] Acne Vulgaris — Prevention / Patient Education
paragraphs.text:
Acne Vulgaris — Prevention / Patient Education
- Gentle skincare (pH-balanced cleansers, non-comedogenic products).  
- Avoid harsh scrubbing/picking.  
- Limit high glycemic index foods/dairy (individualized).  
- Stress management.  
- Sun protection.

paragraphs.title: Acne Vulgaris
paragraphs.name: [12] Acne Vulgaris — Interprofessional Considerations
paragraphs.text:
Acne Vulgaris — Interprofessional Considerations
- Follow AAD and WHO guidelines for acne and hormonal therapy.  
- Pharmacists must adhere to iPLEDGE program for isotretinoin, educate on teratogenicity.  
- Nurses provide patient education, monitor treatment response.  
- Dermatology consultation recommended for severe/resistant cases.

paragraphs.title: Acute Kidney Injury
paragraphs.name: [13] Acute Kidney Injury — Definition / Overview
paragraphs.text:
Acute Kidney Injury — Definition / Overview
- Acute kidney injury (AKI), previously termed acute renal failure, denotes a sudden and often reversible reduction in kidney function, measured by increased serum creatinine or decreased urine output.  
- AKI is categorized into prerenal, intrarenal (intrinsic), and postrenal etiologies, which may overlap or interrelate.

paragraphs.title: Acute Kidney Injury
paragraphs.name: [14] Acute Kidney Injury — Epidemiology
paragraphs.text:
Acute Kidney Injury — Epidemiology
- AKI occurs in **1% of all hospital admissions**, with an incidence of **2–5% during hospitalization** and up to **67% in ICU admissions**.  
- Contributes to prolonged hospital stays and increased patient morbidity.

paragraphs.title: Acute Kidney Injury
paragraphs.name: [15] Acute Kidney Injury — Etiology / Causes
paragraphs.text:
Acute Kidney Injury — Etiology / Causes
### Prerenal AKI  
- Hypovolemia: hemorrhage, severe burns, gastrointestinal losses (diarrhea, vomiting, high ostomy output).  
- Hypotension from decreased cardiac output: cardiogenic shock, pulmonary embolism, acute coronary syndrome.  
- Hypotension from systemic vasodilation: septic shock, anaphylaxis, anesthesia.  
- Renal vasoconstriction: NSAIDs, iodinated contrast, amphotericin B, calcineurin inhibitors, hepatorenal syndrome.  
- Glomerular efferent arteriolar vasodilation: ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers.  

### Intrinsic Renal AKI  
- **Acute tubular necrosis (ATN)**: prolonged prerenal injury, aminoglycosides, vancomycin, amphotericin B, iodinated contrast, rhabdomyolysis, intravascular hemolysis.  
- **Acute interstitial nephritis (AIN)**: beta-lactam antibiotics, NSAIDs, proton pump inhibitors, 5-ASA, infections, autoimmune conditions (SLE, IgG-related disease).  
- **Glomerulonephritis**: anti-GBM disease, immune complex-mediated diseases (SLE, post-infectious glomerulonephritis, cryoglobulinemia, IgA nephropathy).  
- **Intratubular obstruction**: monoclonal gammopathy (e.g., multiple myeloma), tumor lysis syndrome, hemolytic anemia, ethylene glycol.  

### Postrenal AKI  
- Bladder outlet obstruction: prostatic hypertrophy (older men), pelvic masses (older women), nephrolithiasis (younger patients).  
- Ureteral obstruction: tumors, blood clots, neurogenic bladder.  
- Urethral obstruction: retroperitoneal fibrosis, pregnancy, fecal impaction, pelvic organ prolapse, phimosis.

paragraphs.title: Acute Kidney Injury
paragraphs.name: [16] Acute Kidney Injury — Pathophysiology
paragraphs.text:
Acute Kidney Injury — Pathophysiology
- **Prerenal**: Reduced renal blood flow due to systemic hypoperfusion or selective renal hypoperfusion.  
- **Intrinsic**: Tubular-glomerular damage from ischemia (ATN), toxins, inflammation (AIN, glomerulonephritis), or intratubular obstruction.  
- **Postrenal**: Urinary tract obstruction leads to increased upper tract pressure, decreased renal perfusion, and eventual chronic interstitial nephritis.

paragraphs.title: Acute Kidney Injury
paragraphs.name: [17] Acute Kidney Injury — Clinical Presentation
paragraphs.text:
Acute Kidney Injury — Clinical Presentation
- Sudden decline in kidney function, often with normal BUN/creatinine initially; decreased urine output is a key early sign.  
- Common causes in hospitalized patients:  
  - ATN (45%)  
  - Prerenal disease (21%)  
  - AKI superimposed on CKD (13%)  
  - Urinary tract obstruction (10%)  
  - Glomerulonephritis/vasculitis (4%)  
  - AIN (2%)  
  - Atheroemboli (1%)  
- Urine output patterns:  
  - Oliguria: suggests AKI.  
  - Sudden anuria: acute urinary obstruction, glomerulonephritis, vascular blockage.  
  - Polyuria: postobstructive nephropathy or tubular defects (e.g., AIN).

paragraphs.title: Acute Kidney Injury
paragraphs.name: [18] Acute Kidney Injury — Evaluation / Diagnosis
paragraphs.text:
Acute Kidney Injury — Evaluation / Diagnosis
- **Criteria**:  
  - **KDIGO**: Increase in serum creatinine ≥0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours, or ≥1.5× baseline within 7 days, or urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h for ≥6 hours.  
  - **RIFLE**: Risk (Cr ↑1.5×, GFR ↓25%, urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 h), Injury (Cr ↑2×, GFR ↓50%, urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h for 12 h), Failure (Cr ↑3×, GFR ↓75%, Cr ≥4.0, or urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h for 24 h).  
- **Diagnostic tests**:  
  - Comprehensive metabolic panel, urine electrolytes, osmolality, albumin-to-creatinine ratio.  
  - Serum and urine protein electrophoresis (older patients) to evaluate for monoclonal gammopathy.  
  - Renal ultrasound for obstruction; CT for nephrolithiasis/urolithiasis.  
  - Urine microscopy: muddy brown casts (ATN), white blood cell casts (AIN), sterile pyuria (AIN).  
  - Biomarkers (limited use): NGAL, KIM-1, cystatin C.  
  - **Fluid challenge**: Differentiates prerenal vs. ATN if no contraindications.

paragraphs.title: Acute Kidney Injury
paragraphs.name: [19] Acute Kidney Injury — Differential Diagnosis
paragraphs.text:
Acute Kidney Injury — Differential Diagnosis
- Renal calculi, chronic kidney disease, hypovolemia, gastrointestinal bleeding, decreased cardiac output, urinary tract infection, urinary obstruction.  
- Elevated creatinine unrelated to kidney disease (e.g., creatine supplements).

paragraphs.title: Acute Kidney Injury
paragraphs.name: [20] Acute Kidney Injury — Management / Treatment
paragraphs.text:
Acute Kidney Injury — Management / Treatment
- **Fluid challenge**: First-line for prerenal AKI if no contraindications.  
- **Avoid nephrotoxins**: Adjust medications, discontinue offending agents.  
- **Volume overload**: Use diuretics (e.g., IV furosemide) for symptomatic management; does not alter oliguric ATN progression.  
- **Hyperkalemia management**:  
  - Dietary restriction, insulin/dextrose, beta-agonists, potassium-binding resins, calcium gluconate for ECG changes, dialysis if refractory.  
- **Renal replacement therapy (RRT)**: Indicated for severe hyperkalemia, uremic pericarditis, pulmonary edema, or electrolyte acid-base abnormalities. Options include hemodialysis or continuous renal replacement therapy.  
- **Etiology-specific treatments**:  
  - Vasoactive medications/colloids for hepatorenal syndrome.  
  - Immunosuppressives for glomerulonephritis/vasculitis.  
  - Steroids for AIN.  
  - Surgical intervention for postrenal obstruction (e.g., prostatic hypertrophy, stenting for calculi).

paragraphs.title: Acute Kidney Injury
paragraphs.name: [21] Acute Kidney Injury — Complications
paragraphs.text:
Acute Kidney Injury — Complications
- **Metabolic derangements**: Hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, hyperphosphatemia, hyponatremia.  
- **Volume overload**: Pulmonary edema, peripheral edema.  
- **Cardiovascular**: Heart failure, arrhythmias, myocardial infarction, pericarditis.  
- **Gastrointestinal**: Nausea, vomiting, anorexia, GI bleeding.  
- **Neurologic**: Uremic encephalopathy (lethargy, somnolence, cognitive impairment).

paragraphs.title: Acute Kidney Injury
paragraphs.name: [22] Acute Kidney Injury — Prognosis
paragraphs.text:
Acute Kidney Injury — Prognosis
- **Prerenal AKI**: Complete recovery if treated early; may progress to ATN if insult persists.  
- **In-hospital mortality**: **40–50% overall**, **>50% in ICU patients**.  
- **Long-term**: **12–15% may require permanent dialysis**.  
- **Prognostic factors**: Older age, APACHE III score, persistent creatinine elevation, multiorgan involvement, sepsis.

paragraphs.title: Acute Kidney Injury
paragraphs.name: [23] Acute Kidney Injury — Prevention / Patient Education
paragraphs.text:
Acute Kidney Injury — Prevention / Patient Education
- Avoid nephrotoxic agents (NSAIDs, contrast), dehydration.  
- Monitor blood pressure and adhere to prescribed medications.  
- Dietary modifications: Sodium/fluid restriction, low-potassium diet if indicated, adequate protein intake during catabolic states.  
- Close follow-up with nephrology and primary care providers.

paragraphs.title: Acute Kidney Injury
paragraphs.name: [24] Acute Kidney Injury — Interprofessional Considerations
paragraphs.text:
Acute Kidney Injury — Interprofessional Considerations
- Collaborative care involving nephrologists, pharmacists (medication review), dietitians (nutritional guidance), and primary care providers.  
- Early recognition and intervention by all healthcare team members to reduce morbidity.  
- Patient education on avoiding nephrotoxins and adhering to dietary restrictions.

paragraphs.title: Animal Bites
paragraphs.name: [25] Animal Bites — Definition / Overview
paragraphs.text:
Animal Bites — Definition / Overview
- Animal bites pose significant clinical challenges due to risks of infection, tissue damage, and transmission of diseases such as rabies and tetanus. Injuries range from superficial abrasions to deep punctures or crushed tissue. Management requires evidence-based strategies for wound care, infection prevention, and prophylaxis.

paragraphs.title: Animal Bites
paragraphs.name: [26] Animal Bites — Epidemiology
paragraphs.text:
Animal Bites — Epidemiology
- Approximately **4.5 million animal bites** occur annually in the US, with **750,000 requiring medical attention**.  
- **Dogs** account for **60–90%** of bites, **cats** for **5–20%**, and other species (e.g., rats, monkeys) are rare.  
- **Children** are commonly bitten on the **head/neck** (due to smaller stature), while **adults** often sustain hand/arm injuries.  
- **Infection rates**:  
  - Dog bites: **2–25%** (higher with comorbidities, hand/foot involvement, or delayed care).  
  - Cat bites: **~30%** (puncture wounds increase risk of osteomyelitis, septic arthritis).  
- **Rat-bite fever** carries **10–13% mortality** if untreated.

paragraphs.title: Animal Bites
paragraphs.name: [27] Animal Bites — Etiology / Causes
paragraphs.text:
Animal Bites — Etiology / Causes
- **Domestic cats and dogs** are the primary sources of biting animals.  
- **Pathogens in dog bites**:  
  - Aerobic: *Pasteurella canis*, *Staphylococcus*, *Streptococcus*.  
  - Anaerobic: *Bacteroides*, *Capnocytophaga canimorsus* (higher risk in immunocompromised individuals).  
- **Pathogens in cat bites**:  
  - Aerobic: *Pasteurella multocida*, *Streptococcus*, *Staphylococcus*, *Bartonella henselae* (cat scratch disease).  
  - Anaerobic: *Fusobacterium*, *Capnocytophaga*.  
- **Less common animals**:  
  - **Rats**: *Streptobacillus moniliformis*, *Spirillum minus* (rat-bite fever), leptospirosis.  
  - **Monkeys**: Human-like oral flora (e.g., *Neisseria*, *Streptococcus*), herpes B virus.  
  - **Bats**: Rabies virus.  
- **Other infections**: Tularemia (*Francisella tularensis*), plague (*Yersinia pestis*), fungal infections.

paragraphs.title: Animal Bites
paragraphs.name: [28] Animal Bites — Pathophysiology
paragraphs.text:
Animal Bites — Pathophysiology
- **Mechanical trauma**: Teeth cause punctures, lacerations, crush injuries, or fractures.  
- **Infection mechanisms**: Polymicrobial contamination from oral flora (aerobes/anaerobes) and environmental/skin bacteria.  
- **Systemic spread**: Pathogens may travel via blood (sepsis, endocarditis) or nerves (rabies virus binding to neuromuscular junctions, ascending to the brain).

paragraphs.title: Animal Bites
paragraphs.name: [29] Animal Bites — Clinical Presentation
paragraphs.text:
Animal Bites — Clinical Presentation
- **General signs of infection**: Erythema, swelling, warmth, purulent drainage, lymphangitis.  
- **Specific presentations**:  
  - **Rabies**: Myalgia, fever, paresthesia, confusion, hallucinations, coma.  
  - **Cat scratch disease**: Papule at bite site, lymphadenopathy, myalgia, fever.  
  - **Rat-bite fever**: Fever, headache, maculopapular rash, arthritis, possible multi-organ involvement.  
  - **Tularemia**: Fever, headache, weakness.

paragraphs.title: Animal Bites
paragraphs.name: [30] Animal Bites — Evaluation / Diagnosis
paragraphs.text:
Animal Bites — Evaluation / Diagnosis
- **Laboratory tests**:  
  - Wound cultures (if infected).  
  - Blood cultures (systemic infection).  
  - CBC (leukocytosis suggests infection).  
- **Imaging**:  
  - X-rays: Fractures, foreign bodies, gas (anaerobic infection).  
  - Advanced imaging (CT/MRI): Suspected deep tissue abscess or complications.  
- **Risk assessment**: Tetanus immunization status, rabies exposure risk.

paragraphs.title: Animal Bites
paragraphs.name: [31] Animal Bites — Differential Diagnosis
paragraphs.text:
Animal Bites — Differential Diagnosis
- Skin infections (cellulitis, abscesses, necrotizing fasciitis).  
- Insect bites (e.g., brown recluse spider, ticks).  
- Human bites or self-inflicted injuries.  
- Child abuse or domestic violence (history mismatch).  
- Chronic ulcers (e.g., *Mycobacterium marinum*, autoimmune conditions like pyoderma gangrenosum).  
- Crush injuries, burns, or vasculitis.

paragraphs.title: Animal Bites
paragraphs.name: [32] Animal Bites — Management / Treatment
paragraphs.text:
Animal Bites — Management / Treatment
- **Wound care**:  
  - Thorough irrigation (high-pressure syringe).  
  - Debridement of devitalized tissue.  
  - Delayed closure for high-risk wounds; primary closure only for cosmetic concerns (e.g., face).  
- **Antibiotics**:  
  - **Prophylaxis (penetration ≥epidermis)**: Amoxicillin-clavulanate (first-line).  
    - Penicillin-allergic: Doxycycline + metronidazole or clindamycin + TMP-SMX.  
  - **Systemic infection**: Hospitalization, IV antibiotics (ampicillin-sulbactam).  
  - **Specific pathogens**:  
    - *Bartonella henselae*: Azithromycin.  
    - *Francisella tularensis*: Streptomycin/gentamicin (severe), doxycycline (mild).  
    - Rat-bite fever: Penicillin G/ceftriaxone.  
- **Prophylaxis**:  
  - Tetanus: Update if last dose >5 years; immunoglobulin if >10 years.  
  - Rabies: Vaccine + immunoglobulin (WHO guidelines: days 0, 3, 7, 14) for high-risk exposures.

paragraphs.title: Animal Bites
paragraphs.name: [33] Animal Bites — Complications
paragraphs.text:
Animal Bites — Complications
- Infectious: Cellulitis, abscess, osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, sepsis, meningitis, endocarditis.  
- Non-infectious: Nerve damage, tendon rupture, psychological effects (PTSD).  
- MRSA transmission between animals and humans.

paragraphs.title: Animal Bites
paragraphs.name: [34] Animal Bites — Prognosis
paragraphs.text:
Animal Bites — Prognosis
- Generally excellent with prompt intervention.  
- Dog bites cause **~30–50 annual fatalities** in the US.  
- Increasing severity of injuries requiring hospitalization/surgery.

paragraphs.title: Animal Bites
paragraphs.name: [35] Animal Bites — Prevention / Patient Education
paragraphs.text:
Animal Bites — Prevention / Patient Education
- Responsible pet ownership and avoiding provocation of unfamiliar animals.  
- Tetanus vaccination updates.  
- Rabies preexposure prophylaxis for high-risk individuals (e.g., veterinarians).  
- Immediate wound irrigation with soap/water after a bite.  
- Recognize signs of infection (redness, swelling, pus) and seek care.

paragraphs.title: Animal Bites
paragraphs.name: [36] Animal Bites — Interprofessional Considerations
paragraphs.text:
Animal Bites — Interprofessional Considerations
- Collaborative care involving clinicians, nurses, pharmacists, infectious disease specialists, surgeons, and public health officials.  
- Clinicians: Diagnose, manage wounds, assess rabies/tetanus risk.  
- Nurses: Wound care, patient education, monitoring for complications.  
- Pharmacists: Antibiotic selection, dosing, drug interaction advice.  
- Coordination ensures holistic care, especially for complex cases.

paragraphs.title: Allergic Rhinitis
paragraphs.name: [37] Allergic Rhinitis — Definition / Overview
paragraphs.text:
Allergic Rhinitis — Definition / Overview
- Atopic disease characterized by symptoms of sneezing, nasal congestion, clear rhinorrhea, postnasal drip, and nasal pruritis. It is an IgE-mediated immune response with an immediate phase (IgE, mast cell degranulation) and a late phase (leukotriene-mediated, cytokine release, eosinophil infiltration). Classified as seasonal (intermittent) or perennial (chronic). Associated with systemic allergic conditions (e.g., asthma, atopic dermatitis).

paragraphs.title: Allergic Rhinitis
paragraphs.name: [38] Allergic Rhinitis — Epidemiology
paragraphs.text:
Allergic Rhinitis — Epidemiology
- Prevalence: 15% based on physician diagnosis, up to 30% based on symptoms. Peaks in the second to fourth decades, gradually declines with age. Common in children (14.6% in 13–14-year-olds, 8.5% in 6–7-year-olds). Seasonal AR more common in pediatric populations, chronic in adults.
- Economic impact: 3.6% of adults miss work; 36% report impaired work performance. Indirect costs (lost productivity) dominate the cost burden.
- Risk factors: Family history of atopy, male sex, allergen-specific IgE, serum IgE >100 IU/mL before age 6, higher socioeconomic status. Early exposure to foods/formula, cigarette smoking in infancy may increase risk. "Farm effect" (40% lower risk in those raised on farms) and potential protective effects of breastfeeding (debated) noted.

paragraphs.title: Allergic Rhinitis
paragraphs.name: [39] Allergic Rhinitis — Etiology / Causes
paragraphs.text:
Allergic Rhinitis — Etiology / Causes
- IgE-mediated response to inhaled antigens (e.g., pollens, animal dander, dust mites). Genetic factors: 45–60% concordance in monozygotic twins, 25% in dizygotic twins. Chromosomal regions 3 and 4 linked to allergic responses.

paragraphs.title: Allergic Rhinitis
paragraphs.name: [40] Allergic Rhinitis — Pathophysiology
paragraphs.text:
Allergic Rhinitis — Pathophysiology
- **Early phase (5–15 minutes post-exposure):** IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation releases histamine, leukotrienes, prostaglandins. Histamine causes sneezing (via trigeminal nerve), rhinorrhea, and nasal congestion.
- **Late phase (4–6 hours post-exposure):** Cytokine release (IL-4, IL-13) leads to eosinophil, T-lymphocyte, and basophil infiltration, causing nasal edema and congestion.
- Non-IgE-mediated hyperresponsiveness due to eosinophilic infiltration and mucosal obliteration; triggers include smoke, cold air.

paragraphs.title: Allergic Rhinitis
paragraphs.name: [41] Allergic Rhinitis — Clinical Presentation
paragraphs.text:
Allergic Rhinitis — Clinical Presentation
- Symptoms: Sneezing, nasal congestion, clear rhinorrhea, postnasal drip, nasal pruritis. Associated features: Allergic conjunctivitis, non-productive cough, Eustachian tube dysfunction, chronic sinusitis.
- Physical findings: Mouth breathing, frequent sniffling, transverse supra-tip nasal crease, allergic shiners (dark circles under eyes), nasal mucosa swelling, thin clear secretions, bluish inferior turbinates, cobblestoning. Endoscopic exam may reveal polyps or structural abnormalities.

paragraphs.title: Allergic Rhinitis
paragraphs.name: [42] Allergic Rhinitis — Evaluation / Diagnosis
paragraphs.text:
Allergic Rhinitis — Evaluation / Diagnosis
- Clinical diagnosis based on history and physical. Confirmatory tests: Serum allergen-specific IgE or skin prick testing (reserved for cases unresponsive to empiric treatment). Skin testing preferred for sensitivity and cost-effectiveness. Contraindications: Uncontrolled asthma, unstable cardiovascular disease, pregnancy, beta-blockers, certain medications (H2 antagonists, tricyclics, omalizumab).
- Imaging (e.g., CT) not routine; used to rule out sinusitis or structural issues.

paragraphs.title: Allergic Rhinitis
paragraphs.name: [43] Allergic Rhinitis — Differential Diagnosis
paragraphs.text:
Allergic Rhinitis — Differential Diagnosis
- Vasomotor rhinitis, infectious rhinitis, cerebrospinal fluid leak, non-allergic rhinitis with eosinophilia (NARES), chemical rhinitis, rhinitis of pregnancy, drug-induced rhinitis (e.g., NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors), autoimmune/granulomatous causes (e.g., granulomatosis with polyangiitis), nasal polyposis, neoplasms. Congenital causes (choanal atresia) in children <2 years.

paragraphs.title: Allergic Rhinitis
paragraphs.name: [44] Allergic Rhinitis — Management / Treatment
paragraphs.text:
Allergic Rhinitis — Management / Treatment
- **Avoidance:** Limit exposure to allergens (e.g., allergen-impermeable bedding, HEPA filters, pet isolation). Not always practical.
- **Pharmacological:**
  - **First-line:** Intranasal corticosteroids (beclomethasone, budesonide, fluticasone, mometasone, triamcinolone). Administered with proper technique (aim laterally, avoid septum). Peak effect in days.
  - **Antihistamines:** First-gen (diphenhydramine; sedating, anticholinergic side effects) and second-gen (fexofenadine, loratadine, desloratadine, cetirizine; less sedating).
  - **Intranasal antihistamines (azelastine):** Rapid onset, used with steroids.
  - **Leukotriene receptor antagonists (montelukast, zafirlukast):** Adjunct for severe/refractory cases.
  - **Decongestants:** Oral (pseudoephedrine) or intranasal (xylometazoline); avoid prolonged use (risk of rhinitis medicamentosa).
  - **Immunotherapy:** Subcutaneous (SCIT) or sublingual (SLIT) for 3–5 years. Omalizumab (anti-IgE) for select cases.
  - **Saline irrigation:** Isotonic (adults) or hypertonic (children).
- **Surgical:** For nasal polyps, turbinate hypertrophy, or refractory sinusitis. Budesonide FDA-approved for pregnancy.

paragraphs.title: Allergic Rhinitis
paragraphs.name: [45] Allergic Rhinitis — Complications
paragraphs.text:
Allergic Rhinitis — Complications
- Chronic rhinosinusitis, nasal polyps (benign, bilateral; unilateral raises malignancy concern), adenoid hypertrophy, Eustachian tube dysfunction, asthma (10–40% comorbidity), otitis media with effusion, eosinophilic esophagitis. Immunotherapy risks: Exacerbation of rhinitis/asthma, anaphylaxis (requires emergency preparedness).

paragraphs.title: Allergic Rhinitis
paragraphs.name: [46] Allergic Rhinitis — Prognosis
paragraphs.text:
Allergic Rhinitis — Prognosis
- Symptoms often improve with age. Longitudinal study: 54.9% improved at 23-year follow-up (41.6% symptom-free). Younger onset associated with better outcomes. Immunotherapy (e.g., grass pollen) shows sustained benefit 3 years post-treatment.

paragraphs.title: Allergic Rhinitis
paragraphs.name: [47] Allergic Rhinitis — Prevention / Patient Education
paragraphs.text:
Allergic Rhinitis — Prevention / Patient Education
- Proper nasal spray administration technique (avoid septum, no deep inhalation). Allergen avoidance counseling. Importance of adhering to treatment due to asthma association. Educate on when to seek care (e.g., refractory symptoms, suspected malignancy).

paragraphs.title: Allergic Rhinitis
paragraphs.name: [48] Allergic Rhinitis — Interprofessional Considerations
paragraphs.text:
Allergic Rhinitis — Interprofessional Considerations
- Primary care physicians manage most cases. Referrals to allergists/ENT for immunotherapy, nasal polyps, suspected malignancy, or CSF leaks. Team includes nurses, pharmacists, and specialists for co-management. Global access to specialists varies. Emphasis on self-management education and timely referrals.

paragraphs.title: Arthritis
paragraphs.name: [49] Arthritis — Definition / Overview
paragraphs.text:
Arthritis — Definition / Overview
- Arthritis is defined as acute or chronic joint inflammation, often accompanied by pain and structural damage.  
- Not synonymous with arthralgia (joint pain without inflammation).  
- Over 100 types exist; most common include osteoarthritis (non-inflammatory) and inflammatory types such as rheumatoid arthritis (RA), psoriatic arthritis, gout, pseudogout, and septic arthritis.

paragraphs.title: Arthritis
paragraphs.name: [50] Arthritis — Epidemiology
paragraphs.text:
Arthritis — Epidemiology
- Over one-third of the American population shows arthritis on imaging.  
- **Osteoarthritis**:  
  - 19–30% of adults >45 years have knee osteoarthritis.  
  - 27% have hand or hip osteoarthritis.  
  - Lifetime risk: 40% in men, 47% in women; increases to 60% with BMI >30.  
- **Gout**:  
  - Affects >8 million in the US (prevalence 3.9%), rising to >9% in those >60 years.  
  - Incidence >45/100,000 and increasing.  
- **Rheumatoid arthritis**:  
  - Prevalence ~1% in Caucasians; female lifetime risk 3.6% vs. 1.7% in males.  
- **Septic arthritis**:  
  - Prevalence 0.01% in general population, 0.7% in RA patients.

paragraphs.title: Arthritis
paragraphs.name: [51] Arthritis — Etiology / Causes
paragraphs.text:
Arthritis — Etiology / Causes
- **Osteoarthritis**:  
  - Advancing age, female sex, joint trauma, obesity, genetic mutations in collagen-encoding genes.  
- **Rheumatoid arthritis**:  
  - Autoimmune disorder linked to HLA-DRB1 genes and environmental factors (e.g., smoking).  
- **Gout**:  
  - Prolonged hyperuricemia (genetic mutations <10%), male sex, aging, CKD, alcoholism, diuretics.  
- **Septic arthritis**:  
  - Bacterial seeding (often *Staphylococcus aureus* or streptococci) via hematogenous spread.  
- **Autoimmune associations**:  
  - SLE, Sjogren syndrome, scleroderma, IBD, celiac disease, etc.

paragraphs.title: Arthritis
paragraphs.name: [52] Arthritis — Pathophysiology
paragraphs.text:
Arthritis — Pathophysiology
- **Osteoarthritis**:  
  - Degenerative cartilage loss, subchondral cysts, osteophytes, and interleukin-mediated matrix degradation.  
- **Rheumatoid arthritis**:  
  - Autoimmune synovial inflammation, cytokine release (TNF-α, IL-1, 6, 8), cartilage/bone erosion.  
- **Gout**:  
  - Monosodium urate crystal deposition → IL-1-mediated inflammation.  
- **Pseudogout**:  
  - Calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate crystals → joint damage (osteophytes, subchondral cysts).  
- **Septic arthritis**:  
  - Bacterial toxins/cytokines cause synovial hyperplasia and cartilage degradation.

paragraphs.title: Arthritis
paragraphs.name: [53] Arthritis — Clinical Presentation
paragraphs.text:
Arthritis — Clinical Presentation
- **Symptoms**: Pain, stiffness, decreased range of motion, joint deformities, fatigue, sleep disturbances.  
- **Onset**:  
  - Acute: septic, crystalline, reactive arthritis.  
  - Insidious: OA, RA, psoriatic arthritis.  
- **Joint involvement**:  
  - Monoarticular (e.g., gout, septic), oligoarticular (HLA-B27 spondyloarthropathies), polyarticular (RA, SLE).  
- **Physical findings**:  
  - Inflammatory: swelling, effusion, erythema, warmth.  
  - Non-inflammatory: tenderness, mechanical symptoms (OA).

paragraphs.title: Arthritis
paragraphs.name: [54] Arthritis — Evaluation / Diagnosis
paragraphs.text:
Arthritis — Evaluation / Diagnosis
- **History/physical**: Assess articular vs. non-articular pain, morning stiffness, joint distribution.  
- **Labs**:  
  - Inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP), uric acid, RF, anti-CCP, ANA.  
  - Synovial fluid analysis: cell count, crystals (gout: needle-shaped, negatively birefringent; pseudogout: rhomboid, positively birefringent), cultures.  
- **Imaging**:  
  - X-ray: osteophytes (OA), erosions (RA), chondrocalcinosis (pseudogout).  
  - MRI/CT/ultrasound for detailed soft tissue/bony assessment.

paragraphs.title: Arthritis
paragraphs.name: [55] Arthritis — Differential Diagnosis
paragraphs.text:
Arthritis — Differential Diagnosis
- Non-articular pain (fibromyalgia, myofascial pain, neuropathy, tendinitis).  
- Over 100 arthritis subtypes requiring precise diagnosis before treatment.

paragraphs.title: Arthritis
paragraphs.name: [56] Arthritis — Management / Treatment
paragraphs.text:
Arthritis — Management / Treatment
- **Osteoarthritis**:  
  - Non-pharmacologic: exercise, PT, weight loss, bracing.  
  - Pharmacologic: NSAIDs, capsaicin, duloxetine, intra-articular corticosteroids.  
  - Surgical: joint replacement for refractory cases.  
- **Rheumatoid arthritis**:  
  - DMARDs (e.g., methotrexate), biologics, NSAIDs, glucocorticoids.  
- **Gout**:  
  - Acute: NSAIDs, colchicine, corticosteroids.  
  - Chronic: urate-lowering therapies (e.g., allopurinol).  
- **Septic arthritis**:  
  - Joint drainage and antibiotics.

paragraphs.title: Arthritis
paragraphs.name: [57] Arthritis — Complications
paragraphs.text:
Arthritis — Complications
- Not specified in source.

paragraphs.title: Arthritis
paragraphs.name: [58] Arthritis — Prognosis
paragraphs.text:
Arthritis — Prognosis
- **Osteoarthritis**: Progressive; outcomes improve post-replacement but prostheses require revision (10–15 years).  
- **Rheumatoid arthritis**: Improved with early DMARDs/biologics; higher mortality due to extra-articular manifestations.

paragraphs.title: Arthritis
paragraphs.name: [59] Arthritis — Prevention / Patient Education
paragraphs.text:
Arthritis — Prevention / Patient Education
- Weight loss, exercise, muscle strengthening, diet modification.  
- Medication adherence, smoking cessation, alcohol avoidance.  
- Collaboration with dietitians, PTs, and interdisciplinary teams.

paragraphs.title: Arthritis
paragraphs.name: [60] Arthritis — Interprofessional Considerations
paragraphs.text:
Arthritis — Interprofessional Considerations
- Team includes rheumatologists, orthopedic surgeons, PTs, pharmacists, nurses, and pain specialists.  
- Focus on polypharmacy monitoring, rehabilitation, and early intervention to reduce narcotic dependence.  
- Guidelines recommend interprofessional collaboration (e.g., American College of Rheumatology).

paragraphs.title: Chronic Kidney Disease
paragraphs.name: [61] Chronic Kidney Disease — Definition / Overview
paragraphs.text:
Chronic Kidney Disease — Definition / Overview
- Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is defined by kidney damage or an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) <60 mL/min/1.73 m² persisting for ≥3 months.  
- Classified by the 2012 KDIGO criteria into 6 stages (G1–G5) based on eGFR and 3 stages of albuminuria (A1–A3) based on urinary albumin-creatinine ratio (ACR):  
  - **G1**: eGFR ≥90 mL/min/1.73 m² with kidney damage  
  - **G2**: eGFR 60–89 mL/min/1.73 m²  
  - **G3a**: eGFR 45–59 mL/min/1.73 m²  
  - **G3b**: eGFR 30–44 mL/min/1.73 m²  
  - **G4**: eGFR 15–29 mL/min/1.73 m²  
  - **G5**: eGFR <15 mL/min/1.73 m² or dialysis-dependent  
  - **A1**: ACR <30 mg/g (<3.4 mg/mmol)  
  - **A2**: ACR 30–299 mg/g (3.4–34 mg/mmol)  
  - **A3**: ACR >300 mg/g (>34 mg/mmol)

paragraphs.title: Chronic Kidney Disease
paragraphs.name: [62] Chronic Kidney Disease — Epidemiology
paragraphs.text:
Chronic Kidney Disease — Epidemiology
- Global prevalence: ~10–14%, with albuminuria (~7%) and eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m² (~4%) contributing.  
- In the U.S. (2016): ~26 million affected.  
- Contributed to 2,968,600 disability-adjusted life-years and 2,546,700 life-years lost globally in 2012.

paragraphs.title: Chronic Kidney Disease
paragraphs.name: [63] Chronic Kidney Disease — Etiology / Causes
paragraphs.text:
Chronic Kidney Disease — Etiology / Causes
- **Primary diseases leading to ESRD**:  
  - Type 2 diabetes (30–50%)  
  - Type 1 diabetes (3.9%)  
  - Hypertension (27.2%)  
  - Primary glomerulonephritis (8.2%)  
  - Chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis (3.6%)  
  - Hereditary/cystic diseases (3.1%)  
  - Secondary glomerulonephritis/vasculitis (2.1%)  
  - Plasma cell dyscrasias/neoplasm (2.1%)  
  - Sickle cell nephropathy (<1% in the U.S.)  
- **Categories of disease processes**:  
  - **Prerenal**: Chronic heart failure, cirrhosis, leading to ischemic nephropathy.  
  - **Intrinsic renal**:  
    - Vascular (e.g., nephrosclerosis, renal artery stenosis).  
    - Glomerular (nephritic/nephrotic syndromes; e.g., post-infectious GN, IgA nephropathy, diabetic nephropathy).  
    - Tubulointerstitial (e.g., polycystic kidney disease, MesoAmerican nephropathy).  
  - **Postrenal**: Prostatic disease, nephrolithiasis, congenital anomalies, retroperitoneal fibrosis.

paragraphs.title: Chronic Kidney Disease
paragraphs.name: [64] Chronic Kidney Disease — Pathophysiology
paragraphs.text:
Chronic Kidney Disease — Pathophysiology
- Progressive fibrosis and destruction of renal architecture: glomerulosclerosis, tubulointerstitial fibrosis, vascular sclerosis.  
- Mechanisms:  
  - Inflammatory cell infiltration.  
  - Activation/apoptosis of renal cells.  
  - Extracellular matrix deposition.  
- Accelerating factors:  
  - Systemic/intraglomerular hypertension.  
  - Glomerular hypertrophy.  
  - Calcium phosphate precipitation.  
  - Altered prostanoid metabolism.

paragraphs.title: Chronic Kidney Disease
paragraphs.name: [65] Chronic Kidney Disease — Clinical Presentation
paragraphs.text:
Chronic Kidney Disease — Clinical Presentation
- **Asymptomatic in early stages (1–3)**. Symptoms in stages 4–5:  
  - Nausea, vomiting, anorexia, fatigue, sleep disturbances, oliguria, muscle cramps, edema, pruritus, cognitive changes, pericarditis, pulmonary edema, hypertension.  
- **Physical findings**: Skin pigmentation, excoriations, pericardial rub, uremic frost, hyperreflexia, hypertensive retinopathy.

paragraphs.title: Chronic Kidney Disease
paragraphs.name: [66] Chronic Kidney Disease — Evaluation / Diagnosis
paragraphs.text:
Chronic Kidney Disease — Evaluation / Diagnosis
- **Establishing chronicity**:  
  - History of hypertension, proteinuria, or structural abnormalities.  
  - Persistent eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m² for ≥3 months.  
  - Imaging (e.g., small kidneys with cortical thinning on ultrasound).  
- **Assessment**:  
  - eGFR (using CKD-EPI equation).  
  - Urine ACR (early morning sample).  
  - Imaging: Ultrasound for kidney size/cysts, Doppler for renal artery stenosis.  
  - Biopsy for definitive etiology.

paragraphs.title: Chronic Kidney Disease
paragraphs.name: [67] Chronic Kidney Disease — Differential Diagnosis
paragraphs.text:
Chronic Kidney Disease — Differential Diagnosis
- Acute kidney injury  
- Alport syndrome  
- Antiglomerular basement membrane disease  
- Diabetic nephropathy  
- Multiple myeloma  
- Nephrolithiasis  
- Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis  
- Renal artery stenosis

paragraphs.title: Chronic Kidney Disease
paragraphs.name: [68] Chronic Kidney Disease — Management / Treatment
paragraphs.text:
Chronic Kidney Disease — Management / Treatment
- **General**:  
  - Adjust drug dosages based on eGFR.  
  - Avoid nephrotoxins (e.g., NSAIDs, aminoglycosides).  
- **Slowing progression**:  
  - Control hypertension (systolic <120 mmHg per KDIGO 2021; <130/80 mmHg per ACC/AHA 2017).  
  - Reduce proteinuria (<1 g/d if possible).  
  - Address metabolic acidosis (bicarbonate supplementation to maintain serum level ~23 mEq/L).  
  - Smoking cessation, dietary protein restriction, glycemic control in diabetes.  
- **Renal replacement therapy (RRT)**:  
  - Initiate when eGFR <15 mL/min/1.73 m² or emergent indications (e.g., pericarditis, refractory hyperkalemia).  
  - Options: Hemodialysis (AV fistula preferred), peritoneal dialysis, transplantation.  
- **Indications for RRT**:  
  - Uremic pericarditis/encephalopathy, bleeding diathesis, refractory fluid overload/metabolic disorders.

paragraphs.title: Chronic Kidney Disease
paragraphs.name: [69] Chronic Kidney Disease — Complications
paragraphs.text:
Chronic Kidney Disease — Complications
- **Systemic**:  
  - Fluid overload, hypertension, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, hyperphosphatemia, anemia, cardiovascular disease.  
- **Mineral bone disorder**: Secondary hyperparathyroidism, FGF23 elevation.  
- **Transplant-related**: Infections, malignancies, cardiovascular/metabolic complications.

paragraphs.title: Chronic Kidney Disease
paragraphs.name: [70] Chronic Kidney Disease — Prognosis
paragraphs.text:
Chronic Kidney Disease — Prognosis
- Community-based CKD progresses slowly (eGFR decline ~0.75–1 mL/min/year); 24–45% of stages 3–4 die from cardiovascular events before ESRD.  
- Faster progression in referred CKD (e.g., diabetic nephropathy: ~10 mL/min/year decline).

paragraphs.title: Chronic Kidney Disease
paragraphs.name: [71] Chronic Kidney Disease — Prevention / Patient Education
paragraphs.text:
Chronic Kidney Disease — Prevention / Patient Education
- Screen high-risk groups (diabetes, hypertension, age >65) via urinalysis, ACR, eGFR.  
- Patient education: BP monitoring, low-sodium diet, avoid nephrotoxins, dietary counseling, pregnancy risks (teratogenicity of ACE inhibitors).

paragraphs.title: Chronic Kidney Disease
paragraphs.name: [72] Chronic Kidney Disease — Interprofessional Considerations
paragraphs.text:
Chronic Kidney Disease — Interprofessional Considerations
- Nephrologists, primary care providers, dietitians, pharmacists, and nurses collaborate to manage risk factors, adjust medications, provide dialysis access, and coordinate transplantation.  
- Multidisciplinary care reduces hospitalizations, improves vascular access placement, and enhances outcomes.

paragraphs.title: Dengue Fever
paragraphs.name: [73] Dengue Fever — Definition / Overview
paragraphs.text:
Dengue Fever — Definition / Overview
- Dengue fever is a mosquito-transmitted viral illness caused by any of the four distinct serotypes (DENV-1 to DENV-4) of single-stranded RNA viruses in the genus *Flavivirus*. It is the leading arthropod-borne viral disease globally, often termed "breakbone fever" or "7-day fever" due to its symptoms of severe muscle and joint pain, high fever, and its typical duration.

paragraphs.title: Dengue Fever
paragraphs.name: [74] Dengue Fever — Epidemiology
paragraphs.text:
Dengue Fever — Epidemiology
- Fastest-spreading mosquito-borne viral disease worldwide, with over 100 million cases annually and 20,000–25,000 deaths, primarily among children.  
- Endemic in >100 countries, with epidemic and hyperendemic patterns.  
- Transmission cycles include:  
  - Nonhuman primate to nonhuman primate via mosquitoes.  
  - Human to human via mosquitoes (primarily urban environments).  
- Vectors: *Aedes aegypti* and *Aedes albopictus* (female mosquitoes).  
- Modes of transmission: Perinatal, blood transfusions, breast milk, organ transplantation.  
- Mean age of patients increased from 27.2 (1990–2010) to 34 (post-2010).

paragraphs.title: Dengue Fever
paragraphs.name: [75] Dengue Fever — Etiology / Causes
paragraphs.text:
Dengue Fever — Etiology / Causes
- Caused by four serotypes of *Flavivirus* (DENV-1 to DENV-4).  
- Infection with one serotype confers lifelong immunity to that serotype but not others.

paragraphs.title: Dengue Fever
paragraphs.name: [76] Dengue Fever — Pathophysiology
paragraphs.text:
Dengue Fever — Pathophysiology
- Virions (50-nm) contain 3 structural and 7 nonstructural proteins, a lipid envelope, and capped positive-sense ssRNA.  
- 75% of infections are asymptomatic. Spectrum ranges from self-limiting fever to severe hemorrhage/shock.  
- Incubation: 4–7 days; symptoms last 3–10 days.  
- Pathogenesis involves skin macrophages/dendritic cells as initial targets, followed by lymphatic dissemination and viremia (24–48 hours pre-symptoms).  
- Severe dengue (0.5–5% of cases) linked to:  
  - Second infection with a different serotype.  
  - Immune response and viral factors.  
- Microvascular permeability increases as viral titers decline.

paragraphs.title: Dengue Fever
paragraphs.name: [77] Dengue Fever — Clinical Presentation
paragraphs.text:
Dengue Fever — Clinical Presentation
### Phases:  
1. **Febrile Phase (2–7 days):**  
   - Sudden high-grade fever (≈40°C), facial flushing, skin erythema (blanchable macular rash), myalgias, arthralgias, headache, sore throat, conjunctival injection, anorexia, nausea, vomiting.  
   - Saddleback/biphasic fever in ≈6% of cases (common in DHF/severe dengue).  

2. **Critical Phase (Days 3–7):**  
   - Defervescence (temperature ↓ to 37.5–38°C or lower).  
   - Capillary permeability increased, lasting 1–2 days.  
   - Preceded by rapid platelet drop, elevated hematocrit, leukopenia.  
   - Warning signs: Abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, fluid accumulation (ascites/pleural effusion), mucosal bleeding, lethargy, hepatomegaly, elevated hematocrit, thrombocytopenia.  

3. **Recovery Phase (2–3 days):**  
   - Fluid reabsorption, bradycardia.  
   - **Expanded dengue syndrome:** Atypical manifestations (neurological [seizures, encephalitis], hepatic [hepatitis, failure], renal [AKI], cardiac [myocarditis], respiratory [ARDS], hematologic [HUS]).

paragraphs.title: Dengue Fever
paragraphs.name: [78] Dengue Fever — Evaluation / Diagnosis
paragraphs.text:
Dengue Fever — Evaluation / Diagnosis
- **Probable Dengue:**  
  - Travel to/history of endemic area + fever + ≥2 of: nausea/vomiting, rash, myalgias/arthralgias, positive tourniquet test, leukopenia.  
- **Warning Signs:** Abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, fluid accumulation, mucosal bleeding, lethargy, hepatomegaly >2 cm, elevated hematocrit, thrombocytopenia.  
- **Severe Dengue:** Dengue fever with severe plasma leakage, hemorrhage, impaired consciousness, myocardial/pulmonary/organ dysfunction (e.g., transaminitis >1000 IU/L).  
- **Diagnostic Tests:**  
  - Laboratory: Thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, elevated AST.  
  - Antigen detection: NS1 ELISA, PCR, viral culture.  
  - Serology: IgM/IgG (detectable after several days; cross-reactivity with other *Flaviviruses*).

paragraphs.title: Dengue Fever
paragraphs.name: [79] Dengue Fever — Differential Diagnosis
paragraphs.text:
Dengue Fever — Differential Diagnosis
- Measles, influenza, Zika virus, West Nile infection, chikungunya, malaria, yellow fever.  
- Detailed travel/exposure history and lab testing essential.

paragraphs.title: Dengue Fever
paragraphs.name: [80] Dengue Fever — Management / Treatment
paragraphs.text:
Dengue Fever — Management / Treatment
- **Outpatient (no warning signs):**  
  - Acetaminophen (avoid NSAIDs/aspirin), oral fluid repletion.  
  - Patient education on warning signs.  
- **Hospitalization (warning signs/severe dengue/risk factors):**  
  - IV crystalloids (adjust based on response).  
  - Colloids if shock unresponsive to crystalloids.  
  - Blood transfusion for severe/uncontrolled bleeding.  
  - Platelet transfusion if platelets <20,000/µL and high bleeding risk.  
- **No antiviral agents recommended.**

paragraphs.title: Dengue Fever
paragraphs.name: [81] Dengue Fever — Complications
paragraphs.text:
Dengue Fever — Complications
- Liver injury, cardiomyopathy, pneumonia, orchitis/oophoritis, seizures, encephalopathy, encephalitis.

paragraphs.title: Dengue Fever
paragraphs.name: [82] Dengue Fever — Prognosis
paragraphs.text:
Dengue Fever — Prognosis
- Untreated severe dengue mortality: 10–20%.  
- With supportive care: Mortality ↓ to ≈1%.

paragraphs.title: Dengue Fever
paragraphs.name: [83] Dengue Fever — Prevention / Patient Education
paragraphs.text:
Dengue Fever — Prevention / Patient Education
- **Mosquito avoidance:** Bed nets (daytime use), insecticide-treated materials, DEET/IR3535/icaridin repellents, long sleeves/pants.  
- **Biological control:** *Poecilia reticulata* fish, predatory copepods, *Wolbachia*-infected mosquitoes.  
- **Chemical control:** Larvicides, organophosphorus compounds (fenitrothion, malathion), pyrethroids (bioresmethrin, cypermethrin).  
- **Environmental measures:** Eliminate breeding sites, cover water storage.  
- **Vaccination:** CYD-TDV (live recombinant tetravalent vaccine) approved in 20 endemic countries.

paragraphs.title: Dengue Fever
paragraphs.name: [84] Dengue Fever — Interprofessional Considerations
paragraphs.text:
Dengue Fever — Interprofessional Considerations
- Multidisciplinary team: Infectious disease specialists, CDC consultants, emergency clinicians, internists, primary care providers, nurses.  
- Roles:  
  - Timely diagnosis and supportive care (fluids, transfusions).  
  - Primary care providers educate travelers on mosquito avoidance and preventive measures.  
  - Collaboration with public health authorities for outbreak management.

paragraphs.title: Arginine Vasopressin Disorder (Diabetes Insipidus)
paragraphs.name: [85] Arginine Vasopressin Disorder (Diabetes Insipidus) — Definition / Overview
paragraphs.text:
Arginine Vasopressin Disorder (Diabetes Insipidus) — Definition / Overview
- Arginine vasopressin disorder results from decreased release of antidiuretic hormone (ADH/AVP) or reduced renal response to AVP, causing electrolyte imbalances.  
- Two types: **Arginine Vasopressin Deficiency (AVP-D, formerly Central DI)** and **Arginine Vasopressin Resistance (AVP-R, formerly Nephrogenic DI)**.

paragraphs.title: Arginine Vasopressin Disorder (Diabetes Insipidus)
paragraphs.name: [86] Arginine Vasopressin Disorder (Diabetes Insipidus) — Epidemiology
paragraphs.text:
Arginine Vasopressin Disorder (Diabetes Insipidus) — Epidemiology
- Affects approximately 1 in 25,000 people (0.004% global prevalence).  
- No gender preference.  
- Can develop at any age, with hereditary forms presenting earlier.

paragraphs.title: Arginine Vasopressin Disorder (Diabetes Insipidus)
paragraphs.name: [87] Arginine Vasopressin Disorder (Diabetes Insipidus) — Etiology / Causes
paragraphs.text:
Arginine Vasopressin Disorder (Diabetes Insipidus) — Etiology / Causes
### Arginine Vasopressin Deficiency (AVP-D)  
- **Idiopathic**: 30–50% of cases, often autoimmune (lymphocytic inflammation of pituitary stalk/posterior pituitary).  
- **Familial/Congenital**: Wolfram syndrome, PCSK1 gene deficiency, congenital hypopituitarism, septo-optic dysplasia.  
- **Acquired**: Neurosurgery (10–80% incidence post-craniopharyngioma/surgery), trauma, tumors (e.g., craniopharyngioma, metastases), infiltrative disorders (sarcoidosis, histiocytosis, autoimmune lymphocytic hypophysitis), hypoxic encephalopathy.  
- **Adipsic DI**: Lesions affecting hypothalamic osmoreceptors/thirst centers (e.g., craniopharyngioma, trauma).  

### Arginine Vasopressin Resistance (AVP-R)  
- **Hereditary**: X-linked (AVPR2 gene mutations, 90% of cases) or autosomal (aquaporin-2 gene mutations).  
- **Acquired**: Lithium (20% of chronic users), hypercalcemia (>11 mg/dL), hypokalemia, medications (cidofovir, amphotericin B, NSAIDs), renal diseases (sickle cell, polycystic kidney, Sjögren syndrome).  

### Gestational AVP-D  
- Caused by placental vasopressinase activity, degrading AVP.  

### Primary Polydipsia  
- Psychogenic, drug-induced (anticholinergics, nicotine), hypothalamic lesions, dipsogenic DI.

paragraphs.title: Arginine Vasopressin Disorder (Diabetes Insipidus)
paragraphs.name: [88] Arginine Vasopressin Disorder (Diabetes Insipidus) — Pathophysiology
paragraphs.text:
Arginine Vasopressin Disorder (Diabetes Insipidus) — Pathophysiology
- **AVP-D**: Defective AVP synthesis/release from posterior pituitary due to hypothalamic/pituitary lesions. Serum AVP insufficient to concentrate urine.  
- **AVP-R**: Impaired renal response to AVP due to defective V2 receptors or aquaporin-2 channels, reducing water reabsorption in collecting ducts.  
- **Negative feedback loops**: Osmoregulation (osmolality >295 mOsm/kg triggers AVP release) and baroregulation (volume/pressure changes modulate AVP).

paragraphs.title: Arginine Vasopressin Disorder (Diabetes Insipidus)
paragraphs.name: [89] Arginine Vasopressin Disorder (Diabetes Insipidus) — Clinical Presentation
paragraphs.text:
Arginine Vasopressin Disorder (Diabetes Insipidus) — Clinical Presentation
- **General**: Polyuria (>50 mL/kg/day), dilute urine (osmolality <300 mOsm/L), polydipsia (up to 20 L/day), nocturia.  
- **Children**: Dehydration, constipation, vomiting, fever, failure to thrive.  
- **CNS involvement**: Headaches, visual defects.  
- **AVP-D complications**: Reduced bone mineral density, weakness, fatigue, myalgias.

paragraphs.title: Arginine Vasopressin Disorder (Diabetes Insipidus)
paragraphs.name: [90] Arginine Vasopressin Disorder (Diabetes Insipidus) — Evaluation / Diagnosis
paragraphs.text:
Arginine Vasopressin Disorder (Diabetes Insipidus) — Evaluation / Diagnosis
1. **Confirm hypotonic polyuria**:  
   - 24-hour urine volume (>2.5 L in adults).  
   - Urine osmolality <300 mOsm/L with high-normal serum osmolality.  
2. **Water deprivation test**:  
   - Discontinue if urine osmolality stabilizes or plasma osmolality >300 mOsm/kg.  
   - Administer desmopressin (DDAVP) to differentiate AVP-D (urine osmolality ↑ >100%) vs. AVP-R (minimal ↑).  
3. **Imaging**: MRI sella/suprasellar region for AVP-D.  
4. **Biomarkers**: Plasma copeptin (stable surrogate for AVP), hypertonic saline infusion test.  
5. **Rule out mimics**: Primary polydipsia, osmotic diuresis, glucosuria.

paragraphs.title: Arginine Vasopressin Disorder (Diabetes Insipidus)
paragraphs.name: [91] Arginine Vasopressin Disorder (Diabetes Insipidus) — Differential Diagnosis
paragraphs.text:
Arginine Vasopressin Disorder (Diabetes Insipidus) — Differential Diagnosis
- Primary polydipsia  
- Glucosuria (uncontrolled diabetes mellitus)  
- Osmotic diuresis (mannitol, IV fluids, high-protein diet)  
- Ureteral obstruction, irritable bladder syndrome  
- Nocturia causes: Prostate hypertrophy, nocturnal fluid intake

paragraphs.title: Arginine Vasopressin Disorder (Diabetes Insipidus)
paragraphs.name: [92] Arginine Vasopressin Disorder (Diabetes Insipidus) — Management / Treatment
paragraphs.text:
Arginine Vasopressin Disorder (Diabetes Insipidus) — Management / Treatment
### AVP-D  
- **DDAVP**: First-line (intranasal/oral/subcutaneous). Monitor for hyponatremia.  
- Adjuncts: Low-solute diet, thiazide diuretics, chlorpropamide, carbamazepine, NSAIDs.  

### AVP-R  
- Treat underlying cause (e.g., discontinue lithium, correct hypercalcemia).  
- Low-solute diet, thiazides, NSAIDs, DDAVP (limited efficacy).  

### Gestational AVP-D  
- DDAVP use; resolves postpartum.

paragraphs.title: Arginine Vasopressin Disorder (Diabetes Insipidus)
paragraphs.name: [93] Arginine Vasopressin Disorder (Diabetes Insipidus) — Complications
paragraphs.text:
Arginine Vasopressin Disorder (Diabetes Insipidus) — Complications
- Chronic dehydration, tachycardia, hypotension, weight loss, fatigue, headaches.  
- Kidney damage, brain injury (severe hyponatremia/hypernatremia).

paragraphs.title: Arginine Vasopressin Disorder (Diabetes Insipidus)
paragraphs.name: [94] Arginine Vasopressin Disorder (Diabetes Insipidus) — Prognosis
paragraphs.text:
Arginine Vasopressin Disorder (Diabetes Insipidus) — Prognosis
- **AVP-D**: Depends on etiology (e.g., poor in Wolfram syndrome).  
- **AVP-R**: Excellent if reversible cause (e.g., lithium cessation).  
- **Gestational AVP-D**: Good prognosis with hydration.  
- Mortality risk in adipsic DI or untreated severe cases.

paragraphs.title: Arginine Vasopressin Disorder (Diabetes Insipidus)
paragraphs.name: [95] Arginine Vasopressin Disorder (Diabetes Insipidus) — Prevention / Patient Education
paragraphs.text:
Arginine Vasopressin Disorder (Diabetes Insipidus) — Prevention / Patient Education
- Medication adherence (e.g., DDAVP, thiazides).  
- Low-salt/protein diet.  
- Monitor hydration status; carry water.  
- Avoid triggers (e.g., excessive NSAIDs, heat exposure).  
- Education on recognizing dehydration (dizziness, confusion).

paragraphs.title: Arginine Vasopressin Disorder (Diabetes Insipidus)
paragraphs.name: [96] Arginine Vasopressin Disorder (Diabetes Insipidus) — Interprofessional Considerations
paragraphs.text:
Arginine Vasopressin Disorder (Diabetes Insipidus) — Interprofessional Considerations
- **Team**: Endocrinologists, neurosurgeons (for pituitary tumors), nurses (hydration monitoring), pharmacists (medication review, lithium risks), primary care.  
- Coordinated care for hydration management, electrolyte monitoring, and comorbidities.

paragraphs.title: Dysmenorrhea
paragraphs.name: [97] Dysmenorrhea — Definition / Overview
paragraphs.text:
Dysmenorrhea — Definition / Overview
- Dysmenorrhea is defined as pain during the menstrual cycle, typically located in the lower abdomen and potentially radiating to the inner thighs and back.
- It is a common gynecologic problem that can negatively impact quality of life, with treatment options available to reduce associated morbidity.

paragraphs.title: Dysmenorrhea
paragraphs.name: [98] Dysmenorrhea — Epidemiology
paragraphs.text:
Dysmenorrhea — Epidemiology
- Prevalence ranges from 16% to 91% in individuals of reproductive age, with severe pain observed in 2% to 29%.
- Agarwal et al. reported an 80% prevalence in adolescents, with 40% experiencing severe symptoms.
- Associated with significant absenteeism (12% of monthly school/work activities) and economic impact (estimated 140 million lost working hours annually in the U.S.).

paragraphs.title: Dysmenorrhea
paragraphs.name: [99] Dysmenorrhea — Etiology / Causes
paragraphs.text:
Dysmenorrhea — Etiology / Causes
### Primary Dysmenorrhea
- Linked to prostaglandin (PG) hypersecretion.
- Risk factors: age <30 years, smoking, attempts to lose weight, abnormal BMI, depression/anxiety, longer menstrual cycles, younger age at menarche, nulliparity, history of sexual assault, uterine niche (post-C-section), heavy menstrual flow, family history of dysmenorrhea, disrupted social networks.

### Secondary Dysmenorrhea
- Associated with underlying pathology: endometriosis, large cesarean scar niche, fibroids, adenomyosis, endometrial polyps, interstitial cystitis, pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), intrauterine contraceptive systems.

paragraphs.title: Dysmenorrhea
paragraphs.name: [100] Dysmenorrhea — Pathophysiology
paragraphs.text:
Dysmenorrhea — Pathophysiology
- **Primary Dysmenorrhea**: Prostaglandins (PGF2α, PGE2) from endometrial tissue increase uterine contractions, causing tissue hypoxia and ischemia. Elevated COX-2 expression during menstruation drives PG production. Vasopressin and leukotrienes (C4, D4) may also contribute to contractions.
- **Secondary Dysmenorrhea**: Caused by structural abnormalities (e.g., endometriosis, adenomyosis) or infections (e.g., PID).

paragraphs.title: Dysmenorrhea
paragraphs.name: [101] Dysmenorrhea — Clinical Presentation
paragraphs.text:
Dysmenorrhea — Clinical Presentation
### Primary Dysmenorrhea
- Cyclic, crampy midline pelvic pain starting 2 years post-menarche or with ovulatory cycles.
- Pain begins within hours of menses, peaks 23–48 hours later, resolves within 72 hours.
- Associated symptoms: nausea, vomiting, headaches, dizziness, fatigue, sleep difficulties.

### Secondary Dysmenorrhea
- Pain may occur at any reproductive age, potentially with dyspareunia, menorrhagia, intermenstrual bleeding, or postcoital bleeding.
- Onset not strictly tied to menstrual cycle.

paragraphs.title: Dysmenorrhea
paragraphs.name: [102] Dysmenorrhea — Evaluation / Diagnosis
paragraphs.text:
Dysmenorrhea — Evaluation / Diagnosis
- **History/Physical**: Assess pain location, timing, characteristics, and associated symptoms. Pelvic exam indicated if secondary dysmenorrhea suspected or poor response to treatment.
- **Imaging**: Ultrasound as initial evaluation for secondary causes (endometriosis, fibroids, adenomyosis). MRI/Doppler if inconclusive.
- **Labs**: STI testing if PID suspected; cervical cytology/HPV testing if malignancy suspected.
- **Special Cases**: Laparoscopy for suspected endometriosis in fertility-desiring patients.

paragraphs.title: Dysmenorrhea
paragraphs.name: [103] Dysmenorrhea — Differential Diagnosis
paragraphs.text:
Dysmenorrhea — Differential Diagnosis
### Gynecological
- Endometriosis, obstructive reproductive tract anomalies (imperforate hymen, OHVIRA syndrome), adnexal cysts/torsion, adenomyosis, PID, endometrial polyps, Asherman syndrome, ectopic pregnancy, membranous dysmenorrhea.

### Non-Gynecological
- Irritable bowel syndrome, urinary tract infections, interstitial cystitis, musculoskeletal causes (abdominal wall muscles, sacroiliac joints).

paragraphs.title: Dysmenorrhea
paragraphs.name: [104] Dysmenorrhea — Management / Treatment
paragraphs.text:
Dysmenorrhea — Management / Treatment
### Nonpharmacological
- Heat application (as effective as NSAIDs), regular exercise, balanced diet rich in vitamins/minerals.
- Acupuncture/transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (limited evidence), behavioral counseling.
- Avoid spinal manipulation (no proven benefit).

### Pharmacological
- **First-line**: NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen, fenamates like mefenamic acid) scheduled before menses.
- **Alternatives**: Acetaminophen (with pamabrom/caffeine), combined hormonal contraceptives (pills, patches, rings), progestin-only methods (for endometriosis-related secondary dysmenorrhea).
- **Second-line**: GnRH agonists/antagonists (e.g., leuprolide, elagolix), vasodilators (sildenafil), calcium channel blockers (nifedipine), antispasmodics (hyoscine butylbromide), magnesium (adjunct).

### Surgical
- Laparoscopy for endometriosis resection; endometrial ablation or hysterectomy for refractory cases. Uterine nerve transection not routinely recommended.

paragraphs.title: Dysmenorrhea
paragraphs.name: [105] Dysmenorrhea — Complications
paragraphs.text:
Dysmenorrhea — Complications
- **Primary**: No direct complications but impacts daily activities and quality of life.
- **Secondary**: Infertility, pelvic organ prolapse, heavy bleeding, anemia (depending on etiology).

paragraphs.title: Dysmenorrhea
paragraphs.name: [106] Dysmenorrhea — Prognosis
paragraphs.text:
Dysmenorrhea — Prognosis
- **Primary**: Generally good with NSAIDs; severe cases may require combination therapy.
- **Secondary**: Depends on underlying cause and treatment response. Reassessment recommended after 3–6 months of treatment.

paragraphs.title: Dysmenorrhea
paragraphs.name: [107] Dysmenorrhea — Prevention / Patient Education
paragraphs.text:
Dysmenorrhea — Prevention / Patient Education
- Encourage balanced nutrition, regular exercise, and heat therapy.
- Educate on tracking symptoms and following up for uncontrolled symptoms.
- Highlight dietary factors (e.g., dairy intake, vitamins) linked to reduced pain severity.

paragraphs.title: Dysmenorrhea
paragraphs.name: [108] Dysmenorrhea — Interprofessional Considerations
paragraphs.text:
Dysmenorrhea — Interprofessional Considerations
- Multidisciplinary approach involving physicians, nurses, pharmacists, pelvic physical therapists, and other specialists.
- Prioritize patient-centered, evidence-based care with clear communication among team members to optimize outcomes and address unique patient needs.

paragraphs.title: Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
paragraphs.name: [109] Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD) — Definition / Overview
paragraphs.text:
Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD) — Definition / Overview
- GERD is a condition characterized by retrograde flow of gastric contents into the esophagus or beyond (e.g., oral cavity, larynx, lungs), resulting in esophagitis and inflammation of affected mucosal surfaces.
- Defined by the American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) as chronic symptoms or mucosal damage due to abnormal reflux of gastric contents.
- Classifications include nonerosive reflux disease (NERD) and erosive reflux disease.

paragraphs.title: Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
paragraphs.name: [110] Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD) — Epidemiology
paragraphs.text:
Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD) — Epidemiology
- Western countries: Prevalence 10–20%, with severe disease in 6%.
- Asian countries: Prevalence ~5%.
- Equal prevalence between men and women; Barrett esophagus more common in men (3:1 ratio).
- Increasing prevalence with age (peak incidence in individuals aged 60–70).
- Pediatric population: Incidence 12–50% in children aged 0–18 (2000–2005); universal in preterm infants.
- Pregnancy: Affects 20–30% in first trimester, 40–45% in second, and 60% in third trimester.

paragraphs.title: Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
paragraphs.name: [111] Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD) — Etiology / Causes
paragraphs.text:
Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD) — Etiology / Causes
- **Anatomical/Physiological Defects**:
  - Transient lower esophageal sphincter (LES) relaxation or low resting LES pressure.
  - Hiatus hernia.
  - Increased intra-abdominal pressure (e.g., obesity, pregnancy, ascites).
  - Impaired esophageal motility.
  - Impaired saliva production or esophageal mucosal defense.
- **Risk Factors**:
  - Male sex, white ethnicity.
  - Age ≥50, BMI >30, smoking, alcohol.
  - Dietary factors (fatty, spicy, acidic foods).
  - Medications (nitrates, calcium channel blockers, anticholinergics).
  - Delayed gastric emptying, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH).
  - Anxiety/depression (bidirectional relationship).

paragraphs.title: Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
paragraphs.name: [112] Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD) — Pathophysiology
paragraphs.text:
Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD) — Pathophysiology
- **Key Mechanisms**:
  - Transient LES relaxation (TRLES): Primary mechanism for reflux in healthy individuals and GERD.
  - Hiatal hernia: Disrupts LES-diaphragm relationship and acts as a gastric contents reservoir.
  - Increased intra-abdominal fat: Raises gastroesophageal pressure gradient and TRLES frequency.
  - Impaired esophageal defense: Reduced acid clearance (motility/saliva) and mucosal barrier dysfunction.
- **Inflammatory Pathways**:
  - Cytokine-mediated inflammation via hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF)-2α and nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer (NF-κB).
  - Pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., TNF-α, IL-6) and T-cell infiltration contribute to mucosal damage.

paragraphs.title: Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
paragraphs.name: [113] Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD) — Clinical Presentation
paragraphs.text:
Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD) — Clinical Presentation
- **Typical Symptoms**:
  - Heartburn (burning sensation behind sternum, post-prandial, exacerbated by exercise/recumbency).
  - Regurgitation (sour/burning fluid in throat/mouth).
  - Noncardiac chest pain.
- **Atypical Symptoms**:
  - Chronic cough, asthma, dysphonia, laryngitis, sinusitis, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.
  - Dysphagia (30% with peptic strictures/Schatzki rings).
- **Alarm Symptoms**:
  - Dysphagia, odynophagia, weight loss, anemia, hematemesis/melena.

paragraphs.title: Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
paragraphs.name: [114] Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD) — Evaluation / Diagnosis
paragraphs.text:
Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD) — Evaluation / Diagnosis
- **Initial Approach**:
  - Empiric PPI trial (8–12 weeks) for typical symptoms without alarm features.
  - Alarm symptoms necessitate endoscopy (EGD) and/or pH monitoring.
- **Diagnostic Tools**:
  - **PPI Trial**: Symptom response supports GERD diagnosis.
  - **Endoscopy (EGD)**: Los Angeles classification for esophagitis severity (A–D).
  - **Ambulatory pH Monitoring**:
    - Wireless (48–96-hour) or transnasal (24-hour) pH testing.
    - pH-impedance for nonacid reflux assessment.
  - **Manometry**: Preoperative assessment for motility disorders (e.g., achalasia).
- **Imaging**: Barium studies limited to detecting strictures/hernias; no role in uncomplicated GERD.

paragraphs.title: Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
paragraphs.name: [115] Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD) — Differential Diagnosis
paragraphs.text:
Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD) — Differential Diagnosis
- Coronary artery disease, infectious esophagitis, eosinophilic esophagitis, radiation/chemotherapy-induced esophagitis.
- Esophageal motility disorders (e.g., achalasia, diffuse spasm), benign strictures.
- Peptic ulcer disease, nonulcer dyspepsia, gastroparesis, gastric cancer.
- Rumination, biliary colic.

paragraphs.title: Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
paragraphs.name: [116] Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD) — Management / Treatment
paragraphs.text:
Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD) — Management / Treatment
- **Lifestyle Modifications**:
  - Weight loss (even modest amounts improve symptoms).
  - Elevate bed head, avoid meals 2–3 hours before bedtime.
  - Avoid trigger foods (chocolate, caffeine, alcohol, spicy foods), smoking.
- **Pharmacological Therapy**:
  - **PPIs**: First-line (omeprazole, lansoprazole, etc.); standard/high doses (see Table for comparison).
  - **H2RAs**: Famotidine/cimetidine (ranitidine/nizatidine withdrawn due to NDMA).
  - **P-CABs**: Vonoprazan (potassium-competitive acid blocker; second-line for refractory cases).
  - Adjuncts: Baclofen (reduces TRLES), sucralfate (pregnancy).
- **Endoscopic/Surgical Options**:
  - **Stretta**: Radiofrequency ablation for refractory GERD (LA A/B, no large hernia).
  - **Magnetic Sphincter Augmentation**: titanium ring placement around LES.
  - **Transoral Incisionless Fundoplication (TIF)**: For mild/moderate refractory cases.
  - **Surgical**: Laparoscopic Nissen fundoplication, gastric bypass (obese patients).

paragraphs.title: Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
paragraphs.name: [117] Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD) — Complications
paragraphs.text:
Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD) — Complications
- **Esophageal**:
  - Severe esophagitis (LA C/D), peptic strictures, dysphagia.
  - Barrett esophagus (5–15% of reflux patients; progresses to adenocarcinoma in 5%).
- **Extraesophageal**:
  - Laryngitis, chronic cough, asthma, sinusitis, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.
  - Dental erosions.
- **Systemic**: Iron deficiency anemia, upper GI bleeding.

paragraphs.title: Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
paragraphs.name: [118] Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD) — Prognosis
paragraphs.text:
Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD) — Prognosis
- Most patients respond to medications but often require long-term maintenance.
- Relapse common after discontinuation of therapy.
- Surgical outcomes excellent in uncomplicated cases; morbidity higher in complex medical histories.
- Barrett esophagus increases adenocarcinoma risk (8-fold higher in men).

paragraphs.title: Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
paragraphs.name: [119] Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD) — Prevention / Patient Education
paragraphs.text:
Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD) — Prevention / Patient Education
- Lifestyle modifications (weight management, dietary adjustments, sleep hygiene).
- Avoid known triggers (alcohol, caffeine, spicy foods).
- Regular follow-up for high-risk patients (Barrett esophagus, severe esophagitis).

paragraphs.title: Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
paragraphs.name: [120] Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD) — Interprofessional Considerations
paragraphs.text:
Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD) — Interprofessional Considerations
- Collaboration between primary care clinicians and gastroenterologists improves outcomes.
- Multidisciplinary approach for refractory cases (e.g., surgery, nutrition, psychology).
