paragraphs.title: Gout
paragraphs.name: [121] Gout — Definition / Overview
paragraphs.text:
Gout — Definition / Overview
- Gout is one of the most common causes of chronic inflammatory arthritis in the United States, characterized by deposition of monosodium urate (MSU) monohydrate crystals in joints and periarticular tissues.  
- Historically termed the "disease of kings and king of diseases," it is defined by MSU crystal formation due to hyperuricemia (serum uric acid >6.8 mg/dL/400 µmol/L).  
- First described by Hippocrates, it is a well-studied and manageable rheumatic disease.

paragraphs.title: Gout
paragraphs.name: [122] Gout — Epidemiology
paragraphs.text:
Gout — Epidemiology
- Prevalence: 1–4% globally; 3–6% in men vs. 1–2% in women in Western nations.  
- Rising incidence over recent decades, peaking in older adults but plateauing after age 70.  
- Higher prevalence in African American individuals (OR 1.81 in women, OR 1.26 in men) compared to White Americans.  
- Associated with comorbidities like obesity, hypertension, CKD, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease.

paragraphs.title: Gout
paragraphs.name: [123] Gout — Etiology / Causes
paragraphs.text:
Gout — Etiology / Causes
- Multifactorial: genetic predisposition (heritability of hyperuricemia ~73%), medical comorbidities (e.g., OSA, CKD), and dietary factors (high-purine foods, alcohol, fructose-rich beverages).  
- Genetic defects linked to hyperuricemia (e.g., HGPRT deficiency, PRPP synthetase overactivity).  
- Evolutionary loss of uricase gene in humans, leading to hyperuricemia.  
- Risk factors: diuretics, obesity, Mediterranean diet, sleep apnea, metabolic syndrome.

paragraphs.title: Gout
paragraphs.name: [124] Gout — Pathophysiology
paragraphs.text:
Gout — Pathophysiology
- **Purine Metabolism**: Humans lack uricase, leading to uric acid accumulation. Xanthine oxidase converts xanthine to uric acid.  
- **Hyperuricemia**: Results from overproduction (e.g., tumor lysis, psoriasis) or underexcretion (renal dysfunction).  
- **Crystal Formation**: MSU crystals form in joints (e.g., first MTP joint) due to supersaturation, low temperature, pH changes, and local cation concentrations.  
- **Inflammatory Response**: MSU crystals activate NLRP3 inflammasome → IL-1β release, neutrophil recruitment, and cytokine cascade (TNF-α, IL-6).  
- **Chronic Stage**: Tophi develop as granulomatous deposits, causing joint erosion via osteoclast activation and cartilage degradation.

paragraphs.title: Gout
paragraphs.name: [125] Gout — Clinical Presentation
paragraphs.text:
Gout — Clinical Presentation
- **Acute Gout Flare**: Sudden, severe monoarticular pain (85–90% in lower extremities; 50% first MTP joint), erythema, swelling, and warmth. May mimic cellulitis or septic arthritis.  
- **Chronic Tophaceous Gout**: Subcutaneous tophi (chalk-like nodules) in ears, fingers, knees, and Achilles tendon.  
- **Systemic Symptoms**: Fever, leukocytosis, and malaise during flares.  
- **Atypical Presentations**: Polyarticular involvement (3–14% initial attacks), axial joint involvement (rare), and finger pad tophi in postmenopausal women.

paragraphs.title: Gout
paragraphs.name: [126] Gout — Evaluation / Diagnosis
paragraphs.text:
Gout — Evaluation / Diagnosis
- **Synovial Fluid Analysis**: Gold standard. MSU crystals (needle-shaped, negatively birefringent under polarized light) detected in 100% of tophi and during intercritical periods.  
- **Laboratory Findings**: Elevated WBC, ESR, CRP during flares; serum urate levels may be normal or low during acute attacks.  
- **Imaging**: Ultrasound (double contour sign on cartilage; sensitivity 83%, specificity 76%), dual-energy CT (sensitivity 87%, specificity 84%) for MSU deposits.  
- **Diagnostic Criteria**: ACR/EULAR 2015 criteria (sensitivity 92%, specificity 89%).

paragraphs.title: Gout
paragraphs.name: [127] Gout — Differential Diagnosis
paragraphs.text:
Gout — Differential Diagnosis
- **Acute Flare**: Calcium pyrophosphate crystal deposition (pseudogout), septic arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, osteoarthritis, cellulitis, trauma.  
- **Tophaceous Gout**: Dactylitis, rheumatoid arthritis, osteomyelitis.

paragraphs.title: Gout
paragraphs.name: [128] Gout — Management / Treatment
paragraphs.text:
Gout — Management / Treatment
### Acute Flare
- **NSAIDs**: Indomethacin (50 mg TID), naproxen (500 mg BID), ibuprofen (800 mg TID). Avoid in CKD (CrCl <60 mL/min) or PUD.  
- **Colchicine**: Low-dose (1.8 mg day 1, then 0.6 mg daily); avoid IV due to toxicity.  
- **Corticosteroids**: Prednisolone 30–40 mg/day for 5–10 days; intra-articular for monoarticular flares.  
- **IL-1 Inhibitors**: Anakinra (100 mg SC daily × 3 days) or canakinumab (150 mg SC) for refractory cases.

### Prophylaxis
- **Colchicine**: 0.6 mg daily for 3–6 months when initiating urate-lowering therapy (ULT).  
- **Avoid**: Azathioprine, cyclosporine with colchicine due to toxicity risk.

### Urate-Lowering Therapy (ULT)
- **Xanthine Oxidase Inhibitors (XOIs)**:  
  - **Allopurinol**: Start 100 mg/day (50 mg/day in CKD); titrate to target serum urate <6 mg/dL. Avoid in HLA-B*5801 carriers (test in high-risk populations).  
  - **Febuxostat**: 40–80 mg/day; alternative for allopurinol intolerance. Monitor CV risk (CARES trial suggests increased mortality).  
- **Uricosurics**: Probenecid (250 mg BID–1000 mg TID); contraindicated in CKD (CrCl <60 mL/min) and nephrolithiasis.  
- **Pegloticase**: IV every 2 weeks for refractory gout; contraindicated in G6PD deficiency.  

### Lifestyle Modifications
- **Diet**: DASH diet, low purine intake (avoid seafood, red meat), limit alcohol/fructose.  
- **Weight Loss**: 5–10% reduction lowers serum urate.  
- **Vitamin C**: ≥500 mg/day reduces urate levels.

paragraphs.title: Gout
paragraphs.name: [129] Gout — Complications
paragraphs.text:
Gout — Complications
- **Skeletal**: Tophi, joint deformity, bone loss.  
- **Urological**: Urate nephropathy, nephrolithiasis.  
- **Ocular**: Conjunctivitis, uveitis, scleritis.  
- **Cardiovascular**: Increased risk of MI, stroke, and cardiovascular mortality (HR 1.86, 1.552, respectively).

paragraphs.title: Gout
paragraphs.name: [130] Gout — Prognosis
paragraphs.text:
Gout — Prognosis
- Varies with comorbidities. Early-onset flares correlate with severe disease.  
- Untreated gout leads to recurrent flares, tophi, and joint destruction.  
- OSA linked to hyperuricemia but not an independent cause of gout.

paragraphs.title: Gout
paragraphs.name: [131] Gout — Prevention / Patient Education
paragraphs.text:
Gout — Prevention / Patient Education
- Educate on weight loss, dietary modifications (avoid high-purine foods/liquids), and adherence to ULT/prophylaxis.  
- Regular serum urate monitoring and flare management plans.

paragraphs.title: Gout
paragraphs.name: [132] Gout — Interprofessional Considerations
paragraphs.text:
Gout — Interprofessional Considerations
- Collaborative care involving rheumatologists, primary care providers, pharmacists, and dietitians.  
- Pharmacists ensure medication safety (e.g., HLA testing for allopurinol, drug interactions).  
- Dietitians guide dietary changes; nurses assist in patient education and monitoring.  
- Referral to specialists for refractory cases, unclear diagnosis, or renal impairment.

paragraphs.title: Human Papillomavirus (HPV)
paragraphs.name: [133] Human Papillomavirus (HPV) — Definition / Overview
paragraphs.text:
Human Papillomavirus (HPV) — Definition / Overview
- Human papillomavirus (HPV) is a non-enveloped, double-stranded, circular DNA virus causing epithelial lesions (e.g., cutaneous and anogenital warts) and cancers. Subtypes vary in oncogenic potential, with high-risk types (e.g., 16, 18) linked to malignancies.

paragraphs.title: Human Papillomavirus (HPV)
paragraphs.name: [134] Human Papillomavirus (HPV) — Epidemiology
paragraphs.text:
Human Papillomavirus (HPV) — Epidemiology
- Over 180 HPV subtypes exist, with tropism for specific body sites:
  - **Cutaneous warts**: Subtypes 1, 2, 4, 27, 57 (hands, feet).
  - **Anogenital warts**: Subtypes 6, 11 (low-risk); subtypes 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, 58 (high-risk, linked to cervical/anogenital/oropharyngeal cancers).
- **CDC data**: Genital HPV prevalence ~45.2% (men) and ~39.9% (women) aged 18–59.
- Transmission: Skin-to-skin contact, sexual transmission, fomites.

paragraphs.title: Human Papillomavirus (HPV)
paragraphs.name: [135] Human Papillomavirus (HPV) — Etiology / Causes
paragraphs.text:
Human Papillomavirus (HPV) — Etiology / Causes
- **Virus characteristics**: Papillomaviridae family; enters via skin/mucosal disruption, infects basal stem cells.
- **Genome**: Early (E1–E7) and late (L1, L2) genes. E6/E7 oncoproteins drive carcinogenesis.
- **Risk factors**: 
  - Sexual activity, early initiation, multiple partners.
  - Smoking, oral contraceptives (>5 years), betel nut use, radiation/UV exposure.

paragraphs.title: Human Papillomavirus (HPV)
paragraphs.name: [136] Human Papillomavirus (HPV) — Pathophysiology
paragraphs.text:
Human Papillomavirus (HPV) — Pathophysiology
- **E6/E7 proteins**: Inactivate tumor suppressors p53 and pRb, disrupting cell cycle regulation.
- **Viral lifecycle**: Remains as episome initially; integrates into host DNA at fragile sites.
- **Histopathology**: Hyperkeratosis, papillomatosis, parakeratosis; thrombosed capillaries, elongated rete ridges.

paragraphs.title: Human Papillomavirus (HPV)
paragraphs.name: [137] Human Papillomavirus (HPV) — Clinical Presentation
paragraphs.text:
Human Papillomavirus (HPV) — Clinical Presentation
- **Lesions**: 
  - Cutaneous (verruca vulgaris/plantaris), anogenital (condyloma acuminatum), oropharyngeal.
  - Latent infections may require DNA testing for detection.
- **High-risk subtypes**: Linked to cervical, anal, oropharyngeal cancers and precancerous lesions (e.g., cervical dysplasia).

paragraphs.title: Human Papillomavirus (HPV)
paragraphs.name: [138] Human Papillomavirus (HPV) — Evaluation / Diagnosis
paragraphs.text:
Human Papillomavirus (HPV) — Evaluation / Diagnosis
- **History**: 
  - Cutaneous warts: Hygiene, infectious contacts, pain/bleeding.
  - Anogenital warts: Sexual history, immunocompromise, prior treatment/vaccination.
  - Cervical dysplasia: Menstrual history, Pap smear results, symptoms (bleeding, pain).
- **Physical exam**: 
  - Cutaneous: Hands/feet inspection (palms, soles, interdigital spaces).
  - Anogenital: Speculum/vaginal/anal exam; oropharyngeal exam if indicated.
- **Tests**: 
  - Pap smear (cervical/anal), HPV DNA testing, colposcopy (acetowhite lesions biopsied).
  - Histopathology for excised lesions.

paragraphs.title: Human Papillomavirus (HPV)
paragraphs.name: [139] Human Papillomavirus (HPV) — Differential Diagnosis
paragraphs.text:
Human Papillomavirus (HPV) — Differential Diagnosis
- Corns & calluses, acrochordon, condyloma latum, keratoacanthoma, psoriasis, seborrhea, chancroid, herpes simplex, molluscum contagiosum.

paragraphs.title: Human Papillomavirus (HPV)
paragraphs.name: [140] Human Papillomavirus (HPV) — Management / Treatment
paragraphs.text:
Human Papillomavirus (HPV) — Management / Treatment
- **Cutaneous warts**: 
  - Cryotherapy, surgical removal, immunomodulators (e.g., imiquimod), laser ablation.
- **Anogenital warts**: Similar to cutaneous; consider patient immunocompetence.
- **Cervical dysplasia**:
  - Low-grade/immunocompetent: Monitoring (Pap/HPV testing, colposcopy).
  - High-grade/persistent: Cryotherapy, LEEP, cold knife cone excision.
- **Cancer**: Resection, chemotherapy, radiation.
- **Vaccination**: 9-valent vaccine (subtypes 6,11,16,18,31,33,45,52,58); recommended ages 9–12, females ≤26, males ≤21.

paragraphs.title: Human Papillomavirus (HPV)
paragraphs.name: [141] Human Papillomavirus (HPV) — Complications
paragraphs.text:
Human Papillomavirus (HPV) — Complications
- Poor cosmesis, depression, urethral obstruction, ulceration/infection of condylomata, progression to malignancy, transmission to others, co-infection with other STIs (5–20% risk).

paragraphs.title: Human Papillomavirus (HPV)
paragraphs.name: [142] Human Papillomavirus (HPV) — Prognosis
paragraphs.text:
Human Papillomavirus (HPV) — Prognosis
- Recurrences common; ~60% genital warts resolve spontaneously. 
- Risk of cervical, anal, head/neck cancers, especially in immunocompromised individuals.

paragraphs.title: Human Papillomavirus (HPV)
paragraphs.name: [143] Human Papillomavirus (HPV) — Prevention / Patient Education
paragraphs.text:
Human Papillomavirus (HPV) — Prevention / Patient Education
- HPV vaccination (preferrably pre-sexual activity).
- Safe sex practices (condoms, limited partners), smoking cessation.
- Regular Pap smears and HPV testing for cervical cancer screening.
- Avoid betel nut, UV/radiation exposure.

paragraphs.title: Human Papillomavirus (HPV)
paragraphs.name: [144] Human Papillomavirus (HPV) — Interprofessional Considerations
paragraphs.text:
Human Papillomavirus (HPV) — Interprofessional Considerations
- **Team roles**: 
  - **Infectious disease**: Immunocompromised patients.
  - **ENT**: Oropharyngeal papillomas.
  - **Urology**: Urethral/penile lesions.
  - **Colorectal surgery**: Anal disease.
  - **Dermatology**: Warts/epidermodysplasia verruciformis.
- **Education**: Nurses/pharmacists counsel on vaccination, safe sex, treatment options, and STI screening. Primary care providers emphasize Pap screening and risk reduction.

paragraphs.title: Inflammatory Bowel Disease
paragraphs.name: [145] Inflammatory Bowel Disease — Definition / Overview
paragraphs.text:
Inflammatory Bowel Disease — Definition / Overview
- Chronic inflammatory disease of the gastrointestinal (GI) tract, divided into Crohn disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC).  
- Characterized by repetitive episodes of inflammation due to an abnormal immune response to gut microflora.  
- UC involves diffuse mucosal inflammation of the colon, often starting in the rectum and extending proximally.  
- CD causes transmural ulceration of any GI segment, with skip lesions and possible fistulas/strictures.

paragraphs.title: Inflammatory Bowel Disease
paragraphs.name: [146] Inflammatory Bowel Disease — Epidemiology
paragraphs.text:
Inflammatory Bowel Disease — Epidemiology
- **Incidence (North America):**  
  - UC: 2.2–19.2/100,000 person-years.  
  - CD: 3.1–20.2/100,000 person-years.  
- **Prevalence (US adults):**  
  - UC: 238/100,000.  
  - CD: 201/100,000.  
- More prevalent in North America/Europe vs. Asia/Africa.  
- Bimodal age distribution: 15–30 years (75%) and 10–15% after age 60.  
- CD slightly more common in females; UC equal gender distribution.

paragraphs.title: Inflammatory Bowel Disease
paragraphs.name: [147] Inflammatory Bowel Disease — Etiology / Causes
paragraphs.text:
Inflammatory Bowel Disease — Etiology / Causes
- Genetic susceptibility combined with exaggerated immune response to intestinal flora.  
- **Crohn disease:** Strong link to tobacco use.  
- **Ulcerative colitis:** Smoking may be protective.  
- Diet role debated; *CARD15* gene associated with CD (not UC).

paragraphs.title: Inflammatory Bowel Disease
paragraphs.name: [148] Inflammatory Bowel Disease — Pathophysiology
paragraphs.text:
Inflammatory Bowel Disease — Pathophysiology
- Defective intestinal epithelial barrier (primary failure or inflammation-induced).  
- Impaired mucus production and antimicrobial peptide secretion (e.g., alpha-defensins).  
- Dysregulated inflammation: Elevated TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-23-TH17 pathway cytokines.  
- **UC:** Mucosal inflammation (edema, ulcers, bleeding), continuous from rectum, "lead-pipe" colon in chronic cases.  
- **CD:** Transmural inflammation, skip lesions, cobblestone mucosa, granulomas possible.  
- Extraintestinal manifestations (e.g., arthritis, primary sclerosing cholangitis).

paragraphs.title: Inflammatory Bowel Disease
paragraphs.name: [149] Inflammatory Bowel Disease — Clinical Presentation
paragraphs.text:
Inflammatory Bowel Disease — Clinical Presentation
- **UC:**  
  - Bloody diarrhea (with/without mucus), tenesmus, abdominal pain (left-sided).  
  - Constipation possible in rectal disease.  
- **CD:**  
  - Right lower quadrant pain, non-bloody diarrhea, weight loss, fever.  
  - Fistulas (e.g., rectovaginal), abscesses, growth retardation in children.  
- **Physical exam:** Tachycardia, fever, dehydration, abdominal tenderness. Toxic megacolon: distension, guarding, rebound tenderness.

paragraphs.title: Inflammatory Bowel Disease
paragraphs.name: [150] Inflammatory Bowel Disease — Evaluation / Diagnosis
paragraphs.text:
Inflammatory Bowel Disease — Evaluation / Diagnosis
- **Laboratory tests:**  
  - CBC (anemia, leukocytosis), ESR, hs-CRP, albumin.  
  - Fecal calprotectin/lactoferrin for inflammation.  
  - Serology: p-ANCA (UC), ASCA (CD).  
  - Stool studies: Rule out infection (*Giardia*, *C. difficile*, ova/parasites).  
- **Imaging:**  
  - X-ray: Free air, obstruction, toxic megacolon.  
  - Barium: "Lead pipe" colon (UC), skip lesions (CD).  
  - CT/MRI: Assess perforation, fistulas, strictures.  
- **Endoscopy:** Colonoscopy/EGD with biopsies (crypt abscesses in UC, granulomas in CD).

paragraphs.title: Inflammatory Bowel Disease
paragraphs.name: [151] Inflammatory Bowel Disease — Differential Diagnosis
paragraphs.text:
Inflammatory Bowel Disease — Differential Diagnosis
- Infectious colitis (*E. coli*, *C. difficile*), microscopic/lymphocytic/collagenous colitis.  
- Appendicitis, celiac disease, irritable bowel syndrome, functional abdominal pain.

paragraphs.title: Inflammatory Bowel Disease
paragraphs.name: [152] Inflammatory Bowel Disease — Management / Treatment
paragraphs.text:
Inflammatory Bowel Disease — Management / Treatment
- **Stepwise approach:**  
  1. Aminosalicylates (mesalamine) for mild UC/CD.  
  2. Corticosteroids (oral/systemic) for moderate disease.  
  3. Immunomodulators (anti-TNF agents, azathioprine, methotrexate) for steroid-refractory/severe disease.  
- **UC-specific:** Topical mesalamine for proctitis; colectomy for uncontrolled disease.  
- **CD-specific:** Budesonide for ileocecal disease; surgery for fistulas/strictures.  
- **General:** Bone density monitoring (steroid use: calcium/bisphosphonates).

paragraphs.title: Inflammatory Bowel Disease
paragraphs.name: [153] Inflammatory Bowel Disease — Complications
paragraphs.text:
Inflammatory Bowel Disease — Complications
- **Intestinal:** Hemorrhage, strictures, perforation, toxic megacolon, cholangiocarcinoma, colon cancer.  
- **Extraintestinal:** Osteoporosis, DVT, gallstones, primary sclerosing cholangitis, arthritis, pyoderma gangrenosum.

paragraphs.title: Inflammatory Bowel Disease
paragraphs.name: [154] Inflammatory Bowel Disease — Prognosis
paragraphs.text:
Inflammatory Bowel Disease — Prognosis
- Mortality 1.5–5× higher than general population.  
- Colon cancer risk: Cumulative 30% in UC pancolitis >30 years.  
- Psychological morbidity (depression, anxiety) common.

paragraphs.title: Inflammatory Bowel Disease
paragraphs.name: [155] Inflammatory Bowel Disease — Prevention / Patient Education
paragraphs.text:
Inflammatory Bowel Disease — Prevention / Patient Education
- No diet/supplement prevents symptoms.  
- Lifelong follow-up for disease monitoring and dysplasia surveillance.  
- Education improves compliance and quality of life.

paragraphs.title: Inflammatory Bowel Disease
paragraphs.name: [156] Inflammatory Bowel Disease — Interprofessional Considerations
paragraphs.text:
Inflammatory Bowel Disease — Interprofessional Considerations
- Interprofessional team essential for comprehensive care (gastroenterologists, surgeons, nurses, pharmacists).  
- Dedicated support lines and accessible provider networks for emergencies.  
- Early collaboration to prevent bowel damage and disability.  
- Address psychological health; monitor for depression/anxiety.

paragraphs.title: Metabolic Syndrome
paragraphs.name: [157] Metabolic Syndrome — Definition / Overview
paragraphs.text:
Metabolic Syndrome — Definition / Overview
- Metabolic syndrome is a cluster of metabolic abnormalities (central obesity, insulin resistance, hypertension, dyslipidemia) that increase the risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular diseases and type II diabetes mellitus. Diagnosis requires ≥3 of these abnormalities.

paragraphs.title: Metabolic Syndrome
paragraphs.name: [158] Metabolic Syndrome — Epidemiology
paragraphs.text:
Metabolic Syndrome — Epidemiology
- Prevalence: ~20% of Americans and Europeans affected.  
- Increased globally, paralleling rising obesity rates.  
- Higher prevalence in South Asian Americans despite lower obesity rates compared to non-Hispanic whites.  
- Affects 3% of children and 5% of adolescents globally, with higher rates in low-income countries.  
- Prevalence rises with age, peaking at ~40% in the 6th decade of life. Slightly more prevalent in women in some ethnic groups.

paragraphs.title: Metabolic Syndrome
paragraphs.name: [159] Metabolic Syndrome — Etiology / Causes
paragraphs.text:
Metabolic Syndrome — Etiology / Causes
- Multifactorial: genetic predisposition and environmental/lifestyle factors.  
- Key contributors: obesity, sedentary lifestyle, unhealthy diet, excessive calorie intake.  
- Fetal and early postnatal environmental factors (e.g., maternal lifestyle, intrauterine/postnatal nutrition) influence risk.

paragraphs.title: Metabolic Syndrome
paragraphs.name: [160] Metabolic Syndrome — Pathophysiology
paragraphs.text:
Metabolic Syndrome — Pathophysiology
- Central mechanism: visceral obesity → insulin resistance and chronic inflammation.  
- Insulin resistance impairs glucose metabolism, promotes fat deposition, and drives hypertension and dyslipidemia.  
- Adipose tissue releases pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., TNF-α, leptin, resistin) and free fatty acids, exacerbating insulin resistance and endothelial dysfunction.  
- Contributes to atherosclerosis, vascular stiffness, and thrombogenicity via elevated fibrinogen and PAI-1.

paragraphs.title: Metabolic Syndrome
paragraphs.name: [161] Metabolic Syndrome — Clinical Presentation
paragraphs.text:
Metabolic Syndrome — Clinical Presentation
- **Signs**: Abdominal obesity (elevated BMI/waist circumference), acanthosis nigricans, xanthomas.  
- **Symptoms**: Polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia (suggestive of diabetes). Hypertension may be asymptomatic.

paragraphs.title: Metabolic Syndrome
paragraphs.name: [162] Metabolic Syndrome — Evaluation / Diagnosis
paragraphs.text:
Metabolic Syndrome — Evaluation / Diagnosis
- **Diagnostic Criteria**:  
  - Waist circumference: >40 inches (men), >35 inches (women).  
  - Fasting triglycerides ≥150 mg/dL.  
  - HDL: <40 mg/dL (men), <50 mg/dL (women).  
  - Fasting glucose ≥100 mg/dL.  
  - Blood pressure: SBP ≥130 mmHg or DBP ≥85 mmHg.  
- **Laboratory Tests**: Lipid panel, fasting glucose/HbA1c, basic metabolic panel, C-reactive protein, LFTs, thyroid studies, uric acid.  
- **Imaging**: Coronary calcium score for ASCVD risk assessment; stress testing for symptomatic patients.

paragraphs.title: Metabolic Syndrome
paragraphs.name: [163] Metabolic Syndrome — Differential Diagnosis
paragraphs.text:
Metabolic Syndrome — Differential Diagnosis
- Hypothyroidism, polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS), pheochromocytoma, Cushing syndrome, acromegaly.  
- Secondary causes of hypertension/dyslipidemia (e.g., renal disease, coarctation of the aorta).

paragraphs.title: Metabolic Syndrome
paragraphs.name: [164] Metabolic Syndrome — Management / Treatment
paragraphs.text:
Metabolic Syndrome — Management / Treatment
- **Lifestyle Modifications**:  
  - 7–10% weight loss over 12 months; target BMI <25 kg/m².  
  - ≥150 minutes/week moderate-intensity or ≥70 minutes/week high-intensity exercise.  
  - Diet: Mediterranean-style (vegetables, fruits, whole grains, fish); avoid processed foods, saturated fats, sodium.  
  - Smoking cessation, limited alcohol, sleep hygiene.  
- **Pharmacologic Therapy**:  
  - Dyslipidemia: Statins or per guidelines.  
  - Hypertension: Antihypertensives tailored to comorbidities.  
  - Insulin resistance/diabetes: Metformin, DPP-4 inhibitors, GLP-1 agonists, pioglitazone.  
- **Surgical Management**: Bariatric surgery (e.g., gastric bypass) for BMI ≥40 kg/m² or ≥35 kg/m² with comorbidities.

paragraphs.title: Metabolic Syndrome
paragraphs.name: [165] Metabolic Syndrome — Complications
paragraphs.text:
Metabolic Syndrome — Complications
- Cardiovascular events (MI, stroke, heart failure) with 2-fold increased risk.  
- Type II diabetes mellitus (near-universal progression) with microvascular complications.  
- Obesity-related: obstructive sleep apnea, pulmonary hypertension, osteoarthritis.  
- Increased risk of malignancies (kidney, gallbladder, colon, prostate).

paragraphs.title: Metabolic Syndrome
paragraphs.name: [166] Metabolic Syndrome — Prognosis
paragraphs.text:
Metabolic Syndrome — Prognosis
- Poor prognosis driven by cardiovascular complications.  
- Recent advances in ASCVD management have improved outcomes.

paragraphs.title: Metabolic Syndrome
paragraphs.name: [167] Metabolic Syndrome — Prevention / Patient Education
paragraphs.text:
Metabolic Syndrome — Prevention / Patient Education
- Target BMI <25 kg/m².  
- Regular physical activity, Mediterranean diet, smoking cessation, alcohol moderation.  
- Sleep hygiene and treatment of sleep apnea.

paragraphs.title: Metabolic Syndrome
paragraphs.name: [168] Metabolic Syndrome — Interprofessional Considerations
paragraphs.text:
Metabolic Syndrome — Interprofessional Considerations
- Team includes cardiologist, endocrinologist, dietitian, physical therapist, pharmacist, neurologist, bariatric surgeon, nurse practitioner, social worker.  
- Emphasis on patient education, adherence monitoring, and coordinated care.

paragraphs.title: Onychomycosis
paragraphs.name: [169] Onychomycosis — Definition / Overview
paragraphs.text:
Onychomycosis — Definition / Overview
- Onychomycosis is a fungal infection of the nail unit. When caused by dermatophytes, it is termed *tinea unguium*. The term encompasses infections by dermatophytes, yeasts, and saprophytic molds. An abnormal nail not caused by fungal infection is classified as a dystrophic nail. Onychomycosis affects both fingernails and toenails, but toenail infections are more prevalent.

paragraphs.title: Onychomycosis
paragraphs.name: [170] Onychomycosis — Epidemiology
paragraphs.text:
Onychomycosis — Epidemiology
- Prevalence estimates range from 1% to 8%, with increasing incidence.  
- Key risk factors include aging, diabetes mellitus, tinea pedis, psoriasis, immunodeficiency, and familial history.  
- Genetic susceptibility follows an autosomal dominant pattern.  
- *Trichophyton rubrum* is the dominant causative organism in the United States due to international travel from Asia.

paragraphs.title: Onychomycosis
paragraphs.name: [171] Onychomycosis — Etiology / Causes
paragraphs.text:
Onychomycosis — Etiology / Causes
- **Dermatophytes**: *Trichophyton rubrum* (most frequent), *T. mentagrophytes*, *Epidermophyton floccosum* (account for 90% of toenail and 50% of fingernail infections).  
- **Yeasts**: *Candida albicans* (2% of cases, primarily fingernails).  
- **Nondermatophytic molds**: *Fusarium*, *Aspergillus*, *Acremonium*, *Scytalidium*, *Scopulariopsis brevicaulis* (≈8% of infections).

paragraphs.title: Onychomycosis
paragraphs.name: [172] Onychomycosis — Pathophysiology
paragraphs.text:
Onychomycosis — Pathophysiology
- Infection often precedes with asymptomatic, dry hyperkeratotic tinea pedis.  
- Microtrauma and occlusive footwear create a warm, moist environment, compromising the hyponychial seal and allowing fungal penetration.  
- Dermatophytes colonize the nail bed via the distal hyponychium, progressing proximally with onycholysis and subungual hyperkeratosis.  
- **Histopathology**:  
  - **Acute phase**: Spongiosis, acanthosis, papillomatosis, edema, hyperkeratosis.  
  - **Chronic phase**: Compact hyperkeratosis, hypergranulosis, acanthosis, papillomatosis, sparse perivascular infiltrate.  
- Elevated interleukin-6 and interleukin-10 in nail bed and bloodstream; human beta defensin-2 present in mycotic nails.

paragraphs.title: Onychomycosis
paragraphs.name: [173] Onychomycosis — Clinical Presentation
paragraphs.text:
Onychomycosis — Clinical Presentation
- **Common subtypes**:  
  - **Distal lateral subungual onychomycosis (DSLO)**: Partial distal onycholysis with subungual hyperkeratosis (most common).  
  - **White superficial onychomycosis (WSO)**: White, chalky deposits on the nail surface (easily scraped away).  
  - **Proximal subungual onychomycosis (PSO)**: Involves the nail matrix, associated with immunodeficiency (e.g., AIDS).  
  - **Total dystrophic onychomycosis (TDO)**: Advanced stage with severe hyperkeratosis, nail destruction, and ridging (highest risk of ulceration and infection).  
- Often accompanied by mild, dry, hyperkeratotic tinea pedis (misidentified as xerosis).

paragraphs.title: Onychomycosis
paragraphs.name: [174] Onychomycosis — Evaluation / Diagnosis
paragraphs.text:
Onychomycosis — Evaluation / Diagnosis
- **Mycological tests**:  
  - **KOH wet mount**: 60% sensitive; differentiates dermatophytes from saprophytes.  
  - **Nail biopsy with PAS/Grocott methenamine silver**: 95% sensitive.  
  - **Fungal culture**: Specific but 60% sensitive; requires mycologist interpretation.  
  - **PCR**: 20% higher species-specific detection than culture.  
- **Dermoscopy**: Identifies subungual short spikes, longitudinal striae, and "Aurora Borealis" patterns. Differentiates from transverse onycholysis (microtraumatic dystrophy).  
- **Imaging/clinical**: Baseline nail measurements and photography to track progress (toenail growth ≈1 mm/month).

paragraphs.title: Onychomycosis
paragraphs.name: [175] Onychomycosis — Differential Diagnosis
paragraphs.text:
Onychomycosis — Differential Diagnosis
- Yellow nail syndrome  
- Drug reaction  
- Hypothyroidism  
- Nail malignancy  
- Psoriatic nail  
- Contact dermatitis

paragraphs.title: Onychomycosis
paragraphs.name: [176] Onychomycosis — Management / Treatment
paragraphs.text:
Onychomycosis — Management / Treatment
- **Systemic antifungals**:  
  - **Terbinafine**: 76% mycological cure rate; complete cure rate 38%.  
  - **Itraconazole pulse dosing**: 63% mycological cure rate.  
  - **Fluconazole**: 48% effective.  
- **Topical agents**:  
  - **Efinaconazole**: 55% mycological cure rate; 18% complete cure rate.  
  - **Tavaborole/Ciclopirox**: 36–9.1% complete cure rate.  
- **Adjunctive therapies**:  
  - Periodic debridement, chemical nail avulsion, or combination therapy (topical + systemic).  
  - Prophylactic antifungal powder for tinea pedis.  
- **Monitoring**:  
  - Baseline LFTs (ALT/AST) and hepatitis screening (if endemic exposure).  
  - Avoid systemic therapy in patients with alcohol use disorder, hepatitis, or polypharmacy (risk of drug interactions).  
  - Terbinafine contraindicated with phenothiazines/pimozide (QT prolongation risk).

paragraphs.title: Onychomycosis
paragraphs.name: [177] Onychomycosis — Complications
paragraphs.text:
Onychomycosis — Complications
- Cellulitis  
- Sepsis  
- Osteomyelitis  
- Tissue damage  
- Nail loss

paragraphs.title: Onychomycosis
paragraphs.name: [178] Onychomycosis — Prognosis
paragraphs.text:
Onychomycosis — Prognosis
- Depends on infection type/severity, immune status (e.g., diabetes, HIV), treatment adherence, and underlying conditions (e.g., peripheral vascular disease).  
- Recurrence rate: 5–50%.

paragraphs.title: Onychomycosis
paragraphs.name: [179] Onychomycosis — Prevention / Patient Education
paragraphs.text:
Onychomycosis — Prevention / Patient Education
- Wear proper footwear in public areas (pools, showers).  
- Maintain hand/foot hygiene; avoid shared towels.  
- Use gloves in wet occupations.  
- Prompt evaluation for nail changes; comply with treatment.

paragraphs.title: Onychomycosis
paragraphs.name: [180] Onychomycosis — Interprofessional Considerations
paragraphs.text:
Onychomycosis — Interprofessional Considerations
- **Primary care/dermatologist**: Diagnosis and systemic therapy management.  
- **Pharmacist**: Monitor compliance, drug interactions, and adverse effects (e.g., hepatic toxicity).  
- **Nurses/podiatrists**: Debridement, follow-up, and patient education.  
- **Surgeon**: Referral for nail avulsion in refractory cases.  
- Collaborative care to reduce recurrence and complications.

paragraphs.title: Obstructive Sleep Apnea Syndrome
paragraphs.name: [181] Obstructive Sleep Apnea Syndrome — Definition / Overview
paragraphs.text:
Obstructive Sleep Apnea Syndrome — Definition / Overview
- Obstructive sleep apnea syndrome (OSA) is defined by frequent episodes of apnea and hypopnea associated with symptoms such as excessive daytime sleepiness and cardiovascular morbidity/mortality.  
- Characterized by dynamic collapse of upper airway tissues during sleep, leading to recurrent respiratory events and both short-term symptomatic and long-term physiologic consequences.

paragraphs.title: Obstructive Sleep Apnea Syndrome
paragraphs.name: [182] Obstructive Sleep Apnea Syndrome — Epidemiology
paragraphs.text:
Obstructive Sleep Apnea Syndrome — Epidemiology
- Prevalence ranges from 21-59% in the general population and patients with cardiac disease, respectively.  
- Most common in adult males, but post-menopausal women have rates approaching those of men.  
- In North America: 15-30% in males, 10-15% in females.  
- Higher prevalence in African Americans, independent of body weight.  
- Increasing prevalence attributed to rising obesity rates and improved diagnosis.

paragraphs.title: Obstructive Sleep Apnea Syndrome
paragraphs.name: [183] Obstructive Sleep Apnea Syndrome — Etiology / Causes
paragraphs.text:
Obstructive Sleep Apnea Syndrome — Etiology / Causes
- **Craniofacial factors**: Retrognathia, maxillomandibular deficiency, reduced upper airway patency due to skeletal structure.  
- **Soft tissue factors**: Increased submucosal/lingual adipose tissue, cervical lymphovascular tone, reduced neuromuscular upper airway tone.  
- **Risk factors**: Obesity, male gender, advanced age, smoking, family history of OSA.

paragraphs.title: Obstructive Sleep Apnea Syndrome
paragraphs.name: [184] Obstructive Sleep Apnea Syndrome — Pathophysiology
paragraphs.text:
Obstructive Sleep Apnea Syndrome — Pathophysiology
- Decreased tonic activity of upper airway muscles (laryngeal, supraglottic, oropharyngeal, nasopharyngeal, lingual) during sleep, causing dynamic airway collapse.  
- Obstruction sites: nasal cavity, nasopharynx, oropharynx, base of tongue, laryngeal complex (may involve multiple levels).  
- **Respiratory events**:  
  - Apnea: Cessation of airflow ≥10 seconds.  
  - Hypopnea: ≥30% airflow reduction with ≥4% oxygen desaturation *or* ≥50% reduction with ≥3% desaturation/arousal.  
  - RERA: Breath sequence with increasing effort/flattened waveform causing arousal.

paragraphs.title: Obstructive Sleep Apnea Syndrome
paragraphs.name: [185] Obstructive Sleep Apnea Syndrome — Clinical Presentation
paragraphs.text:
Obstructive Sleep Apnea Syndrome — Clinical Presentation
- **Common symptoms**: Daytime sleepiness (difficulty staying alert), loud snoring, witnessed apneas/choking, morning headaches.  
- **Less common**: Insomnia, chest pain/palpitations, neuropsychiatric changes (mood disorders, cognitive dysfunction), nocturia.

paragraphs.title: Obstructive Sleep Apnea Syndrome
paragraphs.name: [186] Obstructive Sleep Apnea Syndrome — Evaluation / Diagnosis
paragraphs.text:
Obstructive Sleep Apnea Syndrome — Evaluation / Diagnosis
- **History and physical**: Assess symptoms, sleep hygiene, craniofacial anatomy, nasal/tongue abnormalities, tonsillar hypertrophy.  
  - Tools: Updated Friedmann Staging System, flexible fiberoptic laryngoscopy (awake vs. drug-induced sleep endoscopy [DISE]).  
- **Diagnostic testing**:  
  - **Epworth Sleepiness Scale**: Score >10 suggestive of OSA.  
  - **Polysomnography**: Gold standard; calculates:  
    - Apnea-Hypopnea Index (AHI) ≥5 with symptoms *or* AHI ≥15 without symptoms confirms diagnosis.  
    - Severity: Mild (5–14), moderate (15–30), severe (>30).  
  - Home sleep apnea tests: Alternative for select patients.

paragraphs.title: Obstructive Sleep Apnea Syndrome
paragraphs.name: [187] Obstructive Sleep Apnea Syndrome — Differential Diagnosis
paragraphs.text:
Obstructive Sleep Apnea Syndrome — Differential Diagnosis
- Central sleep apnea, primary snoring, laryngospasm, narcolepsy, periodic limb movement disorder, restless leg syndrome, circadian rhythm disorders, sleep hygiene-related issues.

paragraphs.title: Obstructive Sleep Apnea Syndrome
paragraphs.name: [188] Obstructive Sleep Apnea Syndrome — Management / Treatment
paragraphs.text:
Obstructive Sleep Apnea Syndrome — Management / Treatment
### **Education and Behavior**  
- Counsel on risks, complications, motor vehicle collision (MVC) risk, and anesthesia/sedation precautions.  
- Behavioral modifications: Weight loss, exercise, diet, sleep position adjustment, avoid alcohol/sedatives.  

### **Positive Airway Pressure Therapy**  
- **CPAP/BiPAP/APAP**: First-line therapy; improves event frequency, daytime sleepiness, blood pressure, quality of life.  
- Adherence challenges: 20-40% non-adherence.  

### **Alternative/Adjunctive Therapies**  
- **Oral appliances**: Mandibular advancement devices for mild-moderate OSA (dental side effects possible).  
- **Surgery**: Tonsillectomy, uvulopalatopharyngoplasty, maxillomandibular advancement, hypoglossal nerve stimulation (BMI <32, moderate-severe OSA), tracheostomy (last-resort).

paragraphs.title: Obstructive Sleep Apnea Syndrome
paragraphs.name: [189] Obstructive Sleep Apnea Syndrome — Complications
paragraphs.text:
Obstructive Sleep Apnea Syndrome — Complications
- Increased MVC risk (2-3× general population).  
- Neuropsychiatric: Cognitive deficits, mood disorders, sexual dysfunction.  
- Cardiopulmonary: Hypertension, coronary artery disease, arrhythmias, heart failure, pulmonary hypertension, stroke.  
- Metabolic: Insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes complications.  
- Hepatic: Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (2-3× increased incidence).

paragraphs.title: Obstructive Sleep Apnea Syndrome
paragraphs.name: [190] Obstructive Sleep Apnea Syndrome — Prognosis
paragraphs.text:
Obstructive Sleep Apnea Syndrome — Prognosis
- Short-term prognosis favorable with treatment.  
- Untreated OSA linked to increased mortality from cardiopulmonary complications, MVCs, and neurocognitive decline.  
- Treatment improves symptoms but not long-term cardiovascular/mortality outcomes.

paragraphs.title: Obstructive Sleep Apnea Syndrome
paragraphs.name: [191] Obstructive Sleep Apnea Syndrome — Prevention / Patient Education
paragraphs.text:
Obstructive Sleep Apnea Syndrome — Prevention / Patient Education
- Screen for symptoms and risk factors.  
- Educate on pathophysiology, treatment options, lifestyle modifications, and long-term monitoring.

paragraphs.title: Obstructive Sleep Apnea Syndrome
paragraphs.name: [192] Obstructive Sleep Apnea Syndrome — Interprofessional Considerations
paragraphs.text:
Obstructive Sleep Apnea Syndrome — Interprofessional Considerations
- Multidisciplinary care involving clinicians, nurses, sleep specialists, and pharmacists for comprehensive management.  
- Coordination ensures accurate diagnosis, adherence to therapy, and monitoring for complications.  
- Patient counseling and data sharing among team members are critical for optimal outcomes.

paragraphs.title: Acute Otitis Media
paragraphs.name: [193] Acute Otitis Media — Definition / Overview
paragraphs.text:
Acute Otitis Media — Definition / Overview
- Acute otitis media (AOM) is an infection of the middle ear space, representing a spectrum of diseases including AOM, chronic suppurative otitis media (CSOM), and otitis media with effusion (OME). It is the second most common pediatric diagnosis in the emergency department following upper respiratory infections.

paragraphs.title: Acute Otitis Media
paragraphs.name: [194] Acute Otitis Media — Epidemiology
paragraphs.text:
Acute Otitis Media — Epidemiology
- More common in males than females.
- Peak incidence occurs between 6–12 months of life, declining after age 5.
- Approximately 80% of children experience otitis media during their lifetime; 80–90% have otitis media with effusion before school age.
- Less common in adults but occurs in subpopulations with childhood history of recurrent OM, cleft palate, immunodeficiency, or immunocompromised status.

paragraphs.title: Acute Otitis Media
paragraphs.name: [195] Acute Otitis Media — Etiology / Causes
paragraphs.text:
Acute Otitis Media — Etiology / Causes
- **Infectious Factors**: 
  - Bacterial: *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, non-typeable *Haemophilus influenzae* (NTHi), *Moraxella catarrhalis*.
  - Viral: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), coronaviruses, influenza viruses, adenoviruses, human metapneumovirus, picornaviruses.
- **Risk Factors**:
  - Decreased immunity (HIV, diabetes, immunodeficiencies).
  - Genetic predisposition; mucin gene abnormalities (e.g., MUC5B).
  - Anatomic abnormalities (palate, tensor veli palatini, Eustachian tube dysfunction).
  - Ciliary dysfunction, cochlear implants, vitamin A deficiency.
  - Allergies, lack of breastfeeding, passive smoke exposure, daycare attendance, lower socioeconomic status, family history of recurrent AOM.

paragraphs.title: Acute Otitis Media
paragraphs.name: [196] Acute Otitis Media — Pathophysiology
paragraphs.text:
Acute Otitis Media — Pathophysiology
- Begins as inflammation following a viral upper respiratory tract infection, involving mucosa of the nose, nasopharynx, middle ear, and Eustachian tubes.
- Edema obstructs the Eustachian tube, causing negative pressure, mucosal secretion buildup, and bacterial/viral colonization.
- Progresses to suppuration/purulence, clinically presenting as bulging/erythematous tympanic membrane (TM) and purulent fluid.
- Differentiated from chronic serous otitis media (CSOM), which shows thick amber fluid and retracted TM.

paragraphs.title: Acute Otitis Media
paragraphs.name: [197] Acute Otitis Media — Clinical Presentation
paragraphs.text:
Acute Otitis Media — Clinical Presentation
- Otalgia is a key indicator; non-specific symptoms include ear pulling, irritability, headache, disturbed sleep, poor feeding, vomiting, diarrhea.
- Fever (low-grade) in ~66% of cases.
- Otoscopic findings: TM erythema/bulging, purulent fluid (suppurative OM); intact vs. perforated TM.

paragraphs.title: Acute Otitis Media
paragraphs.name: [198] Acute Otitis Media — Evaluation / Diagnosis
paragraphs.text:
Acute Otitis Media — Evaluation / Diagnosis
- **Physical Exam**: Otoscopy (pneumatic preferred for higher sensitivity/specificity).
- **Diagnostic Tools**: Tympanometry, acoustic reflectometry.
- **Laboratory Studies**: Rarely needed; consider sepsis workup in infants <12 weeks with fever and no source.
- **Imaging**: Reserved for suspected intratemporal/intracranial complications (CT/MRI).
- **Tympanocentesis**: For refractory cases to identify pathogens.

paragraphs.title: Acute Otitis Media
paragraphs.name: [199] Acute Otitis Media — Differential Diagnosis
paragraphs.text:
Acute Otitis Media — Differential Diagnosis
- Cholesteatoma, fever in infants/toddlers, hearing impairment, pediatric nasal polyps, nasopharyngeal cancer, otitis externa, human parainfluenza viruses, passive smoking, allergic rhinitis, bacterial meningitis, gastroesophageal reflux, *Haemophilus influenzae* infection, HIV, mastoiditis, pneumococcal infections, primary ciliary dyskinesia, respiratory syncytial virus, rhinovirus, teething.

paragraphs.title: Acute Otitis Media
paragraphs.name: [200] Acute Otitis Media — Management / Treatment
paragraphs.text:
Acute Otitis Media — Management / Treatment
- **Pain Control**: NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen) or acetaminophen.
- **Antibiotics**:
  - First-line: High-dose amoxicillin (10-day course) for non-penicillin-allergic patients.
  - Penicillin allergy: Azithromycin, clarithromycin, cefdinir, cefpodoxime, cefuroxime.
  - Refractory cases: High-dose amoxicillin-clavulanate.
  - TM perforation: Ototopical antibiotics (e.g., ofloxacin).
  - Watchful waiting (controversial in the U.S.) vs. immediate antibiotics per guidelines (e.g., Netherlands).
- **Surgical**: Myringotomy with tube placement for ≥4 episodes in 12 months.

paragraphs.title: Acute Otitis Media
paragraphs.name: [201] Acute Otitis Media — Complications
paragraphs.text:
Acute Otitis Media — Complications
- **Intratemporal**: Conductive/sensorineural hearing loss, TM perforation, CSOM, cholesteatoma, mastoiditis, petrositis, labyrinthitis, facial paralysis, cholesterol granuloma.
- **Intracranial**: Meningitis, brain abscess, subdural empyema, lateral sinus thrombosis, otitic hydrocephalus.
- **Developmental**: Conductive hearing loss may impair language/speech development in children aged 6–24 months.

paragraphs.title: Acute Otitis Media
paragraphs.name: [202] Acute Otitis Media — Prognosis
paragraphs.text:
Acute Otitis Media — Prognosis
- Generally excellent; rare mortality in developed countries with prompt treatment.
- Prognostic factors: Number of episodes, seasonality (winter), complications.
- Recurrent cases may lead to high hearing loss/speech therapy needs.

paragraphs.title: Acute Otitis Media
paragraphs.name: [203] Acute Otitis Media — Prevention / Patient Education
paragraphs.text:
Acute Otitis Media — Prevention / Patient Education
- Vaccination: Pneumococcal and influenza vaccines.
- Avoid tobacco smoke, promote breastfeeding.
- Educate on antibiotic adherence, symptom monitoring, and follow-up.

paragraphs.title: Acute Otitis Media
paragraphs.name: [204] Acute Otitis Media — Interprofessional Considerations
paragraphs.text:
Acute Otitis Media — Interprofessional Considerations
- Team includes primary care providers, otolaryngologists (surgical referrals), audiologists (hearing assessment), speech therapists (developmental delays), nurses (medication education), and pharmacists (drug counseling).
- Early diagnosis and collaborative management reduce complications and improve outcomes.

paragraphs.title: Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome
paragraphs.name: [205] Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome — Definition / Overview
paragraphs.text:
Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome — Definition / Overview
- Most common endocrine disorder in females of reproductive age worldwide.  
- Involves insulin resistance and visceral adiposity, leading to disrupted hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis function.  
- Associated comorbidities: infertility, metabolic syndrome, obesity, type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular risks, depression, obstructive sleep apnea, endometrial cancer, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD).  
- Diagnosis requires exclusion of mimicking disorders.

paragraphs.title: Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome
paragraphs.name: [206] Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome — Epidemiology
paragraphs.text:
Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome — Epidemiology
- Prevalence: 5%–26% depending on diagnostic criteria.  
- Rotterdam criteria (2/3: hyperandrogenism, ovulatory dysfunction, polycystic ovaries) are most commonly used.  
- Higher prevalence in Mexican Americans vs. non-Hispanic whites and African Americans.  
- Phenotypic changes over time: classic PCOS (phenotype A) decreases, with reduced hyperandrogenism and increased FSH levels.

paragraphs.title: Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome
paragraphs.name: [207] Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome — Etiology / Causes
paragraphs.text:
Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome — Etiology / Causes
- Multigenic disorder with epigenetic factors.  
- Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) linked genes to insulin resistance, ovarian steroidogenesis, and PI3K-Akt signaling.  
- Twin studies: ~70% heritability.  
- *DENND1A* gene identified as a risk marker.  
- Epigenetic factors: obesity-related hypermethylation of granulosa cells.  
- Potential roles: fetal androgen exposure, microRNA regulation of GLUT4.

paragraphs.title: Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome
paragraphs.name: [208] Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome — Pathophysiology
paragraphs.text:
Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome — Pathophysiology
- Insulin resistance (70% of cases) → hyperinsulinemia → ovarian androgen excess.  
- Dysregulation of hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis: elevated LH, reduced FSH, altered AMH.  
- Theca cell overexpression of steroidogenic enzymes (e.g., P450c17) → androgen excess.  
- Chronic low-grade inflammation (elevated CRP).  
- Two-thirds of cases: functional ovarian hyperandrogenism (FOH) with 17-OHP overresponse.

paragraphs.title: Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome
paragraphs.name: [209] Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome — Clinical Presentation
paragraphs.text:
Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome — Clinical Presentation
- **Irregular menses**: Defined by postmenarche interval abnormalities (e.g., <21 or >35 days after 3 years postmenarche).  
- **Hyperandrogenism**: Hirsutism (modified Ferriman-Gallwey score ≥4–6), alopecia, acne.  
- **Phenotypes**: 7 categories (A–G) based on hyperandrogenism, hirsutism, oligo-anovulation, and polycystic ovaries.

paragraphs.title: Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome
paragraphs.name: [210] Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome — Evaluation / Diagnosis
paragraphs.text:
Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome — Evaluation / Diagnosis
- **Rotterdam Criteria**: 2/3 of hyperandrogenism, ovulatory dysfunction, or polycystic ovaries/AMH elevation.  
- **Exclusion**: Thyroid disease, hyperprolactinemia, congenital adrenal hyperplasia (test 17-OHP, ACTH stimulation).  
- **Hyperandrogenism workup**: Total/free testosterone (prefer liquid chromatography/mass spectrometry), androstenedione, DHEAS.  
- **Imaging**: Transvaginal ultrasound (follicles per ovary ≥20), AMH (not standalone for diagnosis).  
- **Adolescents**: Require hyperandrogenism + ovulatory dysfunction; avoid ultrasound/AMH.

paragraphs.title: Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome
paragraphs.name: [211] Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome — Differential Diagnosis
paragraphs.text:
Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome — Differential Diagnosis
- Androgenic steroid use, hypothyroidism, late-onset congenital adrenal hyperplasia, idiopathic hirsutism, ovarian malignancies.

paragraphs.title: Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome
paragraphs.name: [212] Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome — Management / Treatment
paragraphs.text:
Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome — Management / Treatment
- **Lifestyle Modification**: 5% weight loss improves metabolic health, ovulation, and symptoms.  
- **Pharmacologic**:  
  - **Hormonal contraceptives**: First-line for menstrual irregularities, hirsutism, acne (e.g., ethinyl estradiol with antiandrogenic progestin).  
  - **Metformin**: Improves menstrual cycles, insulin resistance; adjunct for infertility.  
  - **Antiandrogens**: Spironolactone for hirsutism unresponsive to contraceptives.  
  - **Infertility**: Letrozole first-line; clomiphene citrate + metformin if inadequate response.  
  - **GLP-1 agonists**: Off-label for weight loss, insulin sensitivity, ovulation improvement.  
- **Symptom-based**: Laser hair removal, topical eflornithine, myoinositol (fertility support).

paragraphs.title: Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome
paragraphs.name: [213] Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome — Complications
paragraphs.text:
Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome — Complications
- **Infertility**: Linked to anovulation; 70% face conception challenges.  
- **Obstetric**: Higher risk of miscarriage, gestational diabetes, preeclampsia.  
- **Metabolic**: MASLD (3× increased risk), insulin resistance (33%–66%), type 2 diabetes.  
- **Psychiatric**: Increased depression, anxiety, suicide attempts.  
- **Cancers**: Endometrial hyperplasia/cancer from unopposed estrogen.

paragraphs.title: Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome
paragraphs.name: [214] Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome — Prognosis
paragraphs.text:
Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome — Prognosis
- Hirsutism and acne decrease with age; ovarian volume/follicle number decline.  
- Ovulation improves with age, but fertility success rates drop (e.g., letrozole pregnancy rate 41%–64.8%).  
- Increased long-term risk of diabetes, cardiovascular disease, but no elevated all-cause mortality.

paragraphs.title: Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome
paragraphs.name: [215] Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome — Prevention / Patient Education
paragraphs.text:
Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome — Prevention / Patient Education
- Early diagnosis and lifestyle changes to reduce comorbidities.  
- Weight management, regular screening for metabolic/cardiovascular issues, and mental health support.  
- Family history awareness and genetic counseling considerations.

paragraphs.title: Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome
paragraphs.name: [216] Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome — Interprofessional Considerations
paragraphs.text:
Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome — Interprofessional Considerations
- Multidisciplinary approach: Physicians, dermatologists, reproductive endocrinologists, dietitians, psychiatrists, pharmacists, and nurses.  
- Coordinated care for metabolic health, fertility, mental health, and cosmetic concerns.  
- Patient-centered education and support groups to address stigma and improve adherence.

paragraphs.title: Peptic Ulcer Disease
paragraphs.name: [217] Peptic Ulcer Disease — Definition / Overview
paragraphs.text:
Peptic Ulcer Disease — Definition / Overview
- Peptic ulcer disease (PUD) involves discontinuation in the inner lining of the gastrointestinal (GI) tract due to gastric acid secretion or pepsin, extending into the muscularis propria layer. Common locations include the stomach, proximal duodenum, lower esophagus, distal duodenum, or jejunum.

paragraphs.title: Peptic Ulcer Disease
paragraphs.name: [218] Peptic Ulcer Disease — Epidemiology
paragraphs.text:
Peptic Ulcer Disease — Epidemiology
- Lifetime risk: 5–10%. 
- Decreasing global incidence due to improved hygiene, effective treatments, and judicious NSAID use. 
- Duodenal ulcers are four times more common than gastric ulcers. 
- Duodenal ulcers are more prevalent in men than women.

paragraphs.title: Peptic Ulcer Disease
paragraphs.name: [219] Peptic Ulcer Disease — Etiology / Causes
paragraphs.text:
Peptic Ulcer Disease — Etiology / Causes
### Common:
- *Helicobacter pylori* infection
- NSAID use
- Medications (corticosteroids, bisphosphonates, potassium chloride, fluorouracil)

### Rare:
- Zollinger-Ellison syndrome
- Malignancy (gastric/lung cancer, lymphomas)
- Stress (acute illness, burns, head injury)
- Viral infection
- Vascular insufficiency
- Radiation therapy
- Crohn’s disease
- Chemotherapy

### Hypersecretory conditions:
- Zollinger-Ellison syndrome
- Systemic mastocytosis
- Cystic fibrosis
- Hyperparathyroidism
- Antral G cell hyperplasia

paragraphs.title: Peptic Ulcer Disease
paragraphs.name: [220] Peptic Ulcer Disease — Pathophysiology
paragraphs.text:
Peptic Ulcer Disease — Pathophysiology
- Imbalance between gastric mucosal protective factors (bicarbonate, mucus) and destructive factors (acid, pepsin).
- Risk factors: *H. pylori* infection, NSAID use, first-degree family history of PUD, emigration from a developing nation, African American/Hispanic ethnicity.
- *H. pylori*: Colonizes gastric mucosa, impairs bicarbonate secretion, induces inflammation, and causes gastric metaplasia.
- Histopathology: Gastric ulcers typically on the lesser curvature (antrum/fundus); duodenal ulcers in the duodenal bulb. Ulcers >5 mm with smooth/irregular borders.

paragraphs.title: Peptic Ulcer Disease
paragraphs.name: [221] Peptic Ulcer Disease — Clinical Presentation
paragraphs.text:
Peptic Ulcer Disease — Clinical Presentation
- **Epigastric pain**: 
  - Gastric ulcer: 15–30 minutes post-meal.
  - Duodenal ulcer: 2–3 hours post-meal; nocturnal pain.
- Associated symptoms: Bloating, abdominal fullness, nausea/vomiting, weight loss/gain.
- **Alarm symptoms** (require urgent referral):
  - Unintentional weight loss
  - Progressive dysphagia
  - Overt GI bleeding
  - Iron deficiency anemia
  - Recurrent emesis
  - Family history of upper GI malignancy

paragraphs.title: Peptic Ulcer Disease
paragraphs.name: [222] Peptic Ulcer Disease — Evaluation / Diagnosis
paragraphs.text:
Peptic Ulcer Disease — Evaluation / Diagnosis
- **Endoscopy**: 
  - Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD): Gold standard (90% sensitivity/specificity).
  - Indicated for patients >50 years, new-onset dyspeptic symptoms, or alarm symptoms.
- **H. pylori testing**:
  - Urea breath test (high sensitivity/specificity; post-treatment confirmation at 4–6 weeks).
  - Stool antigen test.
  - Serologic testing (antibodies).
  - Endoscopic biopsy (culture if refractory or antibiotic resistance suspected; 4–6 sites).
- **Imaging**:
  - Barium swallow if EGD contraindicated.
  - CT abdomen with contrast for complications (perforation, obstruction).
- **Labs**: CBC, LFTs, amylase/lipase, serum gastrin (Zollinger-Ellison suspicion).

paragraphs.title: Peptic Ulcer Disease
paragraphs.name: [223] Peptic Ulcer Disease — Differential Diagnosis
paragraphs.text:
Peptic Ulcer Disease — Differential Diagnosis
- Gastritis
- GERD
- Gastric cancer
- Pancreatitis
- Biliary colic/cholecystitis
- Myocardial infarction (inferior wall/right ventricular involvement)
- Mesenteric ischemia/vasculitis

paragraphs.title: Peptic Ulcer Disease
paragraphs.name: [224] Peptic Ulcer Disease — Management / Treatment
paragraphs.text:
Peptic Ulcer Disease — Management / Treatment
### Medical Therapy:
- **Antisecretory agents**:
  - Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs; first-line over H2-receptor antagonists).
  - Long-term PPI use requires calcium supplementation (fracture risk).
- **H. pylori eradication**:
  - Triple therapy: PPI + two antibiotics (clarithromycin, metronidazole, or amoxicillin) for 7–14 days.
  - Quadruple therapy (bismuth-based) if first-line fails.
- **NSAID-associated PUD**:
  - Discontinue NSAIDs or switch to lower dose.
  - Prostaglandin analogs (misoprostol) for prophylaxis.
- **Other medications**: Avoid corticosteroids, bisphosphonates, anticoagulants if possible.

### Surgical Therapy:
- Indicated for refractory ulcers (>5 mm after 8–12 weeks of PPI), noncompliance, or complications.
- Procedures: Vagotomy, partial gastrectomy.

paragraphs.title: Peptic Ulcer Disease
paragraphs.name: [225] Peptic Ulcer Disease — Complications
paragraphs.text:
Peptic Ulcer Disease — Complications
- Upper gastrointestinal bleeding
- Gastric outlet obstruction
- Perforation
- Penetration
- Gastric cancer

paragraphs.title: Peptic Ulcer Disease
paragraphs.name: [226] Peptic Ulcer Disease — Prognosis
paragraphs.text:
Peptic Ulcer Disease — Prognosis
- Excellent after successful treatment of underlying cause.
- Recurrence rates: >60% in most series.
- NSAID-induced gastric perforation rate: 0.3% per patient per year.
- Mortality rates have significantly decreased.

paragraphs.title: Peptic Ulcer Disease
paragraphs.name: [227] Peptic Ulcer Disease — Prevention / Patient Education
paragraphs.text:
Peptic Ulcer Disease — Prevention / Patient Education
- Avoid NSAIDs, alcohol, tobacco, caffeine.
- Use lowest effective NSAID dose with prophylaxis (e.g., misoprostol) if necessary.
- Weight loss (association with obesity).
- Stress reduction counseling.

paragraphs.title: Peptic Ulcer Disease
paragraphs.name: [228] Peptic Ulcer Disease — Interprofessional Considerations
paragraphs.text:
Peptic Ulcer Disease — Interprofessional Considerations
- Primary care providers, emergency physicians, nurses, pharmacists, and dietitians collaborate for comprehensive care.
- Nurses: Monitor patients, provide education, update team on status.
- Pharmacists: Ensure medication compliance and explain regimens.
- Dietitians: Address obesity as a potential trigger.
- Coordination improves outcomes and reduces morbidity.

paragraphs.title: Bacterial Pneumonia
paragraphs.name: [229] Bacterial Pneumonia — Definition / Overview
paragraphs.text:
Bacterial Pneumonia — Definition / Overview
- Inflammation of lung parenchyma and alveolar spaces caused by various bacteria, triggering an intricate interplay with the host immune response.

paragraphs.title: Bacterial Pneumonia
paragraphs.name: [230] Bacterial Pneumonia — Epidemiology
paragraphs.text:
Bacterial Pneumonia — Epidemiology
- Global annual incidence: 450 million CAP cases, 95% in developing countries, contributing to ~4 million deaths annually.
- Europe: 206–470 cases/100,000 patients/year; China: 298–2210 cases/100 patient-years.
- US: 649–847 CAP hospitalizations/100,000 patient-years, disproportionately affecting low-income and minority groups.
- Highest incidence in ages <4 years and ≥65 years.
- US estimates: 2.2–8 million annual hospitalizations; CAP-related mortality: 100,000 deaths/year.
- Global CAP mortality: 2.6–18.5% at hospitalization, up to 31–44.5% within 1 year.

paragraphs.title: Bacterial Pneumonia
paragraphs.name: [231] Bacterial Pneumonia — Etiology / Causes
paragraphs.text:
Bacterial Pneumonia — Etiology / Causes
- **Community-Acquired Pneumonia (CAP):** 
  - *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, *Haemophilus influenzae*, *Staphylococcus aureus*, Group A *Streptococci*, *Moraxella catarrhalis*, anaerobes, aerobic Gram-negative bacteria (e.g., *Klebsiella pneumoniae*, *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*).
  - Atypical: *Legionella* spp., *Mycoplasma pneumoniae*, *Chlamydia pneumoniae*, *Chlamydia psittaci*.
  - Opportunistic: *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*, *Nocardia* spp.
- **Hospital-Acquired Pneumonia (HAP)/Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia (VAP):** 
  - *K. pneumoniae*, *E. coli*, *P. aeruginosa*, *S. aureus* (including MRSA), *Enterobacter* spp., *Acinetobacter baumannii* complex.

paragraphs.title: Bacterial Pneumonia
paragraphs.name: [232] Bacterial Pneumonia — Pathophysiology
paragraphs.text:
Bacterial Pneumonia — Pathophysiology
- Lower respiratory tract exposed to environmental pathogens. Bacterial invasion triggers innate immune response: 
  - Toll-like receptor recognition → neutrophilic infiltration.
  - Alveolar macrophages attempt bacterial clearance.
- Bacterial virulence factors: 
  - Polysaccharide capsules (*S. pneumoniae*), adhesion proteins (*M. pneumoniae*), pili (*Legionella pneumophila*).
- Inflammatory cytokines (IL-1, TNF, IL-6, IL-8, G-CSF) drive symptoms: fever, leukocytosis, purulent secretions.
- Alveolar-capillary membrane leakage → hypoxia, fibrosis, dyspnea.
- Pleuritic pain via phrenic nerve irritation; hemoptysis from parenchymal necrosis.

paragraphs.title: Bacterial Pneumonia
paragraphs.name: [233] Bacterial Pneumonia — Clinical Presentation
paragraphs.text:
Bacterial Pneumonia — Clinical Presentation
- **Symptoms:** Fever, cough (productive/nonproductive), dyspnea, chest pain, fatigue, headache, myalgia, arthralgia.
- **Physical findings:**
  - Fever/hypothermia, tachypnea, tachycardia/bradycardia, cyanosis, decreased chest expansion, dull percussion, crackles/rales, bronchial breath sounds, egophony, hypoxia.
  - **Infants:** Tachypnea, nasal flaring, intercostal retraction, abdominal distension.
  - **Children <5 years:** Tachypnea, chest indrawing, abdominal pain.
  - **Elderly:** Early confusion, reduced fever/rigor/sputum production.
  - **Etiology-specific signs:** Relative bradycardia (*Legionella*), dental issues (anaerobes), gag reflex impairment (aspiration pneumonia).

paragraphs.title: Bacterial Pneumonia
paragraphs.name: [234] Bacterial Pneumonia — Evaluation / Diagnosis
paragraphs.text:
Bacterial Pneumonia — Evaluation / Diagnosis
- **Clinical assessment:** Prognostic scores (CURB-65, CORB, SMART-COP, PSI).
- **Laboratory:** CBC, CRP, blood cultures (in severe cases), sputum Gram stain/culture, urine antigen/PCR for specific pathogens.
- **Radiological:** Chest X-ray (consolidations, parapneumonic effusions) as gold standard; CT for complex cases.
- **Bronchoalveolar lavage:** In intubated patients.

paragraphs.title: Bacterial Pneumonia
paragraphs.name: [235] Bacterial Pneumonia — Differential Diagnosis
paragraphs.text:
Bacterial Pneumonia — Differential Diagnosis
- **Children:** Asthma, bronchiolitis, croup, epiglottitis, respiratory distress syndrome.
- **Adults:** Acute/chronic bronchitis, acute pulmonary edema, ARDS, foreign body aspiration, asthma, atelectasis, bronchiectasis, COPD exacerbation, fungal/PCP pneumonia, interstitial lung disease, organizing pneumonia, respiratory failure, viral pneumonia.

paragraphs.title: Bacterial Pneumonia
paragraphs.name: [236] Bacterial Pneumonia — Management / Treatment
paragraphs.text:
Bacterial Pneumonia — Management / Treatment
- **Risk stratification:** CURB-65, clinical judgment.
- **Empirical antibiotics:** 
  - Outpatients (no comorbidities): Penicillin, macrolide, tetracycline.
  - Outpatients (comorbidities): Respiratory fluoroquinolone or amoxicillin/clavulanate + macrolide.
  - Inpatients: Beta-lactam + macrolide or respiratory fluoroquinolone; adjust per susceptibility.
  - *P. aeruginosa*: Piperacillin-tazobactam, ceftazidime, cefepime, ciprofloxacin, meropenem.
- **Adjunctive therapies:** Antipyretics, corticosteroids (controversial; consider in severe CAP), chest physiotherapy (limited evidence).
- **Nonpharmacological:** Smoking cessation counseling, vaccination (influenza, pneumococcus, COVID-19), dysphagia management, early mobilization, hydration, nutrition, positioning (lateral decubitus in consolidation).

paragraphs.title: Bacterial Pneumonia
paragraphs.name: [237] Bacterial Pneumonia — Complications
paragraphs.text:
Bacterial Pneumonia — Complications
- Lung fibrosis, necrotizing pneumonia, empyema, pulmonary abscess, cavitation, meningitis, sepsis, multiorgan failure, death.

paragraphs.title: Bacterial Pneumonia
paragraphs.name: [238] Bacterial Pneumonia — Prognosis
paragraphs.text:
Bacterial Pneumonia — Prognosis
- Influenced by age, comorbidities (malignancy, COPD), immunosuppression, alcohol misuse, hospital setting, ventilatory support.
- *S. pneumoniae* mortality: ~30% untreated; higher with *Pseudomonas*, MRSA, polymicrobial infections.
- Predictors of poor prognosis: PSI score, persistent tachypnea/hypoxia/confusion/acidosis, APACHE II >21 or SOFA >6 in VAP.

paragraphs.title: Bacterial Pneumonia
paragraphs.name: [239] Bacterial Pneumonia — Prevention / Patient Education
paragraphs.text:
Bacterial Pneumonia — Prevention / Patient Education
- Smoking cessation, alcohol moderation, dental hygiene, hand hygiene.
- Vaccination: Pneumococcal (older adults/immunocompromised), annual influenza vaccine.
- Early medical attention for high-risk groups (dyspnea, rigors, fever).

paragraphs.title: Bacterial Pneumonia
paragraphs.name: [240] Bacterial Pneumonia — Interprofessional Considerations
paragraphs.text:
Bacterial Pneumonia — Interprofessional Considerations
- Multidisciplinary approach: Physicians, nurses (VAP prevention, vaccination), pharmacists (antimicrobial stewardship), physiotherapists (mobility), dieticians (nutrition), speech therapists (dysphagia), psychologists (substance use).
- Early mobilization, oral care in aged care facilities, comorbidity management, and follow-up critical.

paragraphs.title: Rheumatoid Arthritis
paragraphs.name: [241] Rheumatoid Arthritis — Definition / Overview
paragraphs.text:
Rheumatoid Arthritis — Definition / Overview
- Systemic autoimmune disease characterized by inflammatory arthritis and extra-articular involvement.  
- Chronic inflammatory disorder caused by gene-environment interactions (e.g., tobacco use), primarily affecting synovial joints.  
- Typically begins in small peripheral joints symmetrically, progressing proximally if untreated.  
- Joint inflammation leads to cartilage loss and bone erosions.  
- Early RA: symptom duration <6 months; established RA: >6 months.  
- Untreated RA is progressive, associated with morbidity and increased mortality.

paragraphs.title: Rheumatoid Arthritis
paragraphs.name: [242] Rheumatoid Arthritis — Epidemiology
paragraphs.text:
Rheumatoid Arthritis — Epidemiology
- Global prevalence: ~0.24% (Global Burden of Disease 2010 Study).  
- Higher prevalence in Western/Northern Europe, North America, Australia; lower in Central/South America, East Asia, Africa.  
- Annual incidence in the US and northern Europe: ~40 per 100,000 persons.  
- Female lifetime risk: 3.6% vs. 1.7% in males.  
- Peak incidence: 65–80 years.  
- Urban prevalence: 0.69% vs. rural 0.54%.  
- High-income countries: 0.49% prevalence vs. low-income: 0.35%.  
- Heritability: ~40–65% for seropositive RA, 20% for seronegative RA.  
- First-degree relative with RA: 3x increased risk; second-degree: 2x.

paragraphs.title: Rheumatoid Arthritis
paragraphs.name: [243] Rheumatoid Arthritis — Etiology / Causes
paragraphs.text:
Rheumatoid Arthritis — Etiology / Causes
- **Genetic factors**:  
  - HLA-DRB1 alleles (*04, *01, *10) with "shared epitope."  
  - Polymorphisms in *PAD14, PTPN22, CTLA4, IL-2RA, STAT4, TRAF1, CCR6, IRF5*.  
  - SNPs in *PSORS1C1, PTPN22, MIR146A* linked to severe disease.  
- **Environmental factors**:  
  - Smoking (strongest risk factor, interacts with HLA-DRB1 in ACPA+ individuals).  
  - Silica, asbestos, textile dust, *Porphyromonas gingivalis* infection.  
  - Gut dysbiosis (increased *Actinobacteria, Collinsella, Eggerthella, Faecalibacterium*).  
- **Epigenetics**:  
  - Hypermethylation of *PTPN11* intron enhancer in RA fibroblast-like synoviocytes (FLS).

paragraphs.title: Rheumatoid Arthritis
paragraphs.name: [244] Rheumatoid Arthritis — Pathophysiology
paragraphs.text:
Rheumatoid Arthritis — Pathophysiology
- Autoimmunity begins at distant sites (lung, GI/gums) with modified proteins (e.g., citrullination via peptidyl arginine deiminase enzymes).  
- ACPA and RF autoantibodies precede clinical symptoms by years.  
- Synovium infiltrated by immune cells (T helper 1/17, B cells, macrophages, FLS).  
- FLS become invasive, producing matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) and RANKL, leading to osteoclast-mediated bone erosions.  
- Key cytokines: TNF, IL-6, GM-CSF, IL-17, IL-1, promoting inflammation and tissue destruction.  
- Complement activation by immune complexes exacerbates inflammation.

paragraphs.title: Rheumatoid Arthritis
paragraphs.name: [245] Rheumatoid Arthritis — Clinical Presentation
paragraphs.text:
Rheumatoid Arthritis — Clinical Presentation
- **Musculoskeletal**:  
  - Insidious onset of joint pain/swelling, typically in small joints (hands/feet).  
  - Symmetric involvement, morning stiffness, progressive proximal spread.  
  - Advanced disease: ulnar deviation, swan neck/boutonniere deformities, reduced grip strength.  
- **Extra-articular**:  
  - Rheumatoid nodules (olecranon, pressure points).  
  - Interstitial lung disease (5–16% prevalence, associated with ACPA, anti-CarP, *MUC5B* variant).  
  - Secondary Sjögren’s syndrome (dry eyes/mouth).  
  - Rare: Felty syndrome (splenomegaly, neutropenia), vasculitis, scleritis.

paragraphs.title: Rheumatoid Arthritis
paragraphs.name: [246] Rheumatoid Arthritis — Evaluation / Diagnosis
paragraphs.text:
Rheumatoid Arthritis — Evaluation / Diagnosis
- **Diagnostic criteria (2010 ACR/EULAR)**:  
  - Requires ≥6 points across 4 domains:  
    1. Joint involvement (large/small joints, counted differently).  
    2. Serology (RF, ACPA: low/high positive = 2/3 points).  
    3. Acute phase reactants (elevated CRP/ESR = 1 point).  
    4. Symptom duration ≥6 weeks = 1 point.  
- **Laboratory**:  
  - RF (sensitivity 69%, specificity 85%), ACPA (sensitivity 67%, specificity 95%).  
  - Anemia of chronic disease, thrombocytosis, neutropenia (Felty syndrome).  
  - Synovial fluid: leukocyte count 1,500–25,000/μL (predominantly PMNs), low C3/C4.  
- **Imaging**:  
  - X-rays: periarticular osteopenia, erosions in advanced disease.  
  - MRI/ultrasound: detect synovitis and erosions before radiographic changes.

paragraphs.title: Rheumatoid Arthritis
paragraphs.name: [247] Rheumatoid Arthritis — Differential Diagnosis
paragraphs.text:
Rheumatoid Arthritis — Differential Diagnosis
- Osteoarthritis  
- Psoriatic arthritis  
- Systemic lupus erythematosus  
- Sjögren syndrome  
- Polymyalgia rheumatic  
- Chronic gouty arthritis  
- Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease

paragraphs.title: Rheumatoid Arthritis
paragraphs.name: [248] Rheumatoid Arthritis — Management / Treatment
paragraphs.text:
Rheumatoid Arthritis — Management / Treatment
- **Goals**: Early diagnosis, remission, prevent joint damage.  
- **Pharmacological**:  
  - **DMARDs**: Methotrexate (first-line), hydroxychloroquine, sulfasalazine, leflunomide.  
  - **Biologics**: TNF inhibitors (etanercept, infliximab), IL-6 inhibitors (tocilizumab), abatacept (T-cell costimulator), rituximab (anti-CD20).  
  - **JAK inhibitors**: Tofacitinib, baricitinib.  
- **Non-pharmacological**:  
  - Physical therapy, counseling, patient education.  
- **NSAIDs**: Symptom relief (e.g., celecoxib for GI safety).  
- **Corticosteroids**: Short-term bridge therapy or for flares.  
- **Monitoring**: Disease activity scores (DAS28, CDAI), screen for infections, hepatitis, TB.  
- **Vaccinations**: Pneumococcus, hepatitis, influenza, HPV, HZV, COVID-19.

paragraphs.title: Rheumatoid Arthritis
paragraphs.name: [249] Rheumatoid Arthritis — Complications
paragraphs.text:
Rheumatoid Arthritis — Complications
- Progressive joint damage/deformities.  
- Interstitial lung disease (ILD).  
- Accelerated atherosclerosis, coronary artery disease.  
- Lymphoma (non-Hodgkin’s, higher in active RA).  
- Osteoporosis, increased fracture risk.  
- Venous thromboembolism.  
- Depression, increased mortality (3x general population).

paragraphs.title: Rheumatoid Arthritis
paragraphs.name: [250] Rheumatoid Arthritis — Prognosis
paragraphs.text:
Rheumatoid Arthritis — Prognosis
- No cure; progressive without treatment.  
- Early treatment (≤6 months) improves function but mortality similar to late treatment.  
- 40% develop disability within 10 years.  
- Poor prognostic factors: high autoantibody titers, HLA-DRB1, early onset, female gender.

paragraphs.title: Rheumatoid Arthritis
paragraphs.name: [251] Rheumatoid Arthritis — Prevention / Patient Education
paragraphs.text:
Rheumatoid Arthritis — Prevention / Patient Education
- Avoid smoking, maintain balanced diet, regular exercise, healthy weight.  
- Recognize early symptoms for timely intervention.  
- Regular monitoring for comorbidities (cardiovascular, lung, bone).

paragraphs.title: Rheumatoid Arthritis
paragraphs.name: [252] Rheumatoid Arthritis — Interprofessional Considerations
paragraphs.text:
Rheumatoid Arthritis — Interprofessional Considerations
- Team includes rheumatologists, nurses, pharmacists, occupational therapists, social workers, mental health professionals.  
- Education on disease management, medication adherence, lifestyle modifications.  
- Coordination for comorbidities, rehabilitation, and psychosocial support.  
- Encourage support groups and mental health counseling for depression.
