paragraphs.title: Sleep Disorders
paragraphs.name: [253] Sleep Disorders — Definition / Overview
paragraphs.text:
Sleep Disorders — Definition / Overview
- Sleep disorders are conditions that disturb normal sleep patterns, leading to inadequate or non-restorative sleep. They interfere with physical, mental, social, and emotional functioning and impact overall health, safety, and quality of life. The International Classification of Sleep Disorders, Third Edition (ICSD-3), categorizes sleep disorders into:  
  - Insomnia  
  - Sleep-disordered breathing  
  - Central disorders of hypersomnolence  
  - Circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorders  
  - Parasomnias  
  - Sleep-related movement disorders

paragraphs.title: Sleep Disorders
paragraphs.name: [254] Sleep Disorders — Epidemiology
paragraphs.text:
Sleep Disorders — Epidemiology
- **Insomnia**: Affects ~10% of adults, with higher prevalence in women (17.6% vs. 10.1% in men). Chronic in >40% with severe symptoms.  
- **Sleep-disordered breathing (SDB)**: Prevalence increases with age; ~50% of older adults report sleep problems. Men have higher prevalence than premenopausal women (2:1). Wisconsin Sleep Cohort Study showed increases from 26.4% to 33.9% in men and 13.2% to 17.4% in women over time.  
- **Central hypersomnolence**: Narcolepsy prevalence ~44.3/100,000; idiopathic hypersomnia ~10.3/100,000.  
- **Circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorders**:Overall prevalence 0.13–0.17%, higher in adolescents (7–16% for delayed sleep phase syndrome).  
- **Parasomnias**: NREM parasomnias ~3%, nightmares ~43.8%, REM sleep behavior disorder ~8.7/100,000.  
- **Sleep-related movement disorders**: Restless leg syndrome (RLS) affects 9% women vs. 5.4% men. Periodic limb movement disorder ~40/100,000.  
- **Racial/ethnic differences**: Hispanics and Chinese have higher odds of SDB and short sleep; Black individuals have 1.8x higher risk of sleep apnea syndrome vs. White individuals.

paragraphs.title: Sleep Disorders
paragraphs.name: [255] Sleep Disorders — Etiology / Causes
paragraphs.text:
Sleep Disorders — Etiology / Causes
- **Insomnia**: Environmental, genetic, psychological, and behavioral factors leading to hyperarousal.  
- **Sleep-disordered breathing**: Obesity, upper airway mechanics, breathing control issues. Includes obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), central sleep apnea (CSA), obesity hypoventilation syndrome.  
- **Central hypersomnolence**: Narcolepsy type 1/2, idiopathic hypersomnia, Kleine-Levin syndrome, hypersomnia due to medical/psychiatric disorders, medication/substance use, sleep insufficiency.  
- **Circadian rhythm disorders**: Misalignment with environment (shift work, jet lag) or altered internal circadian timing (delayed/advanced sleep phase syndromes).  
- **Parasomnias**: Environmental, genetic, or gene-environment interactions. Subtypes: NREM-related (confusional arousals, sleepwalking) and REM-related (RBD, nightmares).  
- **Sleep-related movement disorders**: Restless leg syndrome (familial/genetic or iron deficiency).

paragraphs.title: Sleep Disorders
paragraphs.name: [256] Sleep Disorders — Pathophysiology
paragraphs.text:
Sleep Disorders — Pathophysiology
- Not specified in source.

paragraphs.title: Sleep Disorders
paragraphs.name: [257] Sleep Disorders — Clinical Presentation
paragraphs.text:
Sleep Disorders — Clinical Presentation
- **Insomnia**: Difficulty falling/staying asleep (≥30 minutes), daytime consequences (fatigue, sleepiness, poor attention, irritability).  
- **Hypersomnia**: Excessive daytime sleepiness, unintentional sleep episodes, cognitive impairment. Narcolepsy may include cataplexy, hallucinations, sleep paralysis.  
- **Unusual behaviors**: RBD (kicking, punching during dreams), sleepwalking, sleep-related eating, night terrors, confusional arousals. Symptoms exacerbated by stress, sleep deprivation, or medications (e.g., z-drugs).

paragraphs.title: Sleep Disorders
paragraphs.name: [258] Sleep Disorders — Evaluation / Diagnosis
paragraphs.text:
Sleep Disorders — Evaluation / Diagnosis
- **Questionnaires**: Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS), Fatigue Severity Scale (FSS), Insomnia Severity Index (ISI).  
- **Sleep diary**: Tracks bedtime, awakenings, naps.  
- **Sleep studies**: Polysomnography (PSG, gold standard for OSA), home sleep apnea testing (HSAT).  
- **Laboratory tests**: Arterial blood gases, thyroid function, iron studies, CSF hypocretin-1 (for narcolepsy).  
- **Actigraphy**: Assesses sleep-wake cycles for circadian disorders.  
- **Multiple sleep latency testing (MSLT)**: Measures daytime sleepiness severity.

paragraphs.title: Sleep Disorders
paragraphs.name: [259] Sleep Disorders — Differential Diagnosis
paragraphs.text:
Sleep Disorders — Differential Diagnosis
- PTSD, depression, anxiety disorder, bipolar disorder, opioid abuse, alcoholism, stimulant abuse, COPD, hyperthyroidism.

paragraphs.title: Sleep Disorders
paragraphs.name: [260] Sleep Disorders — Management / Treatment
paragraphs.text:
Sleep Disorders — Management / Treatment
- **Insomnia**:  
  - **Non-pharmacological**: CBT-I (gold standard), sleep restriction, stimulus control, relaxation techniques, sleep hygiene education.  
  - **Pharmacological**: Histamine H1 blockers (avoid in elderly), benzodiazepines, z-drugs (caution: black box warning for complex behaviors), melatonin agonists (ramelteon), orexin antagonists (suvorexant).  
- **OSA**: PAP therapy, lifestyle changes, oral appliances, surgery.  
- **Narcolepsy**: Modafinil (first-line), stimulants (amphetamines), anti-depressants for cataplexy, sodium oxybate.  
- **Circadian disorders**: Light therapy, melatonin.  
- **RLS**: Gabapentin enacarbil.

paragraphs.title: Sleep Disorders
paragraphs.name: [261] Sleep Disorders — Complications
paragraphs.text:
Sleep Disorders — Complications
- Increased risk of accidents, mood/anxiety disorders, cognitive decline, cardiovascular diseases (e.g., hypertension, heart failure), cerebrovascular events (linked to periodic limb movement disorder).

paragraphs.title: Sleep Disorders
paragraphs.name: [262] Sleep Disorders — Prognosis
paragraphs.text:
Sleep Disorders — Prognosis
- Varies by cause. Insomnia related to OSA resolves with treatment; chronic insomnia correlates with depression/anxiety. Persistent hypersomnia despite therapy may indicate poorer outcomes.

paragraphs.title: Sleep Disorders
paragraphs.name: [263] Sleep Disorders — Prevention / Patient Education
paragraphs.text:
Sleep Disorders — Prevention / Patient Education
- Sleep hygiene: Regular sleep schedule, avoid screens/caffeine, optimal sleep environment.  
- Caution with sedative-hypnotics (avoid driving/operating machinery).

paragraphs.title: Sleep Disorders
paragraphs.name: [264] Sleep Disorders — Interprofessional Considerations
paragraphs.text:
Sleep Disorders — Interprofessional Considerations
- Team includes clinicians, specialists (pulmonology, neurology), pharmacists, nurses, psychologists, dieticians, surgical consults.  
- Coordination for sleep studies, medication management, behavioral therapy, and patient education is essential for optimal outcomes.

paragraphs.title: Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs)
paragraphs.name: [265] Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs) — Definition / Overview
paragraphs.text:
Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs) — Definition / Overview
- STIs involve transmission of organisms between sexual partners via oral, anal, or vaginal contact.  
- Include curable (gonorrhea, chlamydia, syphilis, trichomoniasis) and treatable but incurable conditions (herpes, HPV, HIV).  
- Symptoms broadly categorized as discharge/dysuria or ulcerative lesions.

paragraphs.title: Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs)
paragraphs.name: [266] Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs) — Epidemiology
paragraphs.text:
Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs) — Epidemiology
- **HPV**: Most common STI globally; ~80% of sexually active individuals infected at some point.  
- **US Data (2020)**:  
  - Chlamydia: 1.6 million cases.  
  - Gonorrhea: 677,769 cases (45% increase from 2016).  
  - Primary/Secondary Syphilis: 133,945 cases (52% increase).  
  - Congenital Syphilis: 2,148 cases (235% increase).  
- **Global Data**:  
  - 376 million new curable STIs annually (trichomoniasis, chlamydia, gonorrhea, syphilis).  
  - Over 500 million people globally infected with HSV-2.

paragraphs.title: Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs)
paragraphs.name: [267] Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs) — Etiology / Causes
paragraphs.text:
Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs) — Etiology / Causes
- **Chancroid**: *Haemophilus ducreyi*.  
- **Chlamydia**: *Chlamydia trachomatis* (serotypes D-K).  
- **Genital Herpes**: Herpes simplex virus 1 (HSV-1) or 2 (HSV-2).  
- **Gonorrhea**: *Neisseria gonorrhoeae*.  
- **Granuloma Inguinale**: *Klebsiella granulomatis*.  
- **HIV/AIDS**: Enveloped retrovirus.  
- **HPV**: Double-stranded DNA virus.  
- **Lymphogranuloma Venereum**: *Chlamydia trachomatis* (serovars L1, L2, L3).  
- **Mycoplasma genitalium**: *Mycoplasma genitalium*.  
- **Syphilis**: *Treponema pallidum*.  
- **Trichomoniasis**: *Trichomonas vaginalis*.  
- **Risk Factors**: Unprotected sex, multiple partners, history of STIs, sexual assault, substance use.

paragraphs.title: Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs)
paragraphs.name: [268] Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs) — Pathophysiology
paragraphs.text:
Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs) — Pathophysiology
- STIs invade via mucosal abrasions; transmitted through sexual contact, IV drug use, or childbirth.  
- Bacterial, viral, or parasitic organisms trigger immune responses, causing tissue damage and systemic symptoms.  
- Untreated infections lead to complications (e.g., infertility, cancers, disseminated disease).

paragraphs.title: Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs)
paragraphs.name: [269] Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs) — Clinical Presentation
paragraphs.text:
Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs) — Clinical Presentation
- **Chancroid**: Painful genital ulcers, tender lymphadenopathy.  
- **Chlamydia**:  
  - Women: Discharge, bleeding, pelvic pain (often asymptomatic).  
  - Men: Dysuria, testicular pain.  
- **Genital Herpes**: Vesicular lesions, prodromal tingling/itching.  
- **Gonorrhea**: Similar to chlamydia; may include systemic symptoms (e.g., joint pain).  
- **HPV**: Asymptomatic or anogenital warts (condylomata acuminata).  
- **Syphilis**: Primary (painless chancre), secondary (rash, condylomata lata), latent, tertiary (neuro/cardiovascular complications).  
- **Trichomoniasis**: Foul-smelling discharge, "strawberry cervix."

paragraphs.title: Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs)
paragraphs.name: [270] Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs) — Evaluation / Diagnosis
paragraphs.text:
Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs) — Evaluation / Diagnosis
- **Chancroid**: Clinical diagnosis; Gram stain shows "school of fish" pattern.  
- **Chlamydia/Gonorrhea**: NAAT (vaginal swab, urine, urethral sample).  
- **Herpes**: NAAT, viral culture.  
- **Syphilis**: Nontreponemal (VDRL, RPR) + treponemal assays.  
- **HIV**: Antibody tests, PCR.  
- **PID**: Clinical criteria (cervical motion tenderness, discharge, elevated CRP/ESR).  
- **Pregnancy Screening (CDC)**:  
  - First visit: HIV, hepatitis B/C, syphilis.  
  - High-risk: Chlamydia, gonorrhea.  
  - Third trimester: Rescreen high-risk or untested women.

paragraphs.title: Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs)
paragraphs.name: [271] Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs) — Differential Diagnosis
paragraphs.text:
Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs) — Differential Diagnosis
- Broad approach by organ system:  
  - **Cardiovascular/CNS**: HIV, syphilis, herpes.  
  - **GI/Respiratory**: HIV, HSV, chlamydia, gonorrhea, HPV.  
  - **Genitourinary/Integumentary**: All STIs.

paragraphs.title: Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs)
paragraphs.name: [272] Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs) — Management / Treatment
paragraphs.text:
Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs) — Management / Treatment
- **Chancroid**: Azithromycin 1g or ceftriaxone 250mg IM.  
- **Chlamydia**: Doxycycline 100mg twice daily for 7 days or azithromycin 1g.  
- **Gonorrhea**: Ceftriaxone 500mg IM + doxycycline.  
- **Syphilis**: Benzathine penicillin G (dosage varies by stage).  
- **Trichomoniasis**: Metronidazole 500mg twice daily for 7 days (women); 2g single dose (men).  
- **Herpes**: Acyclovir, valacyclovir, or famciclovir for primary/suppressive therapy.  
- **HIV**: Antiretroviral therapy (HAART).  
- **PID**: Ceftriaxone + doxycycline + metronidazole.

paragraphs.title: Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs)
paragraphs.name: [273] Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs) — Complications
paragraphs.text:
Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs) — Complications
- **Untreated STIs**: Infertility, systemic infections, scarring, cancers (HPV), congenital anomalies (syphilis, HIV).  
- **Pregnancy Risks**: Preterm labor, stillbirth, neonatal infections.

paragraphs.title: Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs)
paragraphs.name: [274] Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs) — Prognosis
paragraphs.text:
Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs) — Prognosis
- Depends on early detection, treatment adherence, and access to healthcare.  
- Untreated cases may progress to severe morbidity/mortality.

paragraphs.title: Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs)
paragraphs.name: [275] Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs) — Prevention / Patient Education
paragraphs.text:
Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs) — Prevention / Patient Education
- **Vaccines**: HPV (2-dose series for ages 11-12, up to age 26).  
- **PrEP**: Emtricitabine/tenofovir for high-risk HIV individuals.  
- **Doxycycline PEP**: Post-exposure prophylaxis for chlamydia/gonorrhea/syphilis.  
- **Counseling**: Safe sex practices, regular screening, and behavior modification.

paragraphs.title: Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs)
paragraphs.name: [276] Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs) — Interprofessional Considerations
paragraphs.text:
Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs) — Interprofessional Considerations
- Collaboration among physicians, nurses, pharmacists, counselors, and public health specialists.  
- Coordination for patient education, treatment adherence, and resource allocation.  
- Centralized data collection to monitor STI trends and guide interventions.

paragraphs.title: Type 1 Diabetes
paragraphs.name: [277] Type 1 Diabetes — Definition / Overview
paragraphs.text:
Type 1 Diabetes — Definition / Overview
- Type 1 diabetes (T1D) is an immune-mediated disease characterized by destruction of insulin-producing pancreatic β-cells, resulting in absolute insulin deficiency. Distinct from type 2 diabetes, it requires lifelong exogenous insulin replacement to prevent hyperglycemia and diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). Management includes insulin therapy, glucose monitoring, education, and lifestyle modifications.

paragraphs.title: Type 1 Diabetes
paragraphs.name: [278] Type 1 Diabetes — Epidemiology
paragraphs.text:
Type 1 Diabetes — Epidemiology
- T1D is one of the most frequent chronic diseases in children but can occur at any age.  
- Represents 5–10% of all diabetes cases.  
- Global incidence varies: highest in Finland and Northern Europe (~400 times higher than in China/Venezuela).  
- Incidence of DKA at diagnosis ranges from 15–70% in children.  
- Slight male predominance noted.

paragraphs.title: Type 1 Diabetes
paragraphs.name: [279] Type 1 Diabetes — Etiology / Causes
paragraphs.text:
Type 1 Diabetes — Etiology / Causes
- **Autoimmune destruction** of pancreatic β-cells in genetically susceptible individuals.  
- **Genetic factors**:  
  - Strong association with HLA class II alleles (DRB1, -DQA1, -DQB1), accounting for ~40% of familial aggregation.  
  - HLA-DR4-DQ8 and DR3-DQ2 present in ~90% of children with T1D.  
- **Environmental triggers**:  
  - Viral infections (Coxsackie virus, enteroviruses, cytomegalovirus, rubella, influenza B, mumps, SARS-CoV-2).  
  - Dietary factors (cow’s milk, cereal exposure), childhood vaccinations, pregnancy/perinatal conditions.

paragraphs.title: Type 1 Diabetes
paragraphs.name: [280] Type 1 Diabetes — Pathophysiology
paragraphs.text:
Type 1 Diabetes — Pathophysiology
- **Stage 1 (Preclinical)**: Asymptomatic; normal glucose tolerance, ≥2 pancreatic autoantibodies.  
- **Stage 2 (Dysglycemia)**: Impaired fasting glucose (100–125 mg/dL), impaired glucose tolerance (140–199 mg/dL 2-hour post-OGTT), or HbA1c 5.7–6.4%.  
- **Stage 3 (Clinical onset)**: Symptomatic hyperglycemia with HbA1c ≥6.5%, fasting glucose ≥126 mg/dL, or random glucose ≥200 mg/dL.

paragraphs.title: Type 1 Diabetes
paragraphs.name: [281] Type 1 Diabetes — Clinical Presentation
paragraphs.text:
Type 1 Diabetes — Clinical Presentation
- Classic symptoms: polyuria, polydipsia, unintentional weight loss, fatigue, weakness.  
- DKA: fruity-smelling breath, lethargy, coma (more common in children).  
- Adults may present with gradual progression or initial misdiagnosis as type 2 diabetes.

paragraphs.title: Type 1 Diabetes
paragraphs.name: [282] Type 1 Diabetes — Evaluation / Diagnosis
paragraphs.text:
Type 1 Diabetes — Evaluation / Diagnosis
- **Diagnostic criteria for diabetes**:  
  - Fasting plasma glucose ≥126 mg/dL (confirmed).  
  - Random plasma glucose ≥200 mg/dL with symptoms.  
  - 2-hour post-75g OGTT ≥200 mg/dL.  
  - HbA1c ≥6.5%.  
- **T1D differentiation**:  
  - Autoantibody testing (GAD65, IA-2, ZnT8, ICA, IAA).  
  - C-peptide levels to assess β-cell function.  
- Regular HbA1c monitoring (every 3 months).

paragraphs.title: Type 1 Diabetes
paragraphs.name: [283] Type 1 Diabetes — Differential Diagnosis
paragraphs.text:
Type 1 Diabetes — Differential Diagnosis
- Type 2 diabetes  
- Monogenic diabetes  
- Cystic fibrosis-related diabetes  
- Chronic pancreatitis-related diabetes  
- Posttransplantation diabetes mellitus  
- Steroid-induced diabetes  
- Psychogenic polydipsia

paragraphs.title: Type 1 Diabetes
paragraphs.name: [284] Type 1 Diabetes — Management / Treatment
paragraphs.text:
Type 1 Diabetes — Management / Treatment
- **Insulin replacement**:  
  - **Multiple daily injections (MDI)**: Basal (long-acting: glargine, detemir, degludec) + prandial (rapid-acting: lispro, aspart, glulisine).  
  - **Continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion (CSII)**: Insulin pump with basal + bolus dosing; advanced systems include CGM-integrated automated delivery.  
- **Glucose monitoring**:  
  - Capillary blood glucose meters (≥4 times daily).  
  - Continuous glucose monitors (CGMs) for real-time data and hypoglycemia alerts.  
- **Education**:  
  - Carbohydrate counting, insulin-to-carb ratios.  
  - Hypoglycemia recognition/treatment (glucagon for severe cases).  
  - Sick day rules, ketone testing.  
- **Lifestyle**: Physical activity guidance, consistent carbohydrate intake.

paragraphs.title: Type 1 Diabetes
paragraphs.name: [285] Type 1 Diabetes — Complications
paragraphs.text:
Type 1 Diabetes — Complications
- **Acute**: Hypoglycemia, DKA.  
- **Chronic**: Nephropathy, neuropathy (peripheral/autonomic), retinopathy, cardiovascular disease (coronary artery disease, heart failure), peripheral arterial disease, stroke, foot infections/ulcers.

paragraphs.title: Type 1 Diabetes
paragraphs.name: [286] Type 1 Diabetes — Prognosis
paragraphs.text:
Type 1 Diabetes — Prognosis
- Improved morbidity/mortality with modern insulin therapy and metabolic control.  
- 2–5 times higher mortality risk compared to the general population.  
- Timely complication screening and glycemic control reduce severe outcomes.

paragraphs.title: Type 1 Diabetes
paragraphs.name: [287] Type 1 Diabetes — Prevention / Patient Education
paragraphs.text:
Type 1 Diabetes — Prevention / Patient Education
- Importance of blood glucose control, complication screening, and lifestyle modifications.  
- Education on hypoglycemia symptoms and treatment.  
- Encourage support groups and adherence to follow-up.

paragraphs.title: Type 1 Diabetes
paragraphs.name: [288] Type 1 Diabetes — Interprofessional Considerations
paragraphs.text:
Type 1 Diabetes — Interprofessional Considerations
- **Team approach**: Endocrinologists, diabetes educators, nurses, dietitians, pharmacists, mental health professionals, podiatrists, ophthalmologists, social workers.  
- **Roles**:  
  - Nurses: Care coordination, patient education, monitoring.  
  - Pharmacists: Insulin dosing, medication reconciliation.  
  - Dietitians: Carbohydrate management, nutrition planning.  
  - Mental health professionals: Address diabetes distress, eating disorders.  
- Emphasis on individualized treatment plans and collaborative communication.

paragraphs.title: Type 2 Diabetes
paragraphs.name: [289] Type 2 Diabetes — Definition / Overview
paragraphs.text:
Type 2 Diabetes — Definition / Overview
- Chronic metabolic disorder characterized by persistent hyperglycemia due to impaired insulin secretion, resistance to insulin, or both.  
- Chronic hyperglycemia, combined with metabolic aberrations, causes organ damage, leading to microvascular (retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy) and macrovascular complications, increasing cardiovascular disease risk 2- to 4-fold.

paragraphs.title: Type 2 Diabetes
paragraphs.name: [290] Type 2 Diabetes — Epidemiology
paragraphs.text:
Type 2 Diabetes — Epidemiology
- Global prevalence of diabetes mellitus (DM) was 425 million in 2017.  
- In 2015, ~10% of the US population had DM (7 million undiagnosed).  
- Prevalence increases with age: ~25% of adults >65 years have DM.  
- Rising due to obesity, physical inactivity, and energy-dense diets.

paragraphs.title: Type 2 Diabetes
paragraphs.name: [291] Type 2 Diabetes — Etiology / Causes
paragraphs.text:
Type 2 Diabetes — Etiology / Causes
- **Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (T1DM):** Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells (5–10% of DM cases), often triggered by genetic susceptibility + environmental factors (viral infections, toxins).  
- **Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM):** Insulin resistance + beta-cell dysfunction (90% of DM cases), associated with obesity, physical inactivity, and age >45.  
- **Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM):** Hyperglycemia first detected in pregnancy (7% of pregnancies; increases future T2DM risk).  
- **Monogenic Diabetes:** Single-gene mutations (e.g., MODY, neonatal diabetes; 1–5% of DM cases).  
- **Secondary Diabetes:** Caused by pancreatitis, hormonal disorders (e.g., Cushing’s), or drugs (e.g., corticosteroids).

paragraphs.title: Type 2 Diabetes
paragraphs.name: [292] Type 2 Diabetes — Pathophysiology
paragraphs.text:
Type 2 Diabetes — Pathophysiology
- **T1DM:** Autoimmune-mediated beta-cell destruction; associated with HLA genes (DR3-DQ2, DR4-DQ8). LADA (latent autoimmune diabetes in adults) is a slower-onset variant.  
- **T2DM:** Insulin resistance + progressive beta-cell dysfunction. Adipose tissue promotes insulin resistance via inflammatory mechanisms (e.g., FFA release, adipokine dysregulation). Involves incretin defects (e.g., GLP-1), hyperglucagonemia, and gut microbiota abnormalities.

paragraphs.title: Type 2 Diabetes
paragraphs.name: [293] Type 2 Diabetes — Clinical Presentation
paragraphs.text:
Type 2 Diabetes — Clinical Presentation
- **Common Symptoms:** Polyuria, polydipsia, fatigue, recurrent infections, delayed wound healing, neuropathy (numbness/tingling), blurred vision.  
- **T1DM:** May present with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) as initial manifestation (30% of cases).

paragraphs.title: Type 2 Diabetes
paragraphs.name: [294] Type 2 Diabetes — Evaluation / Diagnosis
paragraphs.text:
Type 2 Diabetes — Evaluation / Diagnosis
- **Screening:**  
  - Annual screening for ages >40; more frequent with risk factors (obesity, family history, hypertension, etc.).  
- **Diagnostic Criteria:**  
  - Fasting Plasma Glucose (FPG) ≥126 mg/dL.  
  - 2-hour plasma glucose ≥200 mg/dL during 75-g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT).  
  - HbA1c ≥6.5% (standardized to NGSP/DCCT assay; limited by conditions like anemia).  
  - **GDM:** 1-step (75-g OGTT with thresholds: fasting ≥92 mg/dL, 1-hour ≥180 mg/dL, 2-hour ≥153 mg/dL) or 2-step approach (50-g glucose challenge test followed by 100-g OGTT if positive).

paragraphs.title: Type 2 Diabetes
paragraphs.name: [295] Type 2 Diabetes — Differential Diagnosis
paragraphs.text:
Type 2 Diabetes — Differential Diagnosis
- Drug-induced hyperglycemia (e.g., corticosteroids, neuroleptics).  
- Genetic beta-cell/insulin action defects.  
- Metabolic syndrome.  
- Infections.  
- Endocrinopathies (e.g., acromegaly, Cushing’s, pheochromocytoma).  
- Iron overload (hemochromatosis).  
- Exocrine pancreatic disorders (e.g., pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis).

paragraphs.title: Type 2 Diabetes
paragraphs.name: [296] Type 2 Diabetes — Management / Treatment
paragraphs.text:
Type 2 Diabetes — Management / Treatment
- **Lifestyle:** Diet (low saturated fat, refined carbs; high fiber, monounsaturated fats) + aerobic exercise (90–150 min/week). Weight loss for obese patients.  
- **T2DM Pharmacotherapy:**  
  - First-line: Metformin.  
  - Second-line: Sulfonylureas, DPP-4 inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists (e.g., liraglutide), SGLT2 inhibitors (e.g., empagliflozin), pioglitazone (if fatty liver), alpha-glucosidase inhibitors.  
  - Prefer agents without hypoglycemia risk (e.g., DPP-4i, SGLT2i, GLP-1 RA).  
- **T1DM:** Basal-bolus insulin or insulin pump therapy.  
- **Goals:**  
  - HbA1c <7%.  
  - BP <130/85 mmHg (ACE/ARB preferred).  
  - LDL-C <100 mg/dL (<70 mg/dL if atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease).  
  - Statins first-line; add ezetimibe/PCSK9 inhibitors if needed.  
- Regular monitoring: Fundoscopy, urine albumin, lipid panel.

paragraphs.title: Type 2 Diabetes
paragraphs.name: [297] Type 2 Diabetes — Complications
paragraphs.text:
Type 2 Diabetes — Complications
- **Acute:** Hypoglycemia, DKA, hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state, coma.  
- **Chronic Microvascular:** Retinopathy (4.4% vision-threatening in US), nephropathy (1% end-stage renal disease), neuropathy.  
- **Chronic Macrovascular:** Coronary artery disease, peripheral artery disease, cerebrovascular disease. Annual cardiovascular event rate: 1.4–4.7% in middle-aged individuals.

paragraphs.title: Type 2 Diabetes
paragraphs.name: [298] Type 2 Diabetes — Prognosis
paragraphs.text:
Type 2 Diabetes — Prognosis
- Increased atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) risk. Excess mortality ~15% higher in T2DM.  
- Improved outcomes with glycemic control, BP management, statins, and ACE/ARB therapy.

paragraphs.title: Type 2 Diabetes
paragraphs.name: [299] Type 2 Diabetes — Prevention / Patient Education
paragraphs.text:
Type 2 Diabetes — Prevention / Patient Education
- Self-monitoring of blood glucose and symptoms of hypoglycemia (tachycardia, sweating, confusion; treat with 15–20g carbs).  
- Regular eye/foot exams, foot care.  
- Smoking cessation, limit alcohol.  
- Lifestyle modifications (diet, exercise, weight management).

paragraphs.title: Type 2 Diabetes
paragraphs.name: [300] Type 2 Diabetes — Interprofessional Considerations
paragraphs.text:
Type 2 Diabetes — Interprofessional Considerations
- Team includes primary care, endocrinologist, ophthalmologist, nephrologist, cardiologist, vascular surgeon, and diabetes nurse.  
- Referrals for complications; education on lifestyle changes, medication adherence, and preventive care.

paragraphs.title: Venous Thromboembolism (VTE)
paragraphs.name: [301] Venous Thromboembolism (VTE) — Definition / Overview
paragraphs.text:
Venous Thromboembolism (VTE) — Definition / Overview
- Venous thromboembolic (VTE) disease encompasses deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism (PE), representing the third leading cardiovascular diagnosis globally. It is associated with significant morbidity, mortality, and healthcare costs.

paragraphs.title: Venous Thromboembolism (VTE)
paragraphs.name: [302] Venous Thromboembolism (VTE) — Epidemiology
paragraphs.text:
Venous Thromboembolism (VTE) — Epidemiology
- Annual incidence: 300,000–600,000 cases in the U.S., with 100,000–300,000 VTE-related deaths yearly. In Europe, >500,000 annual deaths.
- 60% of VTE cases are hospital-acquired, making it the leading preventable cause of death in hospitalized patients.

paragraphs.title: Venous Thromboembolism (VTE)
paragraphs.name: [303] Venous Thromboembolism (VTE) — Etiology / Causes
paragraphs.text:
Venous Thromboembolism (VTE) — Etiology / Causes
- **Patient factors**: Age >40 years, obesity, varicose veins, immobility, oral contraceptives, smoking.
- **Disease states**: Malignancy, spinal cord injury, nephrotic syndrome, congestive heart failure, inflammatory bowel disease, recent myocardial infarction.
- **Procedures**: Pelvic/hip fractures, orthopedic surgeries (hip/knee).
- **Hematologic disorders**: Factor V Leiden mutation, protein C/S deficiency, antithrombin III deficiency, lupus anticoagulant, dysfibrinogenemia, prothrombin mutation, polycythemia vera, paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria.
- **Other**: Pregnancy, validated risk models (Caprini, Padua, Briggs/Brigham and Women’s, IMPROVE, Premier).

paragraphs.title: Venous Thromboembolism (VTE)
paragraphs.name: [304] Venous Thromboembolism (VTE) — Pathophysiology
paragraphs.text:
Venous Thromboembolism (VTE) — Pathophysiology
- Thrombus formation in deep veins (legs, pelvis, arms) may propagate proximally. Embolization to pulmonary vasculature causes gas exchange impairment, alveolar edema, or necrosis.
- Chronic recurrent PE may lead to pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale.
- Paradoxical embolism possible with right-to-left shunts (e.g., patent foramen ovale).

paragraphs.title: Venous Thromboembolism (VTE)
paragraphs.name: [305] Venous Thromboembolism (VTE) — Clinical Presentation
paragraphs.text:
Venous Thromboembolism (VTE) — Clinical Presentation
- **DVT**: Unilateral limb pain, swelling, warmth, tenderness (physical signs have low diagnostic yield).
- **PE**: Sudden dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, cough, hemoptysis. Massive PE: syncope, hypotension, shock.
- **Physical exam**: Tachypnea (>18/min), tachycardia (>100/min), fever, rales, S3/S4 gallop, pleural friction rub.
- **Chronic VTE**: Pulmonary hypertension signs (right ventricular hypertrophy, tricuspid regurgitation, hepatomegaly, edema).

paragraphs.title: Venous Thromboembolism (VTE)
paragraphs.name: [306] Venous Thromboembolism (VTE) — Evaluation / Diagnosis
paragraphs.text:
Venous Thromboembolism (VTE) — Evaluation / Diagnosis
- **Pretest probability**: Modified Wells criteria (score ≥4 indicates high probability).
- **Low probability**: D-dimer assay (high negative predictive value; age-adjusted cutoff for older adults).
- **High/moderate probability**: CTPA or VQ scan for PE; proximal/whole-leg ultrasound for DVT.
- **PERC rule**: Avoids D-dimer in low-risk PE if all criteria met (age <50, pulse <100, SpO₂ >94%, no leg swelling, hemoptysis, trauma/surgery, prior VTE, estrogen use).
- **Additional tests**: Echocardiography for right-heart strain in massive PE; ABG, troponin, BNP, ECG, chest X-ray have limited diagnostic utility.

paragraphs.title: Venous Thromboembolism (VTE)
paragraphs.name: [307] Venous Thromboembolism (VTE) — Differential Diagnosis
paragraphs.text:
Venous Thromboembolism (VTE) — Differential Diagnosis
- **DVT**: Cellulitis, arterial insufficiency, lymphedema, hematoma.
- **PE**: Congestive heart failure, acute respiratory distress syndrome, pneumonia, myocardial infarction.

paragraphs.title: Venous Thromboembolism (VTE)
paragraphs.name: [308] Venous Thromboembolism (VTE) — Management / Treatment
paragraphs.text:
Venous Thromboembolism (VTE) — Management / Treatment
- **Anticoagulation**: First-line (DOACs: apixaban, rivaroxaban preferred; warfarin requires bridging with heparin).
  - **Duration**: 3–6 months for initial VTE; 4–6 weeks for isolated distal DVT (low recurrence risk).
  - **Special populations**: 
    - Cancer: LMWH.
    - Pregnancy: LMWH (minimum 6 weeks postpartum, total 3 months).
    - Obesity: Use actual weight for LMWH dosing.
- **Thrombolytics**: For massive PE (hemodynamic instability) or DVT with compartment syndrome.
- **Vena cava filters**: Contraindications to anticoagulation only.
- **Outpatient management**: PESI score ≤65 or simplified criteria (age <80, no comorbidities, stable vitals).

paragraphs.title: Venous Thromboembolism (VTE)
paragraphs.name: [309] Venous Thromboembolism (VTE) — Complications
paragraphs.text:
Venous Thromboembolism (VTE) — Complications
- **Long-term**: Post-thrombotic syndrome, pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale.
- **Bleeding**: Most common complication (especially with advanced age, hepatic/renal dysfunction).
- **Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT)**: Thrombosis with thrombocytopenia 5–10 days post-heparin exposure.
- **Warfarin-induced skin necrosis**: Rare (<0.1%), linked to protein C deficiency.

paragraphs.title: Venous Thromboembolism (VTE)
paragraphs.name: [310] Venous Thromboembolism (VTE) — Prognosis
paragraphs.text:
Venous Thromboembolism (VTE) — Prognosis
- **Mortality**: 4.5% in-hospital for acute VTE; 10% with active cancer; 14% for unstable PE at 30 days.
- **Recurrence**: 17.7% at 5 years with cancer; 8.6% without.

paragraphs.title: Venous Thromboembolism (VTE)
paragraphs.name: [311] Venous Thromboembolism (VTE) — Prevention / Patient Education
paragraphs.text:
Venous Thromboembolism (VTE) — Prevention / Patient Education
- **Thromboprophylaxis**: Reduces VTE incidence by 30–65%. Betrixaban approved for extended prophylaxis in acutely ill medical patients.
- **Orthopedic surgery**: AAOS/ACCP guidelines recommend 10–14 days (or up to 35 days if low bleeding risk) of chemoprophylaxis (LMWH, fondaparinux, DOACs, warfarin, aspirin) ± mechanical methods.
- **Hospital protocols**: Interprofessional collaboration for VTE prevention and treatment protocols.

paragraphs.title: Venous Thromboembolism (VTE)
paragraphs.name: [312] Venous Thromboembolism (VTE) — Interprofessional Considerations
paragraphs.text:
Venous Thromboembolism (VTE) — Interprofessional Considerations
- **Team approach**: Clinicians, nurses, pharmacists, administrators required for protocol development, patient education, and adherence monitoring. Pharmacists ensure dosing accuracy and monitor compliance; nurses provide education and complication surveillance.

paragraphs.title: Tinea Corporis
paragraphs.name: [313] Tinea Corporis — Definition / Overview
paragraphs.text:
Tinea Corporis — Definition / Overview
- Tinea corporis (ringworm) is a superficial dermatophyte skin infection caused by fungi of the genera *Trichophyton*, *Epidermophyton*, and *Microsporum*.  
- Presents as annular, scaly plaques with central clearing and an active, erythematous, raised border. Often pruritic, with potential for confluence in immunocompromised individuals.

paragraphs.title: Tinea Corporis
paragraphs.name: [314] Tinea Corporis — Epidemiology
paragraphs.text:
Tinea Corporis — Epidemiology
- Highly prevalent worldwide.  
- Common in children, particularly prepubertal age group.  
- Risk factors: excessive heat, high humidity, fitted clothing, close contact with infected individuals/animals, poor hygiene.  
- Immunocompromised individuals are more susceptible and at higher risk for severe manifestations like Majocchi granuloma.

paragraphs.title: Tinea Corporis
paragraphs.name: [315] Tinea Corporis — Etiology / Causes
paragraphs.text:
Tinea Corporis — Etiology / Causes
- Caused by dermatophytes:  
  - *Trichophyton rubrum* (80–90% of cases)  
  - *Trichophyton mentagrophytes*  
  - *Microsporum audouinii*  
  - *Trichophyton tonsurans* (associated with tinea capitis and tinea corporis gladiatorum in athletes)  
  - *Microsporum canis* (linked to contact with cats/dogs)  
- Transmission via direct skin contact, contaminated objects, or soil.

paragraphs.title: Tinea Corporis
paragraphs.name: [316] Tinea Corporis — Pathophysiology
paragraphs.text:
Tinea Corporis — Pathophysiology
- Dermatophytes infect keratinized tissue.  
- Susceptibility linked to defects in innate/adaptive immunity, including defensin β4 deficiency.  
- Risk factors: diabetes mellitus, immunosuppression, Cushing syndrome, excessive sweating, advanced age.  
- Histopathology: KOH preparation reveals septate, branching hyphae.

paragraphs.title: Tinea Corporis
paragraphs.name: [317] Tinea Corporis — Clinical Presentation
paragraphs.text:
Tinea Corporis — Clinical Presentation
- Pruritic annular lesions with sharp margins, erythematous scaly edges, and central clearing.  
- Lesions expand centrifugally, often on trunk, neck, arms, or legs.  
- Inflammation severity varies; vesicles may occur at active border.

paragraphs.title: Tinea Corporis
paragraphs.name: [318] Tinea Corporis — Evaluation / Diagnosis
paragraphs.text:
Tinea Corporis — Evaluation / Diagnosis
- Clinical diagnosis via history and physical examination.  
- Confirmatory tests:  
  - **KOH microscopy**: Septate, hyaline hyphae (false negatives in 15% of cases).  
  - **Fungal culture**: Sabouraud dextrose agar; growth within 5 days to 4 weeks.  
  - **Dermoscopy**: Identifies species-specific features (e.g., corkscrew hairs in tinea capitis).  
- Antifungal susceptibility testing for refractory cases.

paragraphs.title: Tinea Corporis
paragraphs.name: [319] Tinea Corporis — Differential Diagnosis
paragraphs.text:
Tinea Corporis — Differential Diagnosis
- Nummular eczema, erythema annulare centrifugum, tinea versicolor, cutaneous candidiasis, subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus, pityriasis rosea, contact dermatitis, atopic dermatitis, seborrheic dermatitis, psoriasis.  
- Severe mimics: secondary syphilis, mycosis fungoides, parapsoriasis.

paragraphs.title: Tinea Corporis
paragraphs.name: [320] Tinea Corporis — Management / Treatment
paragraphs.text:
Tinea Corporis — Management / Treatment
- **Topical therapy** (localized infection):  
  - Clotrimazole 1% (twice daily for 2–3 weeks)  
  - Ketoconazole 2% (once daily)  
  - Miconazole 2% (twice daily)  
  - Naftifine 1% (once daily or twice daily)  
  - Terbinafine 1% (once or twice daily)  
- **Systemic therapy** (extensive/refractory cases):  
  - Terbinafine 250 mg/day for 2 weeks  
  - Itraconazole 100–200 mg/day for 1–2 weeks (take with food)  
  - Fluconazole 50–200 mg/day or 150–200 mg weekly for up to 4 weeks  
  - Griseofulvin 500–1000 mg/day for 2–4 weeks  
- **Resistant cases**: Fosravuconazole for terbinafine-resistant *T. rubrum*.  
- Address predisposing factors (e.g., hygiene, moisture control).

paragraphs.title: Tinea Corporis
paragraphs.name: [321] Tinea Corporis — Complications
paragraphs.text:
Tinea Corporis — Complications
- **Majocchi granuloma**: Deep dermal invasion via follicles, presenting as erythematous nodules/papules; treated with oral terbinafine (250 mg/day for 2–4 weeks).  
- Secondary bacterial infections due to delayed treatment/misdiagnosis.

paragraphs.title: Tinea Corporis
paragraphs.name: [322] Tinea Corporis — Prognosis
paragraphs.text:
Tinea Corporis — Prognosis
- Generally excellent with appropriate therapy.  
- Localized cases resolve in 2–4 weeks with topical treatment.  
- Recurrence possible with persistent risk factors (e.g., immunosuppression, untreated tinea pedis).

paragraphs.title: Tinea Corporis
paragraphs.name: [323] Tinea Corporis — Prevention / Patient Education
paragraphs.text:
Tinea Corporis — Prevention / Patient Education
- Wear loose, breathable clothing; maintain skin hygiene (keep clean and dry).  
- Avoid sharing personal items (towels, clothing).  
- Wash bedding/clothing in hot water.  
- Avoid contact with infected individuals/animals.  
- Compliance with antifungal therapy despite delayed symptom resolution.

paragraphs.title: Tinea Corporis
paragraphs.name: [324] Tinea Corporis — Interprofessional Considerations
paragraphs.text:
Tinea Corporis — Interprofessional Considerations
- **Clinicians**: Diagnose and prescribe therapy.  
- **Pharmacists**: Verify antifungal dosing, check drug interactions (especially azoles), and ensure baseline liver function tests for systemic therapy.  
- **Nurses**: Monitor compliance, counsel on medication use, and report adverse effects.  
- Collaboration required for managing immunocompromised patients and antifungal resistance.

paragraphs.title: Chronic Urticaria
paragraphs.name: [325] Chronic Urticaria — Definition / Overview
paragraphs.text:
Chronic Urticaria — Definition / Overview
- Chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU) is defined as the occurrence of wheals and/or angioedema for ≥6 weeks. Synonymous with "chronic urticaria" and "chronic idiopathic urticaria." A mast cell-mediated condition associated with significant quality-of-life impairment.

paragraphs.title: Chronic Urticaria
paragraphs.name: [326] Chronic Urticaria — Epidemiology
paragraphs.text:
Chronic Urticaria — Epidemiology
- Prevalence: 0.23% to 1.8% (U.S. and international).  
- Female predominance (2:1 ratio).  
- Highest prevalence in adults aged 40–60 years; affects both children and adults.

paragraphs.title: Chronic Urticaria
paragraphs.name: [327] Chronic Urticaria — Etiology / Causes
paragraphs.text:
Chronic Urticaria — Etiology / Causes
- **Autoimmune dysfunction**: Autoantibodies targeting IgE or IgE receptors in 40% of cases (positive autologous serum skin test [ASST]).  
- **Associated autoimmune disorders**: Hypothyroidism (9.8%), rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, Sjögren syndrome, celiac disease, type 1 diabetes.  
- **Infections**: *Helicobacter pylori*, streptococci, staphylococci, *Mycoplasma pneumoniae*, hepatitis viruses, *Giardia lamblia* (causality unproven; potential autoimmune or molecular mimicry links).  
- **Foods/additives**: Rarely causative.  
- **Malignancy**: Conflicting evidence; no established association.

paragraphs.title: Chronic Urticaria
paragraphs.name: [328] Chronic Urticaria — Pathophysiology
paragraphs.text:
Chronic Urticaria — Pathophysiology
- Mast cell and basophil activation → histamine release → vasodilation, increased vascular permeability, dermal edema, and inflammatory cell recruitment.  
- **Immunological activation**: Type 2 (IgG), type 3 (immune complexes), and type 4 (T-cell) hypersensitivity may contribute.  
- **Non-immunological activation**: Reduced threshold for activation by physical/environmental triggers.  
- **Histopathology**: Intervascular edema in upper/mid-dermis, mixed perivascular infiltrates, dilated venules. No leukocytoclasis or vasculitis.

paragraphs.title: Chronic Urticaria
paragraphs.name: [329] Chronic Urticaria — Clinical Presentation
paragraphs.text:
Chronic Urticaria — Clinical Presentation
- **Wheals**: Pruritic, pink-to-red papules/plaques (central pallor), fleeting (<24 hours), no residual ecchymosis/pigmentation. May coalesce; pressure-prone areas often involved.  
- **Angioedema**: Occurs in 40%, pain/discomfort > pruritus, resolves in 72 hours, affects lips, peri-orbital, genitals, extremities.  
- **Secondary changes**: Excoriations, erosions, hemorrhagic crust from scratching.

paragraphs.title: Chronic Urticaria
paragraphs.name: [330] Chronic Urticaria — Evaluation / Diagnosis
paragraphs.text:
Chronic Urticaria — Evaluation / Diagnosis
- **History**: Duration, triggers, systemic symptoms, personal/family history of allergies/autoimmune disease, physical factors, medications, foods.  
- **Physical exam**: Document lesion duration via skin marking pen.  
- **Laboratory tests**: CBC, CRP/ESR (rule out systemic disease). Eosinophilia suggests atopy/parasites.  
- **Testing**: Skin prick testing not useful. ASST and basophil histamine release assay (BHRA) for autoantibodies (research context).  
- **Tools**: Urticaria activity score, control test, quality-of-life index.

paragraphs.title: Chronic Urticaria
paragraphs.name: [331] Chronic Urticaria — Differential Diagnosis
paragraphs.text:
Chronic Urticaria — Differential Diagnosis
- Urticarial vasculitis (wheals >24h, pain, ecchymosis).  
- Papular urticaria (insect bite reaction, persistent papules).  
- Mastocytosis (Darier sign positive).  
- Auto-inflammatory syndromes (e.g., CAPS, Schnitzler).  
- C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency (isolated angioedema).  
- Bullous pemphigoid (pre-bullous pruritus/urticaria).  
- Anaphylaxis (acute, life-threatening).

paragraphs.title: Chronic Urticaria
paragraphs.name: [332] Chronic Urticaria — Management / Treatment
paragraphs.text:
Chronic Urticaria — Management / Treatment
- **First-line**: Second-generation H1-antihistamines (e.g., cetirizine, loratadine) daily; dose ↑ to 4× standard if needed.  
- **Second-line**: Omalizumab (300 mg SC q4 weeks) for H1-refractory cases.  
- **Third-line**: Ciclosporin (off-label; minimize dose/duration due to nephrotoxicity/hypertension risks).  
- **Acute flares**: Short-course systemic corticosteroids.  
- **Not recommended**: Topical corticosteroids.  
- **Alternatives**: Limited evidence for leukotriene antagonists, dapsone, methotrexate, etc.

paragraphs.title: Chronic Urticaria
paragraphs.name: [333] Chronic Urticaria — Complications
paragraphs.text:
Chronic Urticaria — Complications
- Severe pruritus disrupts sleep and quality of life.

paragraphs.title: Chronic Urticaria
paragraphs.name: [334] Chronic Urticaria — Prognosis
paragraphs.text:
Chronic Urticaria — Prognosis
- Self-limited; mean duration 3–5 years.  
- 80% remission within 12 months.  
- 14% persist >5 years; predictors: thyroid autoimmunity, concurrent angioedema.

paragraphs.title: Chronic Urticaria
paragraphs.name: [335] Chronic Urticaria — Prevention / Patient Education
paragraphs.text:
Chronic Urticaria — Prevention / Patient Education
- Avoid NSAIDs/aspirin, triggers (tight clothing, heat).  
- Use H1-antihistamines regularly (not PRN).  
- Educate on symptom management and flares.

paragraphs.title: Chronic Urticaria
paragraphs.name: [336] Chronic Urticaria — Interprofessional Considerations
paragraphs.text:
Chronic Urticaria — Interprofessional Considerations
- Refer to dermatologist/clinical immunologist for H1-refractory cases.  
- Monitor treatment efficacy every 3–6 months.  
- Address psychological burden with counseling/psychotherapy as needed.

paragraphs.title: Vaginal Candidiasis
paragraphs.name: [337] Vaginal Candidiasis — Definition / Overview
paragraphs.text:
Vaginal Candidiasis — Definition / Overview
- Vulvovaginitis caused by *Candida* species, most commonly *Candida albicans*, characterized by inflammation of the vulva and vagina.

paragraphs.title: Vaginal Candidiasis
paragraphs.name: [338] Vaginal Candidiasis — Epidemiology
paragraphs.text:
Vaginal Candidiasis — Epidemiology
- Accounts for approximately one-third of vulvovaginitis cases in reproductive-aged women.  
- Lifetime prevalence: ~70% of women report at least one episode.  
- Recurrent cases (≥4 episodes/year): ~8% of women.  
- *C. albicans* causes 90% of cases; *C. glabrata* accounts for most remaining cases.  
- Underreported due to over-the-counter treatment availability; epidemiological data limited by inconsistent diagnosis methods.

paragraphs.title: Vaginal Candidiasis
paragraphs.name: [339] Vaginal Candidiasis — Etiology / Causes
paragraphs.text:
Vaginal Candidiasis — Etiology / Causes
- *Candida* species (primarily *C. albicans* and *C. glabrata*).  
- Risk factors:  
  - Estrogen use (e.g., oral contraceptives, hormone therapy).  
  - Elevated endogenous estrogens (e.g., pregnancy, obesity).  
  - Diabetes mellitus.  
  - Immunosuppression (e.g., chemotherapy, HIV, transplant).  
  - Broad-spectrum antibiotic use.  
- Not sexually transmitted, though more common in sexually active women.  
- Recurrent cases may involve genetic susceptibility to fungal infections.

paragraphs.title: Vaginal Candidiasis
paragraphs.name: [340] Vaginal Candidiasis — Pathophysiology
paragraphs.text:
Vaginal Candidiasis — Pathophysiology
- *Candida* species penetrate the vaginal mucosa, triggering an inflammatory response.  
- Inflammatory cells: Polymorphonuclear cells and macrophages.  
- Results in symptoms such as irritation, discharge, and edema due to mucosal inflammation.

paragraphs.title: Vaginal Candidiasis
paragraphs.name: [341] Vaginal Candidiasis — Clinical Presentation
paragraphs.text:
Vaginal Candidiasis — Clinical Presentation
- Vulvar/vaginal erythema, excoriations, thick white adherent discharge, and swelling.  
- Symptoms: Itching, burning, dysuria, dyspareunia.  
- Often worsens premenstrually.  
- *C. glabrata* infections typically present with milder symptoms.  
- Cervix is usually normal (no cervical motion tenderness or abnormal discharge).

paragraphs.title: Vaginal Candidiasis
paragraphs.name: [342] Vaginal Candidiasis — Evaluation / Diagnosis
paragraphs.text:
Vaginal Candidiasis — Evaluation / Diagnosis
- **Clinical findings**: Vulvar/vaginal erythema, discharge, and inflammation.  
- **Diagnostic tests**:  
  - Vaginal wet prep: Budding yeast, hyphae, or pseudohyphae.  
  - pH testing: Typically <5.  
  - Potassium hydroxide (KOH) microscopy: Visualize fungal elements.  
  - Fungal culture or PCR (for recurrent/non-responsive cases).  
- Rule out bacterial vaginosis (clue cells, positive Whiff test) and trichomoniasis.  
- Cultures unnecessary for straightforward *C. albicans* cases but indicated for recurrent symptoms.

paragraphs.title: Vaginal Candidiasis
paragraphs.name: [343] Vaginal Candidiasis — Differential Diagnosis
paragraphs.text:
Vaginal Candidiasis — Differential Diagnosis
- Allergic reaction  
- Atopic dermatitis  
- Lichen sclerosis  
- Lichen simplex chronicus  
- Neoplasm  
- Paget disease  
- Physiologic leukorrhea  
- Psoriasis  
- Sexual abuse  
- Vulvodynia

paragraphs.title: Vaginal Candidiasis
paragraphs.name: [344] Vaginal Candidiasis — Management / Treatment
paragraphs.text:
Vaginal Candidiasis — Management / Treatment
- **Acute uncomplicated candidiasis**:  
  - Single-dose fluconazole 150 mg oral or terconazole intravaginally (1–7 days).  
- **Complicated/recurrent candidiasis**:  
  - Extended azole therapy (e.g., intravaginal azole for ≥1 week or fluconazole 150 mg every 3 days × 3 doses).  
  - Suppressive therapy: Weekly fluconazole for 6 months (non-pregnant).  
- **Pregnant patients**: 7-day intravaginal azole (avoid oral fluconazole).  
- **Breastfeeding**: Fluconazole considered safe.  
- **Non-*albicans* species** (e.g., *C. glabrata*): Boric acid 600 mg vaginally for ≥14 days.  
- **Avoid**: Non-prescribed douches, yogurt, garlic, or probiotics (ineffective per evidence).

paragraphs.title: Vaginal Candidiasis
paragraphs.name: [345] Vaginal Candidiasis — Complications
paragraphs.text:
Vaginal Candidiasis — Complications
- Rare but may include severe vulvar erythema, edema, excoriations, fissures.  
- Antifungal adverse effects: Nausea, abdominal pain, headache, rash, alopecia.

paragraphs.title: Vaginal Candidiasis
paragraphs.name: [346] Vaginal Candidiasis — Prognosis
paragraphs.text:
Vaginal Candidiasis — Prognosis
- Recurrence rate: 14–28% in immunocompetent individuals.  
- Recurrence often due to persistent/exogenous *Candida* strains or genetic susceptibility.  
- Triggers: Antibiotics, sexual activity, dietary factors.

paragraphs.title: Vaginal Candidiasis
paragraphs.name: [347] Vaginal Candidiasis — Prevention / Patient Education
paragraphs.text:
Vaginal Candidiasis — Prevention / Patient Education
- Keep vaginal area dry (change wet clothing post-exercise/swimming).  
- Avoid irritants (e.g., scented soaps, douches).  
- Use breathable fabrics.  
- Consider prophylactic antifungals during antibiotic use.  
- Avoid over-the-counter treatments without confirmation to prevent delayed diagnosis.

paragraphs.title: Vaginal Candidiasis
paragraphs.name: [348] Vaginal Candidiasis — Interprofessional Considerations
paragraphs.text:
Vaginal Candidiasis — Interprofessional Considerations
- Managed by gynecologists, primary care clinicians, nurse practitioners.  
- Pharmacists assist with therapy selection and patient counseling.  
- Multidisciplinary approach for complicated cases (e.g., immunosuppressed patients).  
- Emphasize broad differential diagnosis and thorough evaluation for treatment failure.
